articles.title: The Makkah alliance has been called defensive. Now it has to prove it
articles.body:
When Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye signed the Makkah Alliance for Defence in August, most of us read it as a statement of intent. It took barely two months for that to change. On October 5, ministers and commanders met in Riyadh and agreed to activate collective deterrence measures and send forces and capabilities to the Kingdom at speed. The same meeting appointed retired Lt Gen Nauman Mahmood, a Pakistani, as the alliance’s first secretary-general for three years.
Then came Thursday. Two Houthi attacks hit Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, one on the facilities and one on a Saudia aircraft. Three Saudi citizens died, among them a pilot, and people of several nationalities were wounded. Hundreds of flights were cancelled, and European regulators widened their no-fly advisory. By Friday the airport was running normally again. The signal had still been sent: the capital is within reach.
I think this is the moment the alliance has to answer a question it has so far dodged. The pact is modelled on NATO’s Article 5, so an attack on one is treated as an attack on all. Yet all three governments describe it as purely defensive. Both statements can be true only if someone explains where the line sits.
This is not only about Yemen
It helps to remember what kind of war this is. Reuters ties the escalation to the wider US-Iran confrontation. Iranian attacks have choked traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, which makes the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait far more valuable than usual. A month ago the Houthis took ground along that coast. Saudi Arabia has answered with a growing air campaign, Sanaa included, and Yemeni government forces backed by Riyadh have launched a large offensive that their government says is meant to retake everything the Houthis have conquered. The coalition says it hit 324 targets and gave those forces air cover.
So the state this alliance is rushing to protect is also a state on the attack. That does not make Saudi Arabia’s position illegitimate, because it is being struck hard. But it does mean “defensive” cannot be assumed. It has to be shown.
Where the language starts to strain
Prince Khalid bin Salman said the committee would act against the attacks and “all those responsible for them”. I keep coming back to that phrase. It could mean the Houthis. It could mean their sponsors. The statement does not say.
Islamabad has been more careful. Defence Minister Khawaja Asif says Pakistani and Turkish forces are in a supportive role while only Saudi troops fight, and he has described that support as including reconnaissance. His test for the pact to apply is unprovoked aggression or spillover from Yemen into Saudi territory, which is a fair standard. And on October 9 the Foreign Office spokesman said allied forces would not attack from or inside Yemen, dismissing reports of Pakistani strikes as speculation.
I take those statements at face value. Nothing in the public record puts Pakistani or Turkish soldiers in combat in Yemen. But “supportive” covers a lot of ground, and some of the reporting is awkward. Middle East Eye, citing Reuters, says Pakistan flew four plane loads of weapons to Aden for the Saudi-backed government. I could not find any official Pakistani confirmation, so that stays an unverified report for now. If it is accurate, though, it is hard to square with the Foreign Office line. Guarding Saudi cities from missiles is one thing. Arming one side of a ground offensive is another, and people in Pakistan are entitled to know which one their country is doing.
How many troops, exactly?
The numbers in circulation come from reporters, not from the government. In May, Reuters reported that Pakistan had sent 8,000 troops, a fighter squadron and an air-defence system. On October 2 it quoted a Pakistani official saying 30,000 to 40,000 troops were helping guard Saudi land borders and intercept drones and missiles.
The army’s spokesman has now confirmed that Pakistani forces are in the Kingdom in “multiple capabilities and domains” and have been for decades. That is accurate, and it is also a little convenient. A decades-old training and advisory mission is a very different thing from a force of tens of thousands on border defence. Nobody in government has told the public which description fits.
I understand why troop positions are kept quiet. Revealing them can get people killed. But the overall size, purpose and limits of a commitment this large are a matter of public policy, and they should not be treated as an operational secret.
READ: Turkiye completes preparations to submit Mecca defense pact to parliament: Foreign minister
Ankara has not finished its homework
The pact brings together NATO’s second-largest army, the Muslim world’s only nuclear-armed state and the leading Gulf power. On paper that is formidable. In practice, the three are not at the same stage. Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has said Turkiye is still assessing how it can help, and the Turkish parliament has not ratified the agreement. Reports say the government plans to take it to parliament, which would clear the way for a deployment. Until that happens, Ankara’s role rests on executive decisions alone, and a pact that lacks legislative backing at home will be hard to sustain once casualties rise.
Pakistan’s difficult position
Pakistan has the most to balance. Years ago its parliament voted unanimously against sending combat troops into the Yemen conflict, and nobody has formally revoked that stance. Pakistan also has a long border with Iran, which supports the Houthis, and a large Shia community at home. Any sense that the country is slipping from defence into offence would carry costs inside Pakistan as well as abroad.
And Islamabad is not short of other worries. India on the eastern frontier, Afghanistan on the western one, and militancy in Balochistan all take up men and money. The economy is fragile, too. A new $1.2 billion IMF deal comes with a warning that the Middle East conflict is weighing on growth, and the families who depend on Gulf remittances feel every escalation directly.
None of this is an argument for walking away from Riyadh. The bond is old and deep, built on faith, history and shared interest. It is an argument for a commitment that Pakistan can actually carry.
On adding new members
People keep asking whether other Muslim countries will join. The Foreign Office has said expansion is “not on the cards” at the moment. I read that as a pause, not a refusal. A bigger alliance is not automatically a stronger one, since every new member brings its own threat perceptions and its own limits on using force. The pause is reasonable, but only if the three founders can make their own arrangement work first.
Defence is not the same as victory
Say the air defences work perfectly. Yemen’s war would still be there. Missiles can be shot down, but the political, territorial and sectarian quarrels behind this conflict will not be solved by interceptors. The danger is a slow slide: an alliance created to protect civilians gradually becomes responsible for a campaign with no clear end. That slide is most likely if Saudi offensive goals, like taking back the Red Sea coast, start to be treated as the alliance’s own.
What I would ask of the alliance
I would start with three things. First, publish a short statement of what the alliance defends, what triggers collective action and what it will never do. It should cover cross-border operations and arms supplied to forces inside Yemen. Second, brief the legislatures. Pakistan’s parliament should hear in closed session what the troop levels and rules of engagement are, and Turkiye should finish its ratification. Third, say plainly that all this military readiness is meant to bring about talks, and back that with real work through Oman, the UN and regional partners alongside it.
How we will know
The alliance began with the promise that regional powers can look after their own security. Thursday’s attack shows how badly that is needed. But I will not judge it by troop numbers or by how many flags appear at the next meeting. I will watch whether Riyadh’s airports stay open, whether civilians are safer, whether the war stays contained, and whether the governments involved can tell their own citizens, honestly, what they have signed up for.
If they can, this could become a template for regional cooperation. If they cannot, it will be remembered as an alliance that promised more than it defined.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia can fight the Houthis, it may not be able to defeat them
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia can afford a long war. It can buy aircraft, missiles, drones, air-defense systems and intelligence. It can absorb losses that would bankrupt a poorer state. Yet that does not mean it can defeat the Houthis. That distinction has become impossible to ignore. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman reportedly called Donald Trump twice last week and urged Washington to strike the Houthis directly. Trump declined, although Washington agreed to provide intelligence and targeting support. The episode is revealing not because Saudi Arabia lacks military power, but because Riyadh appears to recognize that the Houthi problem is no longer one that firepower alone can solve.
The timing matters. The Houthis have seized Mocha on Yemen’s Red Sea coast and moved toward strategically important islands at the mouth of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. At the same time, attacks attributed to Iran-aligned forces have disrupted Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline, the very infrastructure designed to give Riyadh an alternative route around the Strait of Hormuz. This leaves Saudi Arabia facing a strategic problem that is much harder than defeating an insurgency. It must protect an economic system built around a handful of extraordinarily valuable and geographically exposed nodes. The Houthis do not need to conquer Saudi Arabia. They only need to make Saudi Arabia’s critical infrastructure sufficiently vulnerable, costly and unpredictable.
Saudi Has the Firepower
On paper, the balance is overwhelmingly in Saudi Arabia’s favor. Riyadh spent an estimated $83.2 billion on its military in 2025, making it the world’s eighth-largest military spender. It possesses advanced fighter aircraft, precision weapons, sophisticated air defenses and extensive access to Western intelligence and technology. The Houthis, by comparison, are a much poorer non-state actor operating from one of the Middle East’s most difficult physical environments. Yet the conventional balance has never translated into decisive strategic victory.
Saudi Arabia entered Yemen’s war in 2015 with overwhelming airpower and a clear political objective: prevent the Houthis from consolidating control over Yemen and restore a government friendly to Riyadh. Years of airstrikes imposed enormous damage and slowed Houthi advances, but they did not produce the political outcome Saudi Arabia wanted.
The lesson is that airpower is poorly suited to solving a political problem when the adversary can disperse, regenerate and operate below the threshold of conventional war. The Houthis have spent the past decade adapting precisely to that imbalance. According to ACLED, they conducted nearly 1,000 rocket and missile attacks and more than 350 distinct drone attacks against Saudi and Emirati territory between 2015 and the April 2022 truce. More importantly, the character of those attacks changed. Guided missiles accounted for just 15 percent of Houthi rocket and missile events in 2015, but 89 percent by 2022. Drone attacks also increasingly outnumbered missile attacks.
That evolution points to a fundamental strategic mismatch. Saudi Arabia has generally sought to punish the Houthis by destroying military assets and degrading their operational capacity. The Houthis, meanwhile, have increasingly sought to deny Saudi Arabia the ability to operate securely and predictably. That is the difference between punishment and denial. A military power can destroy a missile launcher. It cannot easily destroy the political and economic incentives behind a dispersed missile force. It can intercept a drone. It cannot guarantee that the next drone will not find another vulnerability. It can strike a command center. It cannot bomb away the geography that gives an adversary access to a strategic maritime chokepoint.
The 2019 attack on Abqaiq and Khurais illustrated the problem dramatically. The assault temporarily knocked out more than half of Saudi oil production and almost 5 percent of global oil supply.
Whether the attack was launched from Iranian or Iraqi territory or claimed by the Houthis, its strategic lesson was unmistakable that a relatively inexpensive asymmetric attack could impose enormous costs on one of the world’s most heavily armed states. That is why Saudi Arabia’s military superiority should not be confused with strategic invulnerability.
The Houthis Are No Longer Fighting Only for Yemen
The most important change in 2026 is that the Houthi threat is no longer primarily territorial. It is increasingly geographic and economic. The seizure of Mocha and the Houthi advance toward Perim Island and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait have altered the strategic map. Bab al-Mandeb is not simply another battlefield. It is one of the world’s principal maritime chokepoints, linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. Reuters reported that Houthi forces reached the strategic island of Perim on September 11, putting them closer to the maritime gateway through which energy and commercial traffic moves between the Middle East, Europe and Asia.
READ: Saudi Arabia says 3 killed in attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid airport
That development matters enormously for Saudi Arabia. For years, Riyadh has invested in reducing its dependence on the Strait of Hormuz. The East-West Pipeline is central to that strategy because it allows Saudi crude to reach the Red Sea port of Yanbu without passing through Hormuz. But the geography of the current conflict is beginning to turn that strategy against Riyadh. Hormuz is under pressure from Iran. Bab al-Mandeb is increasingly exposed to the Houthis. And the East-West Pipeline has itself been disrupted by drone attacks attributed to Iran-aligned forces in Iraq. Reuters reported that the pipeline outage could threaten as much as 4 percent of global oil supply, while Saudi crude production had already fallen sharply from earlier levels.
This is no longer a conventional war in the familiar sense. It is a contest over the reliability of economic geography. That distinction is critical.
Iran and its aligned forces do not need to seize Saudi oil fields. They do not even need to shut down every shipping lane. They only need to increase the risk attached to the routes through which Saudi energy reaches the global market. This is chokepoint warfare. The objective is not necessarily to control every inch of territory. It is to acquire leverage over the narrow points through which enormous volumes of trade must pass.
That is precisely why Houthi capabilities matter beyond Yemen. ACLED has documented how the group previously used drones and missiles against airports and hydrocarbon facilities rather than concentrating solely on battlefield targets. From 2018 to early 2022, 43 percent of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia targeted civilian airports and energy infrastructure. The logic is brutally efficient that attack what the adversary cannot afford to lose. For Saudi Arabia, that means oil infrastructure, ports, pipelines, airports and increasingly maritime routes. The Houthis therefore do not have to win a conventional war. They only have to make the cost of maintaining normality rise faster than Riyadh’s ability or willingness to absorb it.
Can Saudi Afford to Defeat Houthis?
This is where the question of Saudi military capability becomes inseparable from the question of Saudi economic strategy. Riyadh can certainly retaliate. It can intensify airstrikes, deploy more intelligence assets, expand missile defenses and work with regional partners. Saudi Arabia has enough resources to impose substantial costs on the Houthis. The harder question is whether escalation would actually solve the problem. A heavier Saudi campaign could force the Houthis underground. It could destroy launch sites and command infrastructure. But it could also generate the very response Riyadh wants to avoid: more attacks against oil facilities, cities, ports and shipping. That is the escalation paradox.
If Saudi Arabia restrains itself, the Houthis may consolidate their position around Bab al-Mandeb and strengthen their bargaining power. If Saudi Arabia escalates dramatically, the Houthis may retaliate against the infrastructure that makes Saudi Arabia economically powerful but strategically exposed. The request to Trump therefore makes more sense in this context. MBS was not necessarily asking Washington to fight Saudi Arabia’s war for it. He was seeking to alter the cost-benefit equation by adding American military power to the deterrence equation. Trump’s refusal to authorize direct strikes, while allowing intelligence and targeting support, exposes a new strategic reality that Riyadh cannot automatically assume that Washington will absorb the escalation risks associated with every Saudi security problem.
That leaves Saudi Arabia with a difficult choice. It can fight the Houthis alone. But a war of indefinite containment would consume resources and expose critical infrastructure. A campaign designed to achieve decisive victory could be even more dangerous because it would invite retaliation against precisely those assets Saudi Arabia is trying to protect. The central problem, therefore, is not Saudi Arabia’s military weakness. It is Saudi Arabia’s strategic exposure. The Houthis possess less firepower, less money and fewer sophisticated weapons. Yet they can exploit a fundamental asymmetry, the cost of launching an attack can be tiny compared with the cost of defending every potential target.
A cheap drone can force the deployment of expensive interceptors. A single strike on a pipeline can disrupt millions of barrels of potential exports. A credible threat to shipping can raise insurance premiums even without sinking a single tanker. A temporary closure of a chokepoint can create economic consequences far beyond the battlefield. This is why the Houthi challenge should not be measured by the territory the group controls or the number of weapons it possesses. It should be measured by the amount of strategic uncertainty it can impose.
Saudi Arabia therefore faces a paradox that extends far beyond Yemen. It has sufficient military power to fight the Houthis, but military superiority does not guarantee strategic immunity. Riyadh can degrade the group, deter some attacks and impose painful costs. What it cannot easily do is eliminate the geography, economic exposure and asymmetric incentives that make the Houthi strategy possible.
That is the real lesson of the current crisis. Saudi Arabia does not need to become militarily stronger simply to defeat the Houthis. It needs to become strategically harder to coerce. That means diversifying energy routes, hardening critical infrastructure, improving integrated air and missile defense, strengthening maritime security, expanding regional intelligence cooperation and, above all, reducing the number of single points of failure on which its economic model depends. The Houthis have exposed a vulnerability that money and military technology alone cannot solve. Saudi Arabia can win battles against them. But unless Riyadh changes the strategic geometry of the contest, the Houthis may not need to win the war.

articles.title: Why are Houthi missiles breaking through Saudi Arabia’s air defences?
articles.body:
Why are Houthi missiles breaking through Saudi Arabia’s air defences?
Repeated Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid Airport reveal the limitations of even the most high-tech air defences.
Yemen’s Houthis, the armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), are hitting deep inside Saudi Arabia with waves of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones.
Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport has been targeted multiple times by the Houthis since their new military campaign against the kingdom began in September.
An attack on the airport on Saturday killed 12 people and wounded 309, the deadliest attack in the kingdom in more than a decade. Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority was forced to suspend operations and diverted all flights, while the United States and United Kingdom issued new travel warnings for citizens.
The Houthis claimed two other attacks on the air hub earlier this week and on Sunday warned people to avoid Saudi airports.
Houthi weaponry
Saudi Arabia possesses one of the best-equipped militaries in the world, boasting advanced, multilayered air defence systems.
Saudi warplanes have pummelled Houthi positions across Yemen in the past week, seeking to roll back the Iran-backed group’s recent advances against the Yemeni government army, which Riyadh supports.
The Houthis’ own arsenal has come a long way since the group seized control of Sanaa from the government in September 2014.
Their drones and missiles have reached as far as Israel and, as their accuracy has shown, can hit particular targets such as Saudi airports and oil facilities.
Here’s what we know about the Houthis’ weaponry, how their tactics have changed and why Saudi air defences are struggling to keep pace.
How advanced is the Houthi arsenal?
The exact type of weapon used to attack Riyadh airport is unknown, but the Houthis have fired hundreds of drones and missiles at Saudi Arabia since the 2015 intervention. The Iran-backed group has also targeted Israel and allegedly Israeli-linked vessels since the start of the genocide in Gaza in October 2023.
The group has used its weapons in concert, mixing drones and missiles of varying speeds to confound air defences. The same mix has shaped Yemen’s ground war, with the Houthis pounding government positions for weeks before seizing the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive last month.
Among the group’s most advanced options are medium-range ballistic missiles such as the Palestine-2, a two-stage solid fuel missile believed to have a range of 2,000km with hypersonic capabilities. Another is the Toufan, which appears to be a rebranded Iranian Ghadr missile, thought to have a range of between 1,350km and 1,950km.
The reach of those missiles – some carrying cluster warheads – has allowed the Houthis to breach Israel’s air defence network, some 2,000 km from Yemen.
The Houthis also maintain a number of short-range missiles, such as their Burkan and Badr series. They are also believed to be of Iranian origin and have been used in cross-border strikes into Saudi Arabia.
According to Nawaf Obaid, a senior fellow at Kings College War Studies Department, the Houthis’ missile arsenal is essentially derived from Iranian weaponry, with some Chinese technological influences.
“The Houthis have demonstrated little evidence of significant indigenous technological innovation,” he said. “Their domestic capabilities are largely confined to producing certain lower-end missiles and drones.”
Last month, Yemen’s government forces alleged that the Houthis have been receiving help from the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) to develop a new capability – loitering cruise missiles.
Why are Saudi defences struggling to keep up?
Saudi authorities say their forces shot down a number of projectiles over the past week, including a pair of ballistic missiles aimed at the capital on Thursday. But they failed to intercept the projectile that hit Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Saturday.
Nawaf Obaid told Al Jazeera that occasional penetration of Saudi air defences is to be expected, given the size of the kingdom and its border with Yemen.
“As much as you can have a multi-layered air defence system, one will always come through,” he said, pointing out that dozens of Houthi attempts are thwarted for each successful attack.
Wolfgang Pusztai, a security policy and defence analyst, told Al Jazeera that the main focus of Saudi Arabia’s ballistic missile defence system was countering threats from Iran.
However, as the attacks from the Houthis increase, he views it as likely that the Saudis are re-orienting some of these defences towards Yemen.
There is also the issue of interceptor stocks. Saudi Arabia – along with many of the United States’ regional and global allies – has struggled with limited stockpiles of Patriot and THAAD munitions. These were rapidly expended by the US and its allies during the early months of the war with Iran.
Last month, Riyadh had reportedly reached out to a number of friendly countries to deploy air defence or other support to help defend against attacks by the Houthis.
Limitations
However, the Houthis are also fighting under serious constraints. The group is under a UN-mandated arms embargo, a years-long Saudi blockade, as well as fighting on several fronts across Yemen.
“Militarily, the Saudi-led coalition has the upper hand, but the Houthis can still dominate the headlines with occasional strikes against Saudi Arabia,” Obaid said.
“As the world’s largest crude oil exporter and a G20 economy, Saudi Arabia carries global responsibilities that make such attacks disproportionately visible.”
The exact size of the Houthis’ missile arsenal is unknown, calling into question the group’s ability to sustain attacks on Saudi Arabia, while simultaneously fighting a fierce ground war where missiles and drones have been used by the Iran-backed group.
Obaid said that Saudi Arabia’s air campaign in Yemen has focused heavily on targeting the group’s missile depots, underground installations and drone production facilities. The group is “inflicting enormous damage” on the Houthis’ military capabilities, he added.
Pusztai told Al Jazeera that the Houthis likely have just a limited number of short-range ballistic missiles left.
This would mean they would be incapable of launching saturation attacks, where multiple missiles and drones are fired at targets, such as in Saudi Arabia.
Instead, they could focus on aiming single missiles at less-defended civilian targets “to maximise the strategic impact of these attacks, in this case to disrupt civilian air traffic”.

articles.title: Bombs that pushed Iran across the rubicon
articles.body:
Bombs that pushed Iran across the rubicon
Two wars launched by the US and Israel under the false pretext of stopping Iran's nuclear weapon may have made it more likely
TEHRAN – Donald Trump says he went to war to ensure Iran never gets the bomb — dozens of times and counting. Yet the war fought in the name of non-proliferation has acted like a boomerang: far from closing Iran's path to the bomb, it may have pushed Tehran closer to it.
The US and Israel say they attacked Iran twice to prevent it from acquiring a nuclear weapon. Yet at the time of both attacks, both US intelligence and the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) assessed that Tehran was not building one.
 
No evidence has emerged that Iran is currently racing to build a bomb. But a growing number of Western analysts argue the wars themselves have strengthened Tehran's incentive to do so — while inside Iran, calls to revise the nuclear doctrine and reconsider membership in the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) have moved from the margins to the mainstream.
 
The result is the central paradox of the current confrontation: a preventive war that may have produced the very outcome it claimed to prevent.
 
The justification vs. the assessment
Washington's stated rationale has been consistent: Iran must not be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon.
But two key institutions directly contradicted the claim that Iran was actively pursuing one.
US intelligence: Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard testified to Congress in March 2025 that Iran was not building a nuclear weapon and that Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei had not reauthorized the weapons program suspended in 2003. A leaked US intelligence assessment reported by News24 on March 18, 2026, after the US operation known as Midnight Hammer, again found "no effort to rebuild enrichment" and concluded that Tehran had not moved to weaponize.
The IAEA: Director General Rafael Grossi said on June 19, 2025, amid the first war: "We found no indication of an active, systematic plan to build a weapon in Iran." He added that military strikes would only "delay the indispensable diplomatic work" needed for long-term assurance that
Iran does not acquire a weapon.
In other words, both attacks were launched not against an ongoing weaponization program documented by inspectors or spies, but against capabilities and intentions that Washington and Tel Aviv insisted could turn into one.
The second war removed a barrier: the fatwa
For two decades, Iran's principal political-religious barrier to a bomb was explicit: a fatwa by Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei declaring the production, stockpiling and use of nuclear weapons haram (forbidden).
Iranian officials repeatedly cited the fatwa as the reason Iran had the technical capacity but not the intent. Former Foreign Minister and former Atomic Energy chief Ali Akbar Salehi said in February 2024 that Iran possessed "all the pieces" needed for a weapon but had not assembled them — a restraint Tehran attributed to the Leader's ruling.
Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei was martyred in the joint US-Israel airstrike on the morning of February 28, 2026, in his office in central Tehran.
His successor, Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei, has made no clear public statement on the nuclear fatwa. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi acknowledged the uncertainty in an interview with Reuters on March 18, 2026, saying Iran's position against weapons would not undergo "significant change," but adding that fatwas depend on the issuing jurist and that he could not yet judge the new Leader's jurisprudential view. Any change, he said, would depend on the new Leader.
But that key religious prohibition that underpinned this doctrine for 20 years no longer exists — removed by those who coveted Iran's collapse and US domination over Iran.
In Washington and Tel Aviv, a quiet consensus: the bombing is making the bomb more likely
The most striking warning came, paradoxically, from inside Israel's own intelligence establishment. Danny Citrinowicz, who until recently ran the Iran branch of Israeli military intelligence, told The Times of Israel last summer that kinetic action would push Tehran "to cross the Rubicon on the nuclear file." The war, he said, would not prevent an Iranian bomb. It would accelerate it.
Citrinowicz was not alone, and what followed over the next year was something rare in the normally fractious world of arms control: agreement. From different capitals, disciplines and politics, analysts began describing the same mechanism — a state under existential bombardment, watching its declared, inspected sites destroyed, rationally concluding that only an undeclared deterrent could prevent the next round.
At Carnegie, James Acton argued that the premise of "obliteration" was an illusion. Iran, he noted, had almost certainly dispersed fissile material and key equipment before the strikes, and with what it retained it could, if it ever chose weaponization, move "in less than a year, even significantly less than a year." Eric Brewer, a former US intelligence analyst now at the Nuclear Threat Initiative, put it more bluntly to Reuters in May: as far as anyone knows, Iran still has all of its nuclear material, much of it in places American munitions cannot reach.
The institutional voices followed. Daryl Kimball of the Arms Control Association observed that the campaign had exposed the ceiling of force: bombing could neither erase knowledge nor permanently eliminate capability. Ellie Geranmayeh of the European Council on Foreign Relations noted that capability was "largely still in place," and that without inspectors — themselves now sidelined by war — existing stocks could be enriched to weapons grade with alarming speed. Even the press that had initially cheered restraint turned sombre. Time warned that destroyed centrifuges can be rebuilt but a changed strategic calculus cannot be undone; The Guardian editorialised that prevention by bombardment, absent any diplomatic endgame, historically hardens proliferation incentives rather than softening them.
The most systematic verdict arrived in August 2026 from Defense Priorities in Washington. In an explainer titled "A Security Dilemma Made Worse," it concluded that by waging a war that threatened the very survival of the Iranian state, the US and Israel had strengthened Tehran's motive to acquire the one weapon that might deter a third war. Proliferation was not inevitable, it wrote — merely more likely than before the strikes. Trita Parsi at the Quincy Institute and Ali Vaez at the International Crisis Group, neither of them hawks, reached the same destination by a shorter road: Tehran's determination to obtain a deterrent, they wrote, had been "dramatically increased," and rebuilding from under the rubble with an explicit weapons goal was now thinkable in a way it had not been before.
In short, deterrence theory was working — but in reverse. A country that finds conventional deterrence insufficient, and international verification incapable of protecting it, does what threatened states do: it reconsiders.
In Tehran, the unsayable is now said aloud
For years, even raising the question of a bomb in public in Iran was taboo. The fatwa of Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei stood like a wall around the debate: possession itself was forbidden, and that was the end of it. The wall is gone now, and the debate that has rushed into its place would have been unimaginable two years ago.
It began as a whisper. In October 2024, Kamal Kharrazi — the urbane head of the Strategic Council on Foreign Relations — said calmly that if an existential threat emerged, Iran would revise its doctrine. On April 1, 2026, during the US-Israel war against Iran, his house in Tehran was struck by US-Israeli aircraft. His wife was martyred in the attack and he was severely wounded, succumbing to his wounds eight days later. The capability, he noted, existed. Only the Leader's ruling stood in the way. That same month, 39 members of parliament wrote privately to the Supreme National Security Council asking for precisely such a revision.
Then came the first war, and the whispers grew louder. Ali Shamkhani, the veteran security official martyred on the first day of the second war, on February 28 of this year, appeared on state television in October 2025 and said, with the bluntness of a man who felt history had vindicated his doubts, that had he known then what he knows now, he would have supported building the bomb in the 1990s. By September 2025, the private letters had become a public petition: more than seventy MPs wrote to the president and the Council declaring an arsenal "necessary for nuclear deterrence" and openly asking for the fatwa to be reinterpreted — production for deterrence, they argued, was not the same as use.
What is remarkable is not merely the content but the setting. The argument is now made on camera, in parliament, and from the Friday pulpit. When Hojjatoleslam Haj Ali Akbari told worshippers in Tehran on October 9 that the nuclear program "belongs to the Iranian nation" and that there is a domestic demand to revise membership in the NPT, no one in the establishment criticized him. A month earlier, Nezamoddin Mousavi, a former MP close to the Revolutionary Guards, had told Ensaf News what many in the system now say privately: ambiguity did not prevent war.
It was time, he said, to review the doctrine, the worth of the NPT, and the meaning of deterrence after the strikes on Iran's own facilities.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi still holds the official line — no significant change, he told Reuters in March — but even his reassurance contained the seed of doubt. Fatwas, he acknowledged, belong to the jurist who issues them, and the new Leader, Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei, has not yet spoken. In Tehran today, that silence is itself the story.
A 47-year-old dream turned nightmare
Seen from Tehran, the two campaigns were never really about centrifuges. The US and Israel knew better than anyone that Iran was not pursuing a nuclear weapon — their own intelligence services and the IAEA had told them so. What they pursued was a 47-year-old dream: regime change in Iran.
The calculation was that a heavy air campaign, combined with inciting street unrest, would finally realize that old fantasy. But aggression still needs a pretext. And what better pretext than the nuclear file — an issue they had spent more than two decades turning into a lever for global anti-Iran propaganda and for imposing wave after wave of sanctions?
Iran stood firm. The dream did not come true. Instead, it has curdled into a nightmare — one whose ultimate cost for Iran's enemies is still unknown, and still growing. The wars meant to foreclose Iran's nuclear options have instead opened the most serious national debate in its history about whether those options should be reconsidered, and have left Washington and Tel Aviv facing an Iran more convinced than ever that only its own strength can guarantee its survival.

articles.title: Hackers use security cameras to track troops, military targets in Israel, Ukraine - report
articles.body:
Internet-connected security cameras and webcams around the world are increasingly being hacked and turned into military intelligence tools, allowing countries including Israel, Iran, Russia, and Ukraine to monitor troop movements, track targets, and assess attacks, The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday.
The growing threat has emerged across multiple conflicts, including those involving Israel and Iran and Russia and Ukraine, as governments and hackers exploit vulnerabilities in devices originally intended to protect homes, businesses, and public spaces.
According to the report, an estimated 1.2 billion internet-connected cameras operate worldwide, creating an enormous network of potential intelligence-gathering devices. Many are inadequately secured, making them attractive targets for cyber operations.
One incident highlighted in the investigation involved a poultry farmer in northern Israel who discovered that the language settings on a camera overlooking his chicken coop had unexpectedly changed to Arabic during the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran earlier this year.
The farmer contacted the Israel National Cyber Directorate, which determined that hackers had compromised the Chinese-made device. The camera's position provided a view of Israeli security activity near the Lebanese border, giving the intruders potential access to military intelligence rather than simply images of the farm.
The directorate subsequently helped the farmer improve the camera's security and change its viewing angle to prevent the surveillance of military operations, according to the WSJ.
Civilian surveillance becomes military intelligence
The incident illustrates a growing challenge for military and civilian cybersecurity authorities: Cameras installed for routine security purposes can become intelligence assets when hostile actors access them.
In Israel, the threat has already prompted warnings from the National Cyber Directorate about the vulnerability of residential and commercial surveillance equipment.
During the June 2025 Israel-Iran war, the directorate urged homeowners and businesses to secure their cameras, warning that hostile actors could exploit compromised devices to gather intelligence and identify security vulnerabilities.
The agency identified weak passwords, outdated software, and cameras directly exposed to the internet as common security weaknesses.
Israel National Cyber Directorate chief Yossi Karadi subsequently revealed that Iran had infiltrated parking and road cameras during the June conflict to monitor the movements of prominent Israelis.
Speaking at a cybersecurity conference in December 2025, Karadi said Iranian hackers had sought to track Israeli figures for potential attacks.
He also disclosed that Iranian operatives had accessed a street camera overlooking the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot shortly before an Iranian ballistic missile struck the institute during the conflict.
The incident demonstrated how compromised surveillance systems could potentially contribute to both intelligence collection and the assessment of military strikes.
In March 2026, Karadi again warned about Iranian efforts to compromise Israeli surveillance cameras, describing the devices as a valuable intelligence-gathering resource. He said the directorate had blocked 50 camera-hacking attempts that could have enabled broader network intrusions.
Israel also exploited Iranian surveillance networks
The intelligence value of compromised cameras works both ways.
Israel reportedly infiltrated Tehran's traffic camera network to monitor senior Iranian officials and collect information used in planning military operations against the Islamic Republic.
According to a Financial Times investigation published in March, Israeli intelligence agencies used hacked traffic cameras and artificial intelligence to establish patterns of movement among senior Iranian figures ahead of the operation that killed then-supreme leader Ali Khamenei.
The reported operation demonstrated the potential military value of combining widely available surveillance infrastructure with advanced data-processing capabilities.
Rather than relying exclusively on satellites, reconnaissance aircraft, or intelligence operatives, security services can potentially exploit networks that already monitor streets, intersections, and buildings.
Iranian officials have publicly acknowledged concerns about foreign access to the country's surveillance infrastructure.
In November 2025, Gholamreza Jalali, then head of Iran's Passive Defense Organization, alleged that Israel and the US were exploiting Tehran's surveillance systems for intelligence operations.
Jalali claimed that foreign code had been discovered in Iranian systems that redirected camera footage to external servers. The allegations were not independently verified.
Russia, Ukraine exploit the same vulnerabilities
The WSJ investigation also described how Russia and Ukraine have used compromised surveillance systems to obtain battlefield intelligence.
According to the report, both sides have exploited cameras to monitor military activity and improve their understanding of enemy positions and operations.
The same vulnerabilities extend beyond active battlefields. Russian-linked cyber actors have reportedly targeted surveillance cameras in European countries to monitor military movements.
The widespread availability of internet-connected cameras creates opportunities for intelligence collection far from conventional military installations.
Artificial intelligence can increase the usefulness of compromised video networks by helping operators process large amounts of footage, identify relevant activity, and recognize patterns that would otherwise require extensive manual monitoring.
Security warnings for camera owners
Cybersecurity specialists warn that many connected cameras are installed without adequate safeguards or ongoing technical maintenance.
Unlike computers and smartphones, which often receive regular security attention, cameras may operate for years with outdated firmware, weak login credentials, or insufficient protection against unauthorized access.
The growing number of cameras connected to private and commercial networks also creates potential entry points for attacks extending beyond the devices themselves.
Israeli cyber authorities have recommended replacing default passwords with strong, unique credentials, enabling two-factor authentication where available, installing security updates, and monitoring devices for unauthorized access.
The risks are especially high near military facilities, transportation routes, government installations, and other sensitive locations, where a seemingly ordinary camera may capture operationally valuable information.
As warfare increasingly combines conventional military operations with cyberattacks and digital intelligence collection, the WSJ investigation underscores how civilian surveillance infrastructure has become another contested element of modern conflict.

articles.title: 'Worst is yet to come:' Houthis claim responsibility for strikes on Saudi airports
articles.body:
One person was killed, and nearly a dozen were hurt in a new attack on Riyadh's international airport on Sunday, Saudi authorities reported, a day after a strike claimed by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.
Saudi-led coalition forces in Yemen said an unidentified projectile had targeted Riyadh's international airport Terminal 4 on Sunday, causing a fire. Eleven people were wounded in addition to the fatality, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.
Coalition forces also said Saudi air defenses had intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of King Khalid International Airport. They later added that a drone had been intercepted and destroyed in the country's Eastern Province, and a ballistic missile launched towards Khamis Mushait had been intercepted. Emergency alerts were also issued in Abha, in the south, early on Monday, but the danger had since passed, the Saudi Civil Defense said.
The strikes have exposed vulnerabilities in Saudi defense capabilities as the kingdom wages an air campaign against the Houthis, who are fighting a ground war in Yemen against the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.
Footage released by Saudi state television of the Saturday attack on the Riyadh airport showed scores of religious pilgrims lined up at a gate as they prepared to travel to Islam's two holiest sites. A bright orange flash sent people running in panic, while parts of the roof appeared to cave in. The airport was closed after the attack, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.
Houthis claim responsibility for attacks
In a televised speech on Sunday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed responsibility for Saturday's attack and said the group had also struck the airport in Dammam in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province and two facilities of Saudi oil giant Saudi Aramco.
The Saudi government's media office and Aramco did not respond to requests for comment.
The Saudi civil aviation authority confirmed the strike on Dammam's King Fahd International Airport late on Sunday, adding that "damage assessments and safety inspections of airport facilities are under way."
An eyewitness aboard a taxiing aircraft at Dammam told Reuters that around 8:30 p.m. (1730 GMT) on Sunday, they saw a projectile strike the tarmac beside several parked aircraft, causing a fire. The witness said the aircraft returned to the gate. Passengers disembarked and were told to leave.
Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 showed several delays and cancellations on Sunday for arrivals and departures at Dammam airport, the kingdom's third-largest.
The Houthis earlier on Sunday had renewed their warning against using Saudi airports. "We urge everyone to take our warnings seriously, and Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions," the group said.
Britain's embassy in Saudi Arabia, in a post on X, advised British citizens against all but essential travel to Jeddah, Dammam and all airports in the kingdom except the airport in Medina.
US aviation authorities issued a notice to US airlines to use caution while flying to or over the kingdom.
'Worst is yet to come,' Houthis warn
Saudi Arabia has recently stepped up its military involvement in Yemen, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a government counteroffensive after the Houthis seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month.
The Houthis said on Sunday that Saudi Arabia carried out 124 air strikes in Yemen in the past 24 hours. "Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing," Yemen's Houthi-run foreign ministry said in statements carried by Al Masirah television.
US President Donald Trump said on Saturday the United States was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover from the wider war with Iran that the US and Israel launched in February.
In a Telegram post, Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araqchi said he told his Saudi counterpart that Tehran was ready to help facilitate dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen.
Energy conference going ahead
A five-day conference of the international energy organization WPC Energy opened as planned on Sunday at a convention center about 10 km (6 miles) from the Riyadh airport, the Saudi energy ministry said.
A ministerial meeting of the International Energy Forum also went ahead, according to a media advisory from the ministry. It was not clear which ministers attended.
Italy's energy minister, Gilberto Pichetto Fratin, whose country was co-hosting, had said on Friday he would participate remotely via video link.
German officials were trying to organize a return flight for economy minister Katherina Reiche. She was supposed to return to Berlin from Riyadh on Monday, but the ministry said her flight was likely unable to take off.
Separately, Saudi authorities announced that schools in Riyadh would shift in-person classes to remote learning from Sunday until Thursday.
Sunday's attack brought the death toll in attacks on Riyadh's airport to 18 for the week. In Saturday's attack, the dead included four Saudis while the remainder were foreign nationals, Saudi authorities said.

articles.title: US races Russia and China to build a nuclear reactor on the moon
articles.body:
In 2019, Russia tested a nuclear-powered cruise missile. The test failed, and the missile plunged to the bottom of the White Sea in northern Russia. Shortly afterward, a large explosion occurred near the crash site, causing radiation levels in the area to spike. U.S. intelligence officials assessed that the explosion took place during a Russian operation to recover the missile from the seabed. At least five nuclear scientists and employees of Russia's state-owned nuclear energy company, Rosatom, were killed. Russia quickly denied that the missile was nuclear-powered, but Rosatom subsequently all but acknowledged what had happened.
Now imagine a rocket carrying an actual nuclear reactor to the moon crashing into the ocean. It sounds like particularly dangerous science fiction, but until just a few years ago, the possibility of artificial intelligence taking over the world also seemed like nothing more than science fiction. With the world's major powers locked in a frantic race to install a nuclear reactor in space, such a scenario may be just around the corner.
A dangerous undertaking
About two months ago, NASA asked private contractors to prepare to build a nuclear reactor capable of surviving a journey through space and operating without maintenance near the moon's south pole. The target launch date: December 2030. The goal: to beat Russia, which aims to have a reactor operating on the moon by 2036 as part of a not-so-secret partnership with China. In 1961, President John F. Kennedy challenged America's leading scientists to land a man on the moon before the end of the decade. Now the goal is to have a functioning nuclear reactor on the moon within four years.
Even before sending nuclear reactors to the moon, the United States plans to put humans back on its surface as part of the Artemis program. The third test flight is scheduled for summer 2027, while the crewed Artemis 4 mission is planned for early 2028.
The somewhat dystopian race to install a reactor on the moon is probably inevitable, and it has implications for the entire future of space exploration. For example, a lunar day lasts about 14 Earth days, followed by 14 consecutive Earth days of complete darkness. During that time, solar panels cannot generate electricity, and temperatures plunge to minus 130 degrees. A nuclear reactor provides continuous electricity and heat around the clock, regardless of sunlight. Any ambition to reach Mars, let alone establish habitable conditions there, also requires nuclear energy.
Establishing a base on the moon is critical to the search for resources and the launch of missions into the depths of the solar system. All of this makes control over access to lunar resources essential, and the major powers believe a nuclear reactor is the foundation for achieving these ambitions. But it is a dangerous undertaking.
As in the case of the Russian missile in 2019, debris from a reactor falling back to Earth could scatter radioactive materials, as happened in Canada in the 1970s. An explosion or reactor core meltdown on the lunar surface could also render entire areas of the moon off-limits. All three countries promise that their reactors will remain inactive until they reach the moon, but these days it is difficult to take their leaders at their word, especially when the race is also, of course, a display of nationalist power.
Leading scientists warn that governments are moving too quickly at a time when space exploration has experienced a string of failures over the past six years. Chinese, American and Russian rockets have exploded, and space debris regularly falls back to Earth.
"There will always be a space race going on, and if you enter nuclear power into that mix, then it could take a potentially more dangerous turn,” said Edwin Lyman, the director of nuclear power safety at the Union of Concerned Scientists.
A deadline pushed back
When it comes to nuclear power in space, Russia has no rivals. It has launched more than 30 reactors into Earth orbit, primarily aboard Cold War-era satellites in the 1970s and 1980s, and holds the largest stockpile of what is considered the safest nuclear fuel for space missions.
The last space reactor NASA tested, in 2018, used highly enriched uranium, which is lighter and cheaper to launch than other fuels. But its use is dangerous because the material can be turned into a nuclear weapon. That leaves the option of using low-enriched uranium fuel, except that the Americans do not have enough of it and cannot import it from Russia because of a ban imposed in 2024 in response to the war in Ukraine.
To date, the United States has invested more than $20 billion in space nuclear programs. Last month, the Pentagon selected a company called Antares to develop and demonstrate a space microreactor, while NASA is accelerating its timetable out of concern that a Russian-Chinese reactor could effectively establish an exclusion zone on the moon.
Such a move could, in practice, prevent American astronauts and rovers from accessing large areas of the lunar surface. That would itself violate the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, but international agreements are being violated on a daily basis these days.
Despite the sense of urgency, all the major powers have repeatedly pushed back their target dates, and few experts believe they will meet their deadlines. None of them even has a proven lunar lander capable of delivering heavy, potentially radioactive materials to the moon's unforgiving surface.
There is, of course, the option of international cooperation, as has happened time and again in space exploration. But the current global climate leaves little room for optimism.
"Governments have always achieved more by working together than by competing," Katy Huff, head of the Department of Nuclear Engineering at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, told The New York Times. "Collaborative, team-based science in space has always managed to rise above our fraught international politics."

articles.title: Saudi Arabia needs allies against the Houthis, but will it turn to Israel? - analysis
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump lives in a transactional foreign policy universe. You give, you get. You don’t give, don’t expect much.
Israel has given a lot and, in return, gotten a lot. It has fought wing to wing with the US in Iran, provided valuable intelligence and demonstrated the military capabilities Washington wants to see in an ally.
In April, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said, “To our Israeli allies, thanks for being a brave, capable and willing ally on this battlefield. The rest of the world and the rest of our so-called allies saw what real capabilities look like. They should take some notes.”
America’s “legacy” allies – from NATO countries to South Korea – have not stepped up to anywhere near the same degree. They have consequently been on the receiving end of more than just harsh words.
Trump ordered joint military exercises with South Korea scaled back, citing Seoul’s refusal to help with the Iran campaign, and threatened to cut off trade with Spain after Madrid denied Washington the use of its bases for strikes on Iran.
And then there is Saudi Arabia.
Many have been puzzled by Washington’s reluctance to intervene directly in the Saudis’ battle with the Houthis. This battle took a particularly deadly turn on Saturday when the King Khalid Airport in Riyadh was struck by a missile, killing 12 people and injuring more than 300, the most serious attack in Saudi Arabia in a decade.
This came as tensions between the Saudis and the Houthis steadily escalated – Saturday’s attack was the third such attack in a week, since the Saudis launched a counter-offensive against the Houthis to push them back from the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Despite all that, Trump has wavered. Washington has provided intelligence and targeting assistance, but the president has so far stopped short of direct military intervention. On Saturday, he said he was considering joining the Saudi strikes.
Why the hesitation?
The explanations offered range from reluctance to become engaged in another major military campaign less than a month before the midterm elections to concern about weapons stocks depleted by the war in Iran.
Saudi Arabia's refusal to join the Abraham Accords
Another possible explanation is Trump’s frustration with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s steadfast refusal to join the Abraham Accords. Saudi normalization with Israel would have given Trump an important diplomatic prize before the elections.
If this is indeed the case, then it fits into a pattern. In July, the US and Saudi Arabia signed a nuclear cooperation agreement, opening the door to a major commercial role for American companies. Trump then said he would not proceed unless the Saudis joined the Abraham Accords.
You give, you get.
Saudi normalization with Israel has long been the Middle East’s diplomatic holy grail.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s former military secretary, Avi Gil, said in a long, revealing interview with Israel Hayom on Thursday that the desire to bring Saudi Arabia into the Abraham Accords helped explain Israel’s restraint toward Hamas and Hezbollah in the run-up to October 7.
Israel wanted to avoid an escalation that could derail the normalization process. He said the two countries were “closer than people realize” to a deal.
But Israeli action didn’t scuttle the process. Hamas did that all on its own.
Since then, the Saudis have made clear – even as the Iranian threat loomed larger and normalization with Israel made good strategic sense in trying to create a new security architecture for the region – that without a pathway to a Palestinian state, they were not going to normalize.
That leaves a familiar gap between strategic logic and political feasibility, since – with October 7 so fresh and raw – it is highly unlikely that any Israeli government in the foreseeable future would agree to a Palestinian state.
Israel and Saudi Arabia face threats from Iran and its allies. Both have an interest in preventing the Houthis from threatening shipping, airports, and regional stability. Those shared interests provide a strong argument for cooperation. They have not, however, proven enough to overcome the political obstacles to establishing an open relationship.
Further evidence of where Riyadh was looking for its regional security architecture came in August, when it signed a joint defense pact with Pakistan and Turkey. Rather than bringing its relationship with Israel into the open, Saudi Arabia was strengthening an alternative framework with two Muslim powers.
The pact’s promise was sweeping: an attack on one would be considered an attack on all. So far, the response to the Houthi campaign has not matched that rhetoric. Turkey has reportedly begun providing defensive and technical assistance, but that is a long way from joining Saudi Arabia in striking the enemy attacking it.
Signing this pact showed that Saudi Arabia – while interested in maintaining intelligence cooperation with Israel and keeping it discreet – was seeking far-reaching security arrangements elsewhere.
Then an Omani pilot planned to crash a flydubai plane full of Israeli passengers into Ben-Gurion Airport, only to be thwarted by some brave and resourceful passengers and crew members, and Jerusalem got an unvarnished view of where it stands with the Saudis.
Yes, the Saudis allowed a distressed plane full of Israeli passengers to land at a civilian-military airfield in Tabuk. And, yes, Saudi medical personnel cared for Israeli passengers. Both were consequential acts of assistance in a moment of acute danger.
But Riyadh adamantly refused Israel’s request to send its own aircraft to collect the passengers. A replacement flydubai plane brought them home.
Cooperation, but to a point
This exposed the boundary between practical cooperation and public acceptance. Allowing an Israeli plane to pick up the passengers would be one gesture too far on the road to normalization: one which would have been staunchly opposed by much of the Saudi public and undoubtedly weaponized against the Saudis by the Iranians.
Whatever the precise calculations behind that refusal, the political message was clear: cooperation could proceed, but only so far.
Ten days later, Saudi Arabia’s own airport was targeted, and all of a sudden it is looking for allies in its fight with the Houthis.
That attack inevitably led to speculation that this might bring Israeli-Saudi security cooperation into the open and lead to closer ties to combat a common threat. Weakening the Houthis, after all, would serve Israeli interests as well as Saudi ones. The group’s hostility toward Israel is not exactly a secret.
But shared enemies don’t necessarily lead to joint military operations. Public Israeli involvement could carry political costs for Riyadh and provide ammunition for those seeking to portray the Saudi campaign as serving Israel.
The Saudi leadership would have to weigh those costs against the benefits of the assistance. Israel, in turn, would have to decide what risks it should take on the Saudis’ behalf and what it could expect in return.
While the airport attack does not guarantee a breakthrough between Israel and Saudi Arabia, it does force Riyadh to face this question: does it make sense to keep one of its potentially strongest regional partners at arm’s length?
And for Israel, the question is a variation on Trump’s transactional theme: How much should it give when the Saudis are still unwilling to publicly be seen taking?

articles.title: Iran at the threshold, Israel outside the room - opinion
articles.body:
One justification for war with Iran was that time was running out. Tehran, Israelis were told, was “racing” toward nuclear weapons, “a step away” from a bomb.
Yet Iran has been near the nuclear threshold for years. Its distance from a weapon has never depended solely on centrifuges, enriched uranium, or the time needed to produce fissile material. US intelligence assessed that Tehran had acquired capabilities bringing it close to the threshold but had not decided to cross it. A crucial barrier was political.
Six months into the war, it is difficult to say that barrier has strengthened. Nuclear facilities have been damaged, but subsequent US intelligence assessments do not indicate a significant increase in the time Iran would need to produce a weapon.
Questions remain about its enriched uranium stockpile, while discussion in Iran about crossing the threshold has become more open. The war has also opened a front in the Strait of Hormuz and increased Israel’s diplomatic costs, particularly in the United States. Whether it has made Israel safer from nuclear threats remains unclear.
The only effort in the past decade that successfully imposed agreed, monitored, verifiable limits on Iran’s nuclear program was diplomatic. The 2015 agreement dramatically reduced its enriched uranium stockpile, restricted enrichment and centrifuges, and introduced extensive monitoring.
The International Atomic Energy Agency and Western intelligence assessments found Iran compliant with its core nuclear commitments. Missiles, proxies, and other security issues could – and still can – be addressed separately.
When the Trump administration withdrew unilaterally in May 2018 and reimposed sanctions, the IAEA was still verifying compliance. Iran began exceeding the limits afterward. Israel’s push for US withdrawal, followed by the shift from diplomacy to war, demands a sober assessment of this strategy’s costs.
A low-risk diplomatic option remains largely unknown to Israelis. Since 2019, regional states have gathered annually at UN headquarters in New York for the Conference on the Establishment of a Middle East Zone Free of Nuclear Weapons and Other Weapons of Mass Destruction. Its seventh session takes place this November. Iran and the Arab states participate. Israel is invited but stays away.
Israel has long argued that disarmament cannot be separated from regional security; that arrangements must be developed by regional states with their consent; and that states cannot relinquish capabilities considered essential while remaining in conflict with their neighbors.
It has rightly opposed focusing exclusively on its nuclear capabilities while ignoring missiles, chemical and biological weapons, and other threats. These concerns remain relevant.
They do not, however, require postponing disarmament discussions until peace, recognition, normalization, and extensive confidence-building measures have been achieved. Arab states see this approach as an endless series of prerequisites before weapons of mass destruction reach the table.
Peace, confidence-building, arms control, and disarmament can advance in parallel. War only increases the need for communication, escalation prevention, monitoring, and agreements.
Changing the regional landscape
Participation in November would not require Israel to relinquish weapons attributed to it, join the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), abandon nuclear ambiguity, or accept a future treaty in advance. The conference operates by consensus: regional states participate, and decisions cannot be imposed on Israel.
Several longstanding Israeli demands are therefore already met. If Israel wants missiles, delivery systems, escalation prevention, regional security, and confidence-building on the agenda, it should make those demands inside the room.
Participation could itself build mutual confidence. Israel would discuss weapons of mass destruction directly with its neighbors without committing to an outcome. Arab states and Iran would have to accept Israel as a full, equal negotiating partner.
This would not constitute normalization: states conditioning full relations on ending the occupation and reaching an Israeli-Palestinian settlement could retain their positions. But accepting Israel as a legitimate participant would matter to a country that has long insisted recognition and regional relations are essential to disarmament.
The United States also stays away. Alongside its own reservations, Washington has linked its absence to incomplete regional participation and Israel’s opposition to the format.
An Israeli shift could enable an American one. The government formed after October’s elections could invite Washington to join it in November. After months of confrontation with Iran, this would be a significant diplomatic gesture without advance commitments to disarmament, NPT accession, or an unwritten treaty.
There are precedents. Israel participated in Arms Control and Regional Security talks with Arab states in the 1990s and consultations on a weapons of mass destruction conference in 2013–2014; Iran attended one meeting.
Beginning in 1980, Israel joined the UN General Assembly consensus supporting a nuclear-weapon-free Middle East for over two decades, while retaining reservations about how to achieve it. Attending November’s conference would revive a tradition of raising objections and demanding conditions while continuing to talk.
Meanwhile, the regional landscape is changing. Saudi Arabia is expanding its civilian nuclear program and security alliances, including the Mecca Agreement with Turkey and nuclear-armed Pakistan. Iran is reconsidering its nuclear future, and another confrontation remains possible.
Burying one’s nuclear head in the sand does not preserve freedom of action. It leaves others free to shape the reality Israel must confront.
The next government should arrive in New York with Israel’s security interests, reservations, demands, and proposals – and ask Washington to join it. It need not commit to disarmament. Entering the room does not endanger Israel’s security. In today’s regional reality, remaining outside requires an explanation.
The writer is a guest writer at the Mitvim Institute and an advocate for eliminating nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction from the Middle East. She is the founder and executive director of the Middle East Treaty Organization (METO).

articles.title: Yemen fighting expands as Houthis attack Saudi airport: What to know
articles.body:
Yemen fighting expands as Houthis attack Saudi airport again: What to know
Saudi coalition blames Houthi group for the missile strike that struck King Khalid international airport in Riyadh.
Saudi Arabia has said it will “firmly” retaliate against an attack on Riyadh’s international airport on Saturday in which at least 12 people were killed, as Yemen’s Houthis claimed a new attack on Saudi’s main air hub on Sunday which resulted in fresh injuries.
The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said the attack on Sunday evening targeted King Khalid International Airport and had “resulted in injuries”, without elaborating.
A Saudi-led coalition fighting the Iran-aligned group earlier said an “unidentified projectile” struck a passenger terminal at the airport, causing a fire, adding that Saudi air defences also intercepted a missile.
The coalition on Sunday described the attack the previous day as a “full-fledged war crime”.
It comes amid escalating fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces following the collapse of a United Nations-brokered ceasefire largely in place since 2022.
The fighting has raised fears of a wider regional confrontation, with Trump suggesting the US could join Saudi military operations against the Houthis.
Dania Thafer, executive director at the Gulf International Forum, said Saudi Arabia will likely hit back at the Houthis “pretty hard”.
“I still think that the Saudis probably want de-escalation. They don’t want long-term escalation, but the Houthis are making it very difficult by not only being a threat to Saudi national security but also a threat to international maritime security,” Thafer said. “So this battle is much bigger than just a tit-for-tat.”
Here is what you need to know:
What happened at Riyadh airport?
According to Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA), a missile struck King Khalid airport in Riyadh on Saturday. It killed 12 people and wounded 309 others, some of them critically.
The dead included four Saudi nationals, two Bangladeshis and one citizen each from the US, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine and Sudan. It was the deadliest attack on the kingdom in more than a decade.
The Houthis claimed responsibility for the attack on Sunday.
In a statement, spokesman Yahya Saree said the group carried out multiple operations targeting King Khalid Airport.
“Take our warnings seriously, and Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions,” military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a post on X.
Airport operations were suspended, with flights cancelled or diverted. Schools across Riyadh were ordered to switch to remote learning for a week following the attack.
The attacks have disrupted international flights, with several airlines suspending services to Saudi destinations. Later on Saturday, the Saudi-led coalition said a projectile had fallen near King Fahd international airport in Dammam in the country’s east.
Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, said the Iran-backed group was retaliating by attacking what it called Saudi Arabia’s “most precious assets”, which are Aramco oil facilities and the airport in Riyadh.
“Although Saudi Arabia has said it will retaliate, let’s not forget that it’s carried out many air strikes across Yemen, and the Yemeni group is still able to launch ballistic missiles and drones towards Saudi Arabia,” he added.
What other areas have the Houthis targeted?
The Iran-aligned Houthis have launched a series of missile and drone attacks targeting airports, military installations and oil facilities across Saudi Arabia, including areas near the border with Yemen.
On Monday, attacks on King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz airport in the southwestern city of Jizan and Najran international airport wounded three people and caused material damage, according to the GACA.
On Tuesday, attacks on Abha airport and Riyadh airport killed three people and wounded 36 others, according to Saudi authorities.
The Houthis also claimed to have targeted an Aramco oil refinery in Rabigh, on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea coast, with missiles and drones, saying the attack caused a fire. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the claim.
The Houthis imposed a maritime embargo on Saudi Arabia in July following the outbreak of the latest round of fighting.
Yasmeen al-Eryani, the executive director for knowledge production at Sanaa Center, said the Houthis are trying to put “maximum pressure” on Saudi Arabia.
“But they’re also mobilising the internal front lines in a really major way, moving even away from the west coast battle into Taiz and more densely populated areas,” al-Eryani, from the think tank based in government-controlled Aden, told Al Jazeera.
“We could see further mobilisation; they have very high momentum. They will probably continue to capitalise on that momentum, internally,” she said, adding that “the [Houthi] cross-border attacks” will put pressure across the region.
Al-Eryani added that the Houthis were “provoking” Saudi Arabia, the US and regional states, which could potentially join in the conflict.
What is the latest in the fighting?
The Houthi-affiliated media on Sunday reported an air attack on Naqil al-Zarbi in the Hayfan district of Yemen’s Taiz governorate in southwestern Yemen, as well as a missile attack on the Sahar district in the northern province of Saada.
Forces belonging to Yemen’s internationally recognised government also released footage purportedly showing the downing of a Houthi drone over Mount Sabr in Taiz.
Meanwhile, Saudi-led coalition spokesman Major-General Turki al-Maliki said early on Sunday that forces intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis towards al-Kharj province, as well as a drone in the kingdom’s Eastern province.
On Saturday, Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili, the spokesman for Yemeni government forces, said at least 1,150 Houthis were killed in almost 2,000 targeted operations across the country since the internationally recognised government’s counteroffensive began.
He said the army had destroyed Houthi ammunition dumps and at least 180 combat, transport and supply vehicles operated by the Houthis, adding that ground forces “continued to advance their assault”.
Al Jazeera was not able to independently verify the competing claims.
Fighting has intensified across several fronts in Yemen, with Saudi-backed government forces launching the Dawn of Yemen offensive on October 4 to recapture Houthi-held territory, including the port city of Mocha and the island of Mayyun.
While the internationally recognised government’s forces said they had retaken Mocha and the Dhubab district near the strait, the Houthis have disputed the claims.
The Houthis have also tightened their siege of Taiz after capturing territory south of the city earlier this month, including al-Turbah. Taiz has been one of the most heavily contested cities in the war.
Fighting has also spread to Marib and al-Jawf, two governorates east of Sanaa, where government forces have reported advances against Houthi positions.
What has been the international response to the Houthi attack on the airport?
The attack has drawn condemnation from the US and the UN, while several foreign governments have warned their citizens to avoid the airport.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed that an American was among those killed and condemned the attacks.
“These reprehensible attacks demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life. They must stop now,” Rubio said.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the strike, stressing that attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure violate international law.
The US, Canada, Germany and several other countries issued travel warnings, while some diplomatic missions restricted staff movements through the airport.
Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif described the attack as “heinous” and reaffirmed Islamabad’s commitment to Saudi security.
On October 5, Turkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia agreed to activate “deterrence measures” under a mutual defence pact and rapidly deploy forces to the Gulf kingdom to counter attacks by Yemen’s Houthis. This came weeks after the three countries signed the Mecca Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement.
Will the US join Saudi strikes against Yemen’s Houthis?
Trump has left open the possibility of US military involvement but has not announced a decision.
“We may. We’re going to look at it,” Trump told reporters on Saturday.
The US president said he planned to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, describing the attack as “not acceptable”.
According to US media reports, Washington has already provided intelligence sharing, target identification and planning assistance for the latest Saudi-backed offensive.
When the Saudi-led coalition intervened in the civil war in March 2015, Washington provided intelligence, logistical assistance and weapons to support its campaign against the Houthis, but did not directly participate in the coalition’s air strikes.
But in 2021, the Biden administration ended support for the Saudi-led offensive in Yemen, citing the humanitarian crisis. More than 100,000 Yemenis were killed and millions were displaced at the time.

articles.title: Midterm panic pushes Trump to trade Zelensky for cheaper diesel
articles.body:
Midterm panic pushes Trump to trade Zelensky for cheaper diesel
