TEHRAN — With the 2026 U.S. midterm elections a month away and diesel at $6.28 a gallon, Donald Trump went looking for someone to blame and settled on Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelensky, whose official presidential mandate expired long ago and whose continued rule under suspended elections remains constitutionally questionable.
On Friday, after talks with Vladimir Putin, Trump announced that Russia would ship more than 300,000 tons of diesel immediately, 500,000 in November and a million after that.
U.S. Treasury’s General License 135 makes it legal, reportedly until April 7, 2027. Trump signed a Russia sanctions law last month. He thanked Putin anyway.
The fuel crunch traces to the war on Iran, which the United States and Israel opened on February 28 and which has throttled Persian Gulf supply since. Trump blames Ukrainian drones hitting Russian refineries instead. Analysts are unconvinced.
Analyst Tom Kloza called the announcement “more noise from Truth Social,” adding that Ukrainian drones have reportedly crippled about half of Russia’s refining. Ed Hirs of the University of Houston told Newsweek that he expects relief at the pump only well after the election, and only a temporary one, because the pledged volume is small next to the global market.
Saturday brought the insult. “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” Trump told reporters, accusing Zelensky of wanting “to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel.”
The same day, Russian glide bombs reportedly hit Zaporizhzhia, where Ukrainian officials counted at least 21 dead, three of them children. Zelensky called Washington’s waiver “an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged.”
The timing was almost comic. Ukrainian and European officials were in Miami with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner when the announcement landed, and a senior Ukrainian official told the AP that Kyiv had no warning.
A U.S. official gave Axios another version: Trump moved after Zelensky ignored roughly six requests to stop hitting Russian refineries. Ukrainian officials say Washington threatened to cut intelligence sharing.
Sunday’s Truth Social post claimed an “ENERGY CEASEFIRE,” effective immediately. “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” Zelensky said the announcement “was news for me,” and said Ukraine will comply if Moscow does.
Trump tried this on September 14. Neither capital confirmed it then, and both kept striking each other’s energy sites.
The pattern is hard to miss. Washington announces by social media post, informs its partner afterward and calls the result a deal.
Kyiv is asked to stop hitting refineries, absorb strikes on its power grid and, if Trump gets his way, hold an election under bombardment. Moscow may get sanctions relief and export revenue. Stockholm and Berlin claimed they are keeping their sanctions, even if Washington is not.

articles.title: Kremlin says Zelenskyy currently is incapable of 'considered actions'
articles.body:
Kanyshai Butun
11 October 2026•Update: 11 October 2026
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Sunday that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy currently is in a state of “hysteria” and incapable of making "considered actions."
In an interview with Vesti media outlet, Peskov said that if Zelenskyy were capable of measured action, he would show a willingness to pursue peace negotiations with Russia.
“Naturally, being in a state of hysteria, Zelensky is hardly capable of taking any considered actions right now. If he were capable of considered actions, he would be demonstrating an inclination toward peace negotiations,” he said.
Peskov accused Zelenskyy of seeking more money from “all his overseers,” including for air defense and long-range weapons, as well as access to Starlink infrastructure to enable Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russian territory.
He also criticized Zelenskyy’s belief that showing “aggression” toward Russia could be effective.
“This is a tragic mistake for Ukraine. You cannot treat Russia that way. Those who behave like that toward Russia pay a price. Right now, Ukraine is paying the price,” he said.
Peskov’s remarks came two days after US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke by phone and discussed diesel supplies to the US and global markets.
In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump said Russia had agreed to “immediately supply” more than 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to the US and global markets. He said another 500,000 tons would be supplied in November, followed by 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.”
Trump added that a further 3 million tons would be delivered “within a short period,” depending on the condition of Russian diesel refineries.
Putin said Russian diesel supplies to the US and global markets would benefit the world economy.
Zelenskyy criticized the US-Russia diesel agreement, warning that every additional billion dollars Moscow earns from exports would fund weapons production, Shahed drone upgrades, missile manufacturing and the recruitment of foreign fighters. He urged Ukraine’s partners to “restrict Russia’s ability to wage war.”
On Saturday, Trump called on Ukraine to “get a new president,” accusing Zelenskyy of repeatedly failing to reach a deal to end the war with Russia.
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal, because he could have made many deals that, for some reason, he never does,” Trump said.

articles.title: US-Israel relationship may be irreparably damaged, former Biden official warns
articles.body:
Phil Gordon, who served in the Biden administration as then-vice president Kamala Harris's national security advisor, issued a stark warning in an exclusive interview with The Jerusalem Post on Sunday that Israeli-US ties have been severely damaged.
"It's really collapsed. There's no sugarcoating it. I think Israelis need to understand that," Gordon told the Post.
Gordon believes the damage inflicted on relations between Israel and the United States in recent years may be far more enduring than many Israelis realize, potentially extending well beyond the political careers of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and US President Donald Trump.
"I have rarely seen a turnaround in attitudes on an issue as rapid and comprehensive," Gordon said, referring to the dramatic decline in American support for Israel over the past year.
"You have a whole generation of Americans," he continued. "Look at the numbers on sympathy for Israelis versus Palestinians or favorable to Israel. It's really collapsed. There's no sugarcoating it. I think Israelis need to understand that."
Gordon does not rule out the possibility that the deterioration could prove permanent.
Asked why he recently described the damage to the relationship as "perhaps irreparably," he explained that his choice of words was deliberate.
"I write perhaps because I think it's still an open question, but I also don't rule it out," he said. "The more important word is irreparably because it's honestly possible."
Why Gordon is speaking out now
Gordon's interview comes a day after he publicly challenged efforts by Netanyahu supporters to portray a new book and interviews by Brett McGurk, a senior Biden administration official closely involved in negotiations over the Gaza war and the Israeli hostages, as vindication of the prime minister's wartime decisions.
In a post on X, Gordon argued that McGurk's account, while valuable, should not be treated as the definitive version of what happened behind the scenes.
"While Brett's front-row account is valuable, that doesn't mean it is definitive or its perspectives widely shared, including among former members of the Biden administration," Gordon wrote.
"I would say most of my former colleagues think that President Biden should have put more pressure on Israel to conduct the war differently and end it sooner," he added.
Gordon also wrote that few former administration officials believed Biden's biggest mistake had been publicly distancing himself from Israel, what he described as showing "daylight" between Washington and Jerusalem.
Speaking to the Post, Gordon explained why he decided to enter the debate over one of the most contentious periods in recent Israeli-American relations.
"Everything's charged and this is sensitive and important, which is why I thought it was important for me to weigh in with my perspective," he said.
His account focuses particularly on the efforts to secure a hostage agreement during the summer of 2024, including a crucial phone conversation between Biden and Netanyahu that, Gordon says, revealed just how difficult reaching a deal would become.
The July 4 call: 'We were not hearing a yes… but something closer to no'
On July 4, 2024, president Joe Biden called Netanyahu at what American officials believed could be a significant turning point in the negotiations to release Israeli hostages held in Gaza.
According to Gordon, Hamas had just indicated it was willing to abandon one of its central demands, creating what Washington saw as a genuine opportunity for progress.
To understand the significance of that moment, Gordon traced the negotiations back to the spring of 2024.
For months, Hamas had insisted that Israel commit to a permanent ceasefire before any hostages were released. Israel refused to make such a commitment.
That dispute remained the main obstacle throughout May.
But toward the end of that month, Gordon said Israel signaled it could accept a phased ceasefire arrangement in which a permanent ceasefire would remain the ultimate objective without requiring an immediate Israeli commitment.
"With clever drafting, we were able to put together the proposal that President Biden rolled out publicly on May 31," Gordon said.
Under that framework, Israel would not have to commit to a permanent ceasefire during the first phase, but good-faith negotiations over the final arrangements would allow for what Gordon described as "sustainable calm."
The proposal represented a breakthrough because it created a possible path toward a permanent ceasefire without requiring Israel to accept Hamas's original condition upfront.
For weeks, however, Hamas did not respond.
Then, around July 2, Gordon said Hamas finally agreed in principle to the framework.
"Hamas finally came around and sort of agreed, in principle, with the framework, including dropping its demand that a permanent ceasefire be agreed up front," he recalled.
"That felt to us like a significant step forward. Nobody was naive in thinking that this wouldn't be difficult."
With that development, Biden called Netanyahu on July 4 to urge him to move ahead.
"The plan was to really urge him to take the deal," Gordon said.
"This has gone on far too long. The hostages had suffered far too long. There was far too much catastrophic damage, Palestinian lives lost. Humanitarian conditions were horrific."
But Gordon said Netanyahu's response quickly dampened American expectations.
"I think we, the American side, were pretty deflated to hear Netanyahu say, 'Okay, you know, I hear you, Joe, but here are all the things that will have to happen for this to work,'" Gordon recalled.
Netanyahu then began listing those requirements during the call.
"I could tell in that moment that we were not hearing a yes or even a yes, I can work with this, but something closer to no."
According to Gordon, Netanyahu subsequently began what he described as "clarifying" Israel's position, clarifications that Washington regarded as effectively introducing additional conditions into the negotiations.
Philadelphi Corridor, Gallant, and the political question
One of the most consequential Israeli demands involved retaining military forces along the entire Philadelphi Corridor, the narrow strip of territory separating Gaza from Egypt.
Gordon emphasized that Israel had not even fully controlled the corridor when the original proposals were developed.
"In that sense, it really was a new condition," he said.
Netanyahu continued insisting on that position throughout the fall of 2024, despite objections from senior Israeli officials.
Gordon specifically cited then-defense minister Yoav Gallant, who, he said, considered continued control of the entire corridor militarily unnecessary and an obstacle to reaching a deal.
Another disputed condition involved an Israeli screening mechanism for Palestinians returning to northern Gaza, which would have required Israeli forces to remain in central Gaza.
In his earlier X post, Gordon argued that these conditions made an agreement impossible for another six months.
During that period, he wrote, nearly 9,000 additional Palestinians were killed, while more Israeli hostages died, including the six hostages executed by Hamas in August 2024.
He noted that both Israeli conditions were ultimately dropped from the agreement reached in January 2025.
Asked directly whether Netanyahu deliberately delayed the agreement to preserve his governing coalition, Gordon declined to judge the prime minister's motivations.
"I can't speak to or speculate about his motives," he said.
"I know there was a lot of talk that he feared that he would lose his coalition if he compromised on certain issues."
Gordon acknowledged that Netanyahu might genuinely have believed that continued Israeli control of the Philadelphi Corridor was militarily necessary.
"He certainly articulated over and over again that total victory was the only option," Gordon said.
But he added that the political implications were difficult to ignore.
"It also seemed to be the case that keeping his coalition together depended on rejecting that proposal, so yeah, you can draw your own conclusions."
Gordon stressed that no one could know with certainty whether greater flexibility by Netanyahu would have produced an agreement during the summer of 2024.
Nevertheless, he argued that Netanyahu's insistence on those conditions had a clear consequence.
"We do know that by digging in and taking the positions that he did, which seemed to align with his political interests, and certainly aligned with his emphasis on the need for total victory, that made any deal at that time impossible," he said.
A warning for Israel: Arms conditionality is now mainstream among Democrats
For Gordon, one of the most significant consequences of the Israel-Hamas War in the Gaza Strip is not merely the deterioration in relations between Netanyahu and the Biden administration, but a broader transformation in American political attitudes toward Israel.
Positions once considered marginal in debates over US military assistance have increasingly moved into the Democratic mainstream.
"Arms conditionality has now gone from a kind of fringe view to a mainstream Democratic position," Gordon said.
He pointed to the growing number of Democratic senators supporting measures that would condition American assistance to Israel, including legislation concerning Israel's planned development in the E1 area east of Jerusalem in the West Bank.
Gordon cited a Senate proposal he said virtually all Democrats supported and that would withhold assistance over E1.
Although the shift has been particularly pronounced among Democrats, Gordon emphasized that declining support for Israel is not confined to one political party.
"I know people are mostly focused on Democrats, and it's true there's sharper criticism of Israel among Democrats, but it exists in both parties," he said.
A future Israeli government adopting different policies could begin rebuilding the relationship, Gordon argued, but reversing the damage would require a sustained effort.
"I think with a new Israeli government and different policies, the relationship could improve, he said.
"With work on both sides, maybe it can be repaired, but I don't think anybody should underestimate the challenge."
Should Biden have withheld more weapons from Israel?
While sharply critical of Netanyahu, Gordon does not absolve the administration in which he served of responsibility.
Asked what concrete pressure Biden should have applied, he rejected the idea that Washington faced only two options: continuing military assistance without conditions or imposing a comprehensive arms embargo.
"We had great respect for Israel's need to defend itself against Hezbollah, against Iran," Gordon said.
He noted that the threat of Iranian military action was particularly real during that period, including the ballistic missile and drone attack Iran launched against Israel in April 2024.
He explained that this security threat was a major reason the Biden administration did not support broadly withholding weapons.
But Gordon argued that Washington had many other available tools.
"There's an awful lot between doing nothing and withholding all weapons," he said.
"It starts with diplomatic pressure. It starts with calling out Israel and pushing it to accept these agreements. You can take diplomatic measures at the United Nations and elsewhere, and then yes, you can also start conditioning weapons."
He cited the administration's decision to withhold certain 2,000-pound bombs as an example of using military assistance to signal serious disagreement with Israel's conduct of the war and its handling of the humanitarian crisis.
One episode particularly demonstrated the potential effectiveness of American pressure, Gordon argued: Biden's response to the Israeli strike that killed aid workers from World Central Kitchen.
According to Gordon, Biden called Netanyahu and delivered a direct warning.
"You will do these things on the humanitarian front, and I need to see them immediately, or US policy is going to change," Gordon recalled Biden telling Netanyahu.
"Israel did, and opened up further crossings, and that was an example of how US pressure could work."
Gordon also pointed to the pressure McGurk and Steve Witkoff applied during negotiations over the January 2025 agreement, during the presidential transition following Trump's election victory.
"When Brett McGurk and Steve Witkoff were pressing the Israelis to accept the final deal in January, and Trump behind the scenes, I think that kind of pressure also worked," he said.
Iran before the elections: 'A volatile and dangerous stalemate'
Gordon also addressed another question now dominating discussions in Jerusalem and Washington: Could Israel or the United States resume major military operations against Iran before Israel's elections and the US midterms?
He refused to offer a definitive prediction, warning instead that the current confrontation was unusually volatile.
"We've learned over the last two years and beyond not to exclude anything," Gordon said.
"The situation is extremely volatile."
One of his central concerns is that both Washington and Tehran believe time is working in their favor.
"I'm afraid that both the United States and Iran feel that time is on their side," he said.
"The United States thinks that the blockade is working or squeezing Iran or the economy, but Iran feels like midterms looming and pressure on the US economy means it can resist and last longer."
That competing assessment, Gordon argued, explains the current diplomatic and military impasse.
"That's what explains this current stalemate. But it's a volatile and dangerous stalemate."
Gordon fears that the pressure campaign may produce further escalation before Tehran agrees to American demands.
"One is that before Iran collapses, which is sort of the goal, either capitulates or collapses, which is the goal of maximum pressure, it will lash out," he said.
He cited recent Houthi attacks against Riyadh and the earlier attack on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline as examples of how regional escalation can spiral, while noting that the Houthis, rather than Iran directly, were responsible for those attacks.
Gordon also offered a notable assessment of Trump's military decision-making in recent months.
"I would say that over the past couple of months, every time Trump has threatened it and considered it, he's backed off because he has realized that the consequences could be devastating," he said.
"I don't know if that will hold, but I do think it's worth keeping in mind."
Gordon argued that the war has already demonstrated the danger of unintended consequences.
"I think this war, after six months now, has proven to be catastrophic, with all sorts of unintended consequences," he said.
"If Israel or the United States did decide to resume a major escalation, for reasons of Israel's election or our elections, I fear that we would just see even more unintended consequences of the tragic sort that we've been seeing for the past six months."
Gordon's criticism of Trump: A year of missed opportunities in Gaza
Toward the end of the interview, Gordon turned his criticism toward Trump's handling of Gaza during the first year of his administration.
The January 2025 hostage and ceasefire agreement, Gordon argued, had created an opportunity to put Gaza on a different trajectory: bring home the remaining hostages, preserve the ceasefire, establish a new governing arrangement, and begin reconstruction for Palestinians.
Instead, he said, that opportunity was squandered.
"Once we finally got the deal in January 2025, that was an opportunity to at least start putting it on the right path, get all the hostages out, have a ceasefire, a different government in Gaza, and rebuild for Palestinians," Gordon said.
"But instead, Israel broke the ceasefire in March. Trump did nothing about that," he argued.
According to Gordon, a complete blockade on food, water, and medicine followed for two months, dramatically worsening an already severe humanitarian crisis.
He contended that Trump did not begin applying serious pressure for a renewed ceasefire until after Israel struck Doha later that year.
"Trump sometimes gets credit for getting the ceasefire and the 20-point plan in place, and give him credit for that, fine," Gordon said.
"I think it's obviously a good thing that the ceasefire was achieved, and there's a path forward in Gaza."
But he argued that the administration's earlier inaction should not be forgotten.
"People shouldn't forget that it took a year, including turning a blind eye to a complete blockade of Gaza that severely deteriorated the humanitarian situation, and then the entire summer before he got motivated," Gordon said.
"And that was again only after Israel struck in Doha."
For Gordon, the criticism of Netanyahu, Biden and Trump is part of the same broader argument: The Gaza war presented extraordinarily difficult choices, but he believes opportunities to end the fighting and secure the release of hostages were repeatedly missed.
Now, he warns, Israel faces another formidable challenge: Rebuilding the trust and standing it has lost among the American public.
"With work on both sides, maybe it can be repaired," Gordon said.
"But I don't think anybody should underestimate the challenge."

articles.title: Iran is at the breaking point – the regime’s greatest fear is what comes next - opinion
articles.body:
A nation of 90 million is watching its homeland being impoverished, terrorized, plundered, and driven toward the abyss by a ruling cult that would sooner destroy Iran than relinquish power.
For nearly half a century, the Islamic Republic has consumed the country it claims to govern – its wealth, dignity, security, and the hopes of generations. Now, as economic collapse, repression and the specter of war converge, Iran is approaching a historic breaking point: Will the regime that has held it captive since 1979 finally fall – or drag the country into the abyss with it?
Iran is engulfed in chaos, its economy already collapsing. An incompetent government, presided over by a subservient and populist president, convenes emergency meetings as the country descends deeper into crisis.
Yet Iranians no longer heed the regime’s deceptive promises. The government has lost its grip on the economy and inflation, while Tehran’s markets spiral into turmoil. Officials’ hollow pronouncements and empty assurances no longer command the slightest credibility.
Only the regime’s loyalists profit from the status quo, prepared to watch Iran be destroyed for their financial interests. This same circle has pillaged the country from end to end. Poverty and relentless inflation have brought Iran to its knees.
Iran’s regime prepares for a broader war
Since 1979, a criminal cult has ravaged, plundered, and suppressed the country in service of a fraudulent ideology, holding 90 million people captive. Its rulers now proclaim themselves “the superpower of the world,” boast of having “defeated America and Israel,” and warn that “the region will not be safe as long as even one American soldier remains in the Middle East.”
From state media to Friday-prayer pulpits, regime platforms threaten US President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, while Islamic murderers and criminals relentlessly inflame hostility toward Israel and the United States.
The Islamic Republic is preparing for a broader war and has no desire for an agreement with Trump. Through deception and duplicity, it keeps him entangled in diplomacy and proclaims that deception a victory. The regime will not hand Trump the political triumph of an agreement, even at the price of every Iranian’s life and Iran itself reduced to scorched earth.
Iran’s military and security establishment remains committed to warmongering and crisis-making. Trump says Washington does not know whom to talk to in Iran. Then what purpose is served by this hollow theater of negotiations with Islamic murderers and terrorists? Six years of his presidency have pursued this impossible dream without producing a single signed agreement.
Meanwhile, Iranians live with profound insecurity, despair, and abandonment. Executions, torture, arrests, and persecution have become grim fixtures of ordinary life. The struggle for basic subsistence has left society paralyzed, angry, and exhausted. While ordinary citizens are denied prosperity and opportunity, money continues flowing to notorious religious institutions, the shadowy Shi’ite clerical mafia, the machinery of repression, and the regime’s vast propaganda apparatus.
The regime is releasing criminals from prison, arming them with swords, knives, and sledgehammers, and unleashing them to threaten Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi, the only alternative and leader of Iran’s national uprising – including explicit threats against his life.
Alongside the regime stands a jealous, ambitious, and self-aggrandizing opposition: religious-nationalists, reformists, communists, Kurdish separatists (KDPI, Komala), anti-Israel and anti-American terrorists such as the Mujahedin-e Khalq (MEK), discredited human-rights activists, and mercenaries. Much of this opposition acts in concert, little more than puppets performing before cameras.
In the event of an American and Israeli attack, the regime intends to drag Iran into civil war and reactivate Islamic terrorist networks through the mosques. Its organic relationship with al-Qaeda and ISIS is becoming increasingly unmistakable, while Iran’s borders remain open to them. Hashd al-Shaabi, the Fatemiyoun, the Zainabiyoun, and others are integral components of the Islamic Republic’s machinery of repression.
The regime’s propaganda apparatus promotes weapons training, as though a regime nearing collapse is preparing its supporters for urban warfare. Under the banner of confronting America and Israel, it provides military training with an unmistakable objective: to bring war into Iran’s cities, streets, and alleyways. Islamic terrorists know neither peace nor the value of life and security.
Across Iranian cities, the atmosphere is increasingly one of war. People whisper: Will Trump launch the final attack? The country hangs like a pendulum in uncertainty, with law and order unraveling. The mullahs intensify street propaganda to drown out protest, yet a national uprising looms. The regime calls participants in its street spectacles – its “Islam Party” – fedayeen, echoing the political theater of Saddam Hussein and Muammar Gaddafi.
The Revolutionary Guards and security officials squander their days in endless meetings, terrified by the deepening crisis and sheltering behind a bankrupt, discredited government. Agriculture, industry, and production have ground to a halt. There is no coherent plan to regain control. The regime’s security calculations are unraveling.
Iranians await another war in the hope that the bloodthirsty wolf of the Islamic Republic will finally be brought down. They hope Trump will finish the job – or allow Israel to eliminate the regime’s thugs and criminals, layer by layer.
Meanwhile, the regime intensifies killings and executions, hoping to prevent economic misery, relentless inflation, soaring prices, and mounting social anguish from erupting into the “final battle.” Iran is passing through fateful days as urban repression intensifies. The regime’s ultimate nightmare is a popular uprising. A regime that kills its own people for daring to protest will stop at no crime to preserve its rule.
And yet, behind every headline about war, sanctions, missiles, and nuclear negotiations lies another Iran – the Iran of ordinary people who simply want to live. They want to raise their children without fear, put food on the table, walk their streets without repression, speak without looking over their shoulders, and grow old in the country they love.
For nearly half a century, generations of Iranians have watched their lives disappear into prisons, graves, exile, poverty, and shattered dreams. They are not asking the world to give them a country. They already have one – an ancient and beloved homeland called Iran.
They are asking for the chance to take it back. Ninety million people have waited long enough. In memory of the 50,000 slaughtered in Tehran’s streets by the Shi’ite mullahs and IRGC thugs, who cried out, “This is the final battle – Pahlavi will return!” Iran deserves to live again. “Make Iran Great Again!”
Let us hope Washington has the resolve and unwavering will to make it happen.
The writer is a Middle East political analyst. His latest book, Tehran’s Dictator, examines the theocratic era of Ali Khamenei (1989-2026). @EQFard

articles.title: Riyadh vows response to airport attack, Yemen strike reported
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia on Sunday extended the closure of the country’s main international airport, according to an online flight tracker, a day after a missile attack on the facility killed 12 people from several countries and left more than 300 injured in a major escalation of the war between Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis and the kingdom.
Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis claimed responsibility in a televised speech for Saturday’s attack on Riyadh's international airport that killed 12 people and wounded more than 300 others.
Yemen's Houthis on Sunday renewed their warning to airlines, airport workers, and travellers against using Saudi airports, saying the warning should be taken seriously and that the kingdom "bore responsibility for failed interceptions".
Algeria arrests 61 Moroccans accused of planning 'sabotage'
Algerian authorities announced on Sunday that they had arrested 61 Moroccan nationals earlier this month on suspicion of planning "acts of sabotage".
In a statement carried by public media, the General Directorate of National Security (DGSN) referred to "an international Moroccan criminal network" but did not provide details of the alleged plots.
The 61 people, including a former soldier in the Moroccan army, "were preparing to commit acts of sabotage undermining security and public order", the DGSN said.
It added that the suspects had entered Algeria via mountain trails from neighbouring Tunisia.
Relations between Algeria and Morocco have been strained for years, and their shared land border has been closed since 1994. In 2021, Algiers decided to sever diplomatic relations.
FAA tells US airlines to exercise caution in Saudi flights
The Federal Aviation Administration on Sunday told US airlines to exercise caution when flying to or over Saudi Arabia, citing safety threats tied to ongoing military activities and navigation system interference.
The FAA Notice to Airmen, which lasts until December 10, follows strikes Saturday and Sunday on Riyadh's international airport. The attack on Saturday killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.
"Threats could pose a potential risk to aircraft at all altitudes, including overflight, the arrival, and departure phases of flight," the FAA said.
Saudi Arabia signs energy deals with Kuwait, Qatar, Egypt
Saudi Arabia's energy minister signed three memorandums of understanding with Kuwait, Qatar and Egypt to strengthen energy cooperation, the Saudi state news agency said on Sunday.
The agreement with Qatar sets a framework for collaboration in petroleum, natural gas and petrochemicals, including exploring joint opportunities to develop pipelines for transport and exports.
Syria issues first letter of credit for Saudi Aramco deal
Syria's central bank said on Sunday it had issued its first letter of credit in 14 years to facilitate a petroleum products supply deal between the Syrian Petroleum Company and Saudi Aramco.
The bank said the transaction was arranged in coordination with a major US bank, which it did not name, opening a channel to finance oil imports and settle payments through the formal banking system.
The move marks a step toward restoring Syria's access to international banking channels following the removal of US sanctions and its designation as a state sponsor of terrorism.
At least two killed in south Lebanon amid Israeli attacks
Two men were killed in south Lebanon on Sunday, one by Israeli fire and the other by an explosive remnant of war, as they took part in the annual olive harvest, according to state media and local officials.
South Lebanon has been the scene of two wars since 2023 between Israel and Hezbollah, and Israeli troops still occupy a band of territory 10 kilometres (six miles) wide running along the border.
The official National News Agency (NNA) said one of the men was killed in Yater, in Bint Jbeil district, when Israeli "shelling targeted the outskirts of the town while he was inspecting his land and olive harvest".
Two Indian sailors missing after vessel attacked off Oman
Two Indian sailors were missing after a commercial vessel was hit by a "drone attack" Sunday off the coast of Oman, New Delhi's shipping minister said.
Shipping minister Sarbananda Sonowal said the tanker MT Petro Dolphin, with 11 Indian seafarers on board, was attacked at the anchorage area for the port of Sohar in northern Oman.
"While nine of our Indian crew members have been successfully rescued and are safe, two Indian nationals currently remain missing," he said on X.
Sonowal said search and rescue operations by local authorities was underway.

articles.body:
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said an "unidentified projectile" had targeted Riyadh's international airport on Sunday, causing a fire, hours after the Iran-backed Houthis warned airlines and travelers to stay away from Saudi airports.
The coalition also said Saudi air defenses had intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of King Khalid International Airport. No further details were immediately available.
The airport remains closed after an attack there on Saturday killed 12 people and wounded more than 300 others, the deadliest such strike on the kingdom in over a decade, amid an escalation of fighting between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces.
The Indian Embassy in Riyadh confirmed on Sunday that one of the 12 killed in Saturday's strike was an Indian national.
Despite the airport's temporary closure, the Saudi Energy Ministry said a long-planned international energy conference was still going ahead in Riyadh on Sunday.
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said Sunday's projectile had targeted Terminal 4 of the airport, without elaborating.
Earlier, the Houthis had said in a statement on X:
"We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travelers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theater of operations for our forces, with the exception of the airports in (the holy cities of) Mecca and Medina."
"We urge everyone to take our warnings seriously, and Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions."
Houthis warn, 'Worse is yet to come,'
Saudi Arabia has stepped up its military involvement in Yemen in recent weeks, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a Yemeni government counteroffensive after the group seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month.
Yemen's Houthi-run foreign ministry said later on Sunday that further Saudi military action in Yemen would trigger a stronger response, adding that its actions would be guided by the principle of reciprocity.
"Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing," the ministry said in statements carried by Houthi-run Al Masirah television.
President Donald Trump said on Saturday the United States was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover from the wider war on Iran that the US and Israel launched in February.

A five-day WPC Energy Congress is taking place this week at a convention center some 10 km (6 miles) from the airport. State TV said more than 70 ministers, 300 company executives and representatives of over 25 international energy organizations had confirmed their attendance.
It was not immediately clear whether the participants would attend in person or virtually.
A ministerial meeting of the International Energy Forum is also set to go ahead on Sunday, with its plenary session to be held behind closed doors, according to a media advisory. No further details were immediately available.
Separately, Saudi authorities notified parents that in-person classes would be suspended and shifted to remote learning from Sunday until Thursday for all students, teachers and administrative staff.
In Saturday's attack, the third on Riyadh's airport in a week, the 12 dead included 4 Saudis, 2 Bangladeshis and nationals of the United States, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, Saudi authorities said.
Four people were killed in the two previous attacks on the airport earlier in the week. One of the attacks also caused heavy damage to a Saudi commercial plane parked on the tarmac.

articles.title: Oval Office spat to public rebukes: A timeline of Trump-Zelenskyy ties
articles.body:
Oval Office spat to public rebukes: A timeline of Trump-Zelenskyy ties
Trump has long criticised US military support for Ukraine and has lambasted Zelenskyy since his first term.
United States President Donald Trump has called for the removal of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy after blaming the Ukrainian leader for rising diesel prices, which have put pressure on the Republican Party ahead of the November midterm elections.
The criticism on Saturday came as tensions between the US and Ukraine have increased after Trump announced a diesel supply deal with Russia.
“I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” Trump told reporters at the White House on Saturday, saying Zelenskyy had hurt global diesel supplies with strikes on Russian refineries.
“He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers with diesel fuel because Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel throughout the world,” Trump added.
Zelenskyy on Sunday pushed back, vowing to continue striking Russian oil refineries. “Ukraine will be ready to stop striking Russian oil refineries if Russia stops striking our energy infrastructure,” Zelenskyy wrote on X.
“It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but (Russian President Vladimir) Putin does not want to do so,” he said.
This is not the first time Trump has lambasted Zelenskyy. Their tense relationship goes back to Trump’s first term as president, when he pressured Zelenskyy to investigate his rival, Joe Biden, and his son, Hunter Biden.
Here’s a timeline of some of the occasions when Trump has been critical of Zelenskyy:
October 2026: In his remarks at the White House, Trump criticised Zelenskyy over the lack of a peace deal while demanding an end to Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities.
“I said to him, ‘Do what you want. Don’t hit refineries. There’s plenty of targets. Don’t hit refineries.’ And he went out and he hit,” Trump said. “He better damn well stop.”
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals, but for some reason, he never does,” Trump added.
Trump, who has been urging Zelenskyy to stop attacking Russian energy infrastructure for weeks, struck a deal with Putin on Friday to buy diesel from Russia in an attempt to reduce high fuel prices.
The deal marked a stunning reversal of years of Washington’s pressure on Russia over its full scale invasion of Ukraine.
Zelenskyy, meanwhile, said every additional $1bn Russia earns from exports would help pay for weapons components, drone upgrades, missile production and the recruitment of mercenaries.
Moscow would only be ready to stop when its ability to fight diminished, he added.
April 2025: On April 15 , Trump criticised Zelenskyy and implied Kyiv had started the war against Russia, saying the Ukrainian leader was “always looking to purchase” US missiles. “You don’t start a war against someone 20 times your size and hope people give you some missiles,” Trump said.
Then on April 23 , he criticised Zelenskyy for making “very harmful” statements after the Ukrainian president pushed back against the idea of ceding occupied Crimea to Russia in a potential peace deal.
Zelenskyy had ruled out ceding any territory, declaring, “There is nothing to talk about – it is our land, the land of the Ukrainian people”.
In a post on his social media platform, Trump accused Zelenskyy of stoking tension by “boasting” that Kyiv would not legally recognise ceding Crimea to Russia.
“This statement is very harmful to the Peace Negotiations with Russia,” Trump said, adding that Russia invaded the Crimean Peninsula and annexed it back in 2014 “without a shot being fired”.
“It’s inflammatory statements like Zelenskyy’s that makes it so difficult to settle this War,” Trump said. “He can have Peace or, he can fight for another three years before losing the whole Country.”
Despite the tension, the two leaders held a private meeting at the Vatican on April 26, 2025, during Pope Francis’s funeral.
Feb 28, 2025: During their fiery Oval Office meeting, Trump and Vice President JD Vance clashed with Zelenskyy over rare earth mineral agreements, security assurances and peace negotiations with Russia.
Trump warned Zelenskyy, “You’re either going to make a deal [on ending the war with Russia] or we’re out,” and accused the Ukrainian leader of having “disrespected” the United States and “overplayed his hand”.
The US president and Vance also berated Zelenskyy for lacking gratitude and refusing to compromise to end the war, with Trump arguing that Zelenskyy was unready for peace.
The meeting devolved into a shouting match and Zelenskyy departed the White House abruptly.
February 19, 2025: A month after returning to power for a second term, Trump called the Ukrainian president a “dictator without elections” and accused him of wanting to keep the “gravy train” of US military support going while Washington tries to end the war with Russia.
In a lengthy and scathing post on his social media platform Truth Social, Trump accused Zelenskyy of taking US money and embroiling the country in an endless conflict.
He later doubled down on those comments, telling an audience at an investment summit in Miami that Zelenskyy had “done a terrible job, his country is shattered, and millions and millions of people have unnecessarily died”.
“A dictator without elections. Zelenskyy better move fast or he’s not going to have a country left. Gotta move. Gotta move fast cause that war’s going in the wrong direction,” Trump said on stage at the Future Investment Initiative (FII) Institute summit.
“In the meantime, we’re successfully negotiating an end to the war with Russia. Something I’ll admit that only Trump is going to be able to do and the Trump administration – we’re going to be able to do it. I think Putin even admitted that,” he said.
“Biden never tried. Europe has failed to bring peace and Zelenskyy probably wants to, maybe he wants to keep the gravy train going. I don’t know what’s the problem, but he has been able. He’s very upset,” he added.
Trump had been critical of Biden’s financial and military support to Ukraine during the war. He had vowed to end the war within 24 hours of his taking office, but later said he was being “sarcastic”.
2024 Campaign trail: On the 2024 US presidential election campaign trail, Trump repeatedly criticised Zelenskyy for not trying hard enough to end Russia’s war on Ukraine. In September, at an election rally speech in North Carolina, Trump lashed out at Zelenskyy for refusing to negotiate, stating that even the “worst deal” or giving up a small amount of territory would be better than ongoing death and destruction.
July 2019: During his first term, Trump repeatedly urged Zelenskyy to work with Rudy Giuliani and the US attorney general to investigate Democratic political rival Joe Biden. That is according to a five-page memo summarising the July 25 call.
At the time of the call, the Trump administration was also withholding from Ukraine nearly $400m in congressionally approved security assistance, prompting speculation the US president was using the money as leverage to get his desired investigations.
Zelenskyy expressed willingness to look into new cases and cooperate with US investigations, though he and Ukrainian officials later maintained they did not feel directly threatened or pressured during the conversation itself.

articles.title: Pentagon raises US-Iran war toll to 21 killed, over 800 wounded
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Pentagon raises US-Iran war toll to 21 killed, over 800 wounded
The US Department of War has raised the death toll of US personnel in its war on Iran to 21 killed and 865 wounded in an acknowledgement that losses faced during the conflict were greater than previously admitted.
The Pentagon added two non-combatant deaths, including one Major who died in Kuwait on 6 March and a Navy suicide from September, according to The Washington Post.
The publication previously reported in September that the department's internal figures counted 23 service members as having died since the start of the war on 28 February.
The admission is a firm rebuttal of Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, who previously labelled the reporting of a higher death toll as “a complete lie", as well as a correction of previous reporting by the Pentagon, which has underreported the toll since the start of the war due to Trump's own claims that the war has ended.
In a bid to mark deaths in the region tied to continued war with Iran, the department created a new category for those killed after Trump’s declaration.
The Pentagon told The Post in a statement that, rather than correcting its own figures, it is making revisions to how it reports casualties.
The number of US casualties in its war on Iran have been contentious, with US media outlets revealing larger casualty figures than admitted to by the Pentagon throughout the war.
Despite US and Israeli airpower decapitating Iran's leadership and destroying vast swathes of Iranian military assets, Iran's quick response saw ballistic missiles and drones targeting US bases, alongside Iran's Gulf neighbours and Israel.
Iranian attacks on US bases have left the 5th Fleet headquarters in Bahrain and Al Udeid Air Base, the largest US airbase in the region, severely damaged.
Iranian attacks also damaged or destroyed US radar used to track ballistic missiles and aircraft on the ground.
The extent of the damage has led the Department of War to mull pulling troops and withdrawing from bases in the Gulf.
However, in recent weeks, Trump ordered new plans to be drawn up for renewed strikes against Iran, as negotiatons between the two reach an impasse.

articles.title: How Israel's pager operation shattered Nasrallah’s aura of invincibility - opinion
articles.body:
The second anniversary of the pager operation is a reminder that the first thing to explode on September 17, 2024, was not thousands of small devices. It was the carefully cultivated aura of invulnerability that Hassan Nasrallah had built around himself.
For years, the Hezbollah leader had appeared from his hideout, boasting about missiles, tunnels, and “surprises,” asking the Lebanese to believe that his disappearance was strategic brilliance. The terrorist group could see without being seen, strike without being touched.
Then an old-fashioned device exposed the reality. The organization that had cowed Lebanon through fear had been compromised through its own supply chain. Its leader, who threatened to bury his enemies, did not know his men were carrying booby-trapped devices.
This was not simply an intelligence coup worthy of a spy thriller. Israeli intelligence had constructed a false reality in which Hezbollah operated with complete confidence. Public investigations and the book In the War Room trace the idea’s origins to 2002-2006, during Meir Dagan’s tenure.
Around 2014, Mossad and Israeli military intelligence began introducing wireless devices into Hezbollah’s network, monitoring them while retaining the option of detonation. In 2022, they turned to pagers: devices operatives would carry rather than leave in an office or warehouse.
Front companies, licensing arrangements, dummy websites, and stores gave a battery unavailable on the open market a convincing commercial identity. A Taiwanese brand and a supply chain stretching from Hungary to Hong Kong supplied the cover. The Mossad did not simply intercept a shipment. It created the product, marketed it, built its reputation, and cut the price until Hezbollah’s procurement officials chose the trap themselves.
This was the difference between penetrating an organization and shaping the choices it believed were its own. The procurement process offered the appearance of control while delivering precisely what the adversary wanted.
They thought they were vetting a product. In reality, the product was exposing the organization.
Explosives were built into the batteries
A Reuters investigation found that explosives and a concealed detonator were built into the battery, allowing the devices to pass Hezbollah’s security checks. Even when officials noticed that batteries drained faster than advertised, distribution continued.
The message and alert were designed to make recipients bring the device toward their faces and use both hands. The alert tone and explosive charge had been tested to produce the intended response. The Mossad had choreographed the movements of those carrying its bombs.
The bitterest irony was that Nasrallah himself helped the operation. In February 2024, he called mobile phones more dangerous than spies and urged his men to smash them, bury them, or lock them in metal boxes. Hezbollah accelerated its adoption of pagers. His warning did not create the operation, but it drove more men toward the prepared device. The leadership’s fear had become a predictable procurement decision. Hezbollah had chosen its own poisoned remedy.
I see something deeper here than a procurement mistake. An entire security doctrine collapsed: secrecy supposedly meant switching off a phone, while the enemy was manufacturing the alternative.
At 3:30 p.m. on September 17, the devices began to ring. Roughly 3,000 exploded. The next day came the wireless devices, some held by Hezbollah for nearly a decade. Dozens were killed and more than 3,400 wounded. Devices had been distributed among fighters, commanders, support personnel, and affiliated medics. The penetration even reached Iran’s ambassador. The target was the infrastructure that enabled an Iranian-backed militia to operate as a state within Lebanon.
More important, in my view, was the assault on trust. Anyone still carrying a device had reason to fear its battery. Those who watched colleagues fall simultaneously understood that the enemy had helped build the walls behind which they sheltered. The equipment meant to connect the organization had become a source of fear. Replacing it could restore communication, but could not erase the discovery that trusted channels had carried the enemy inside.
Two former Mossad officers described the intended psychological impact. Wafiq Safa, a close Nasrallah associate, later recounted that the attacks left him deeply shaken and barely eating for almost a day. The man who had spent his life instilling fear in the Lebanese discovered, days before his death, that fear had reached his own hideout.
The operation also opened a military campaign. On September 20, Ibrahim Aqil and Radwan Force commanders were killed. Strikes expanded to weapons depots, facilities, and positions. On September 27, Nasrallah was killed beneath the headquarters he had regarded as an impregnable fortress.
Intelligence derives its real power from turning secrets into paralysis and confusion at the moment military force can exploit them. Without the subsequent strikes, the explosions would have remained an extraordinary intelligence feat. Their succession made the operation the opening phase of a broader dismantling.
Nasrallah had built his authority on the belief that obscurity proved knowledge, disappearance meant immunity, and questioning the leadership betrayed resistance. The farther he withdrew, the more formidable he appeared. Secrecy became wisdom beyond scrutiny.
The pagers exposed what that mythology concealed. His disappearance was isolation. His secrecy hid ignorance of what entered his warehouses. His speeches promised deterrence while his security apparatus was already penetrated.
That is the weakness of closed ideological organizations. They confuse loyalty with competence and treat questions as betrayal. Eventually, the leader’s word becomes a vulnerability no one dares challenge. A professional intelligence service could engineer the environment around its target; a terrorist militia had mistaken suspicion and obedience for security.
Two years later, Hezbollah can buy devices, change intermediaries, and rebuild parts of its network. It cannot turn the clock back to before the first ring.
The militia that claimed to protect Lebanon could not even protect its own supply chain. The leader who threatened to bury his enemies was himself buried beneath the concrete, along with the project he had built. And the Shi’ite community asked to believe in divine protection saw that an aura of sanctity could neither stop a signal nor reveal a compromised battery.
The most devastating part was that Hezbollah’s own leadership had led its men, step by step, to the very tool Israel designed to reach them. In doing so, it shattered the image of Nasrallah as an infallible leader.
The writer is a UAE political analyst and former Federal National Council candidate.

articles.title: Saudis might step up strikes on Houthis even further after airport attack, experts tell 'Post'
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia is unlikely to back down in the face of the Houthis following an attack on Riyadh’s airport that killed 12 people and wounded 309, with the kingdom likely stepping up its military campaign against the Iran-backed terror group, regional experts told The Jerusalem Post.
The attack, which marked a significant escalation in the Houthis’ campaign against Saudi Arabia, has exposed the kingdom’s vulnerability to strikes against civilian infrastructure. Bernard Haykel, a senior fellow at the Foundation for the Defense of Democracies (FDD), said Saudi Arabia had long understood the Houthis’ ability to carry out such attacks, particularly with what he described as support from Iran and Iraqi Shiite militias.
“My sense is that they’re not going to buckle. They’re not going to just capitulate to the Houthis because of this,” he explained.
Haykel said Riyadh now faces a choice between reaching an accommodation with the Houthis or intensifying its military campaign against them, adding that he expects the Saudis will pursue the latter course and rely more heavily on Yemeni forces opposed to the group.
“I think that they’re going to ramp up against the Houthis,” he said.
The attack comes as Saudi Arabia faces the consequences of a broader regional conflict that Riyadh had sought to avoid. According to Haykel, Saudi leaders opposed the war against Iran and made considerable efforts to prevent it, but now recognize that they will have to bear some of its costs.
“They realize that they have to pay a price,” he said.
Former ambassador says attack shocked Saudis
Michael Ratney, former US Ambassador to Saudi Arabia and senior advisor at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), said the scale and audacity of the attack had shocked the Saudis, even though they were familiar with the Houthis’ military capabilities.
Ratney noted that the Houthis had already carried out several strikes against airports, including in Riyadh, during the preceding week, while the latest was the most serious of those incidents. “I think they were shocked, but in a way understood that this is what the Houthis are all about,” Ratney explained.
He identified the targeting of civilian airports as a particularly significant escalation. In the past, the Houthis had generally focused on military installations and energy infrastructure, including Saudi military bases and energy facilities.
“For them to target civilian airports with the expectation of civilian casualties is really a new escalation for the Houthis,” Ratney said.
The attacks put Riyadh in a difficult position as it seeks to achieve its military objectives in Yemen without triggering a wider escalation that could expose additional Saudi infrastructure to retaliation.
Ratney said Saudi Arabia’s immediate military priority was to help the Yemeni army retake positions along the coast near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait that the Houthis had seized the previous month.
“They’re determined to get the Houthis off of the Bab el-Mandeb,” he said, adding that Riyadh would probably then look for a way to de-escalate the conflict.
Riyadh growing concerns over lack of American assistance
Both experts pointed to Riyadh's concerns about the limits of American military assistance, especially as Washington deploys forces and resources across the region.
Haykel said Saudi Arabia was disappointed that the United States was not better prepared to help defend the kingdom against attacks from the Houthis and Iran, particularly given the potential shortage of missile-defense systems.
“I think there’s disappointment that the Americans are not better prepared and better able to help in fighting the Houthis and the Iranians,” he said.
At the same time, Haykel said Saudi leaders understand that American military power has limits, particularly when US forces are already heavily committed across the Persian Gulf.
Ratney said the United States was providing some assistance behind the scenes, including intelligence sharing, targeting and operational planning. But he added that Riyadh would prefer more direct American involvement in airstrikes.
“Clearly what they would like is US support on airstrikes, and I think there is some frustration,” he said.
The attack could influence Washington’s willingness to provide more overt military support, Ratney said, although he cautioned that Trump’s response was difficult to predict.
Still, Ratney said neither Saudi Arabia nor the United States appeared eager to escalate the conflict further.
Saudis worried about further strikes on civilian infrastructure
The concern is that intensifying military operations against Iran or the Houthis could provoke disproportionate retaliation, with civilian infrastructure rather than military targets bearing the consequences.
“None of them really want to escalate at this point because they see the result,” Ratney said.
The attack also raises questions about whether Israel could play a greater role in helping Saudi Arabia counter the Houthi threat, given Israel’s experience confronting Iranian-backed groups and its advanced intelligence and air-defense capabilities.
“The political risk of that outweighs any kind of military benefits that they might derive,” Ratney said, explaining that Saudi leaders are reluctant to see Israeli politicians publicly highlight or take credit for cooperation between the two countries.
Haykel was more skeptical about Israel’s ability to deliver a decisive military blow against the Houthis, particularly through intelligence-led operations targeting the group’s leadership.
He said Israel had developed extensive intelligence capabilities against Hezbollah in Lebanon, allowing it to target the organization’s senior figures and commanders. He does not believe Israel currently possesses a comparable level of intelligence on the Houthis in Yemen.
“If the Israelis had the intelligence on the Houthis to, say, destroy the leadership of the Houthis and the second-, third-tier commanders, you know, what they did to Hezbollah, basically, if they could do that in Yemen, that would be an incredible service and help in this war,” Haykel said.
For Riyadh, the immediate challenge remains how to deter further Houthi attacks without becoming trapped in another prolonged and costly conflict in Yemen. Both experts agree that it will be hard.

articles.title: US explores Israeli strikes on Yemen's Houthis; IDF chief warns of election delay
articles.body:
Contrary to a report that American officials had asked Israel to carry out strikes against Iran, the United States instead explored with IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir whether Israel could conduct strikes against Houthi targets in Yemen, amid escalating fighting between the rebels and Saudi Arabia and deadly missile attacks on Riyadh's international airport.
Dramatic footage published Sunday shows the moment of Saturday's missile strike on King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital, which killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300 others.
The Americans are seeking to avoid direct involvement in the escalating crisis, with the US midterm elections scheduled for next month. Zamir warned his American counterparts that an Israeli strike could trigger further escalation with the Houthis and potentially with Iran. He also cautioned that such a development could lead to the indefinite postponement of Israel's elections, currently scheduled for October 27.
In a conversation between Zamir and the commander of US Central Command (CENTCOM), Adm. Brad Cooper, the two also discussed the possibility of future strikes against Iran. However, their talks did not involve concrete plans for military action in the immediate future.
Both the Israeli Air Force and the IDF's Military Intelligence Directorate remain on constant alert for possible escalation with Iran, which is still considered Israel's primary military front.
The Israeli and American militaries have maintained close coordination in recent months, continuing the cooperation established following the declaration of a ceasefire and the conclusion of Operation Roaring Lion in April.
Meanwhile, the IDF's Military Intelligence Directorate is working to build an extensive target bank in Iran, covering missile capabilities, strike systems, military buildup and facilities connected to the Iranian nuclear program. The IDF Spokesperson's Unit declined to comment.
Just over a week ago, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned during a visit to the Tel Nof Air Base that Israel's enemies might attempt to launch attacks ahead of the upcoming elections.
"There are signs that our enemies will try to attack us ahead of the elections," Netanyahu said. "From here, from the Air Force base, from the long arm of the State of Israel, I am sending you a message: Don't mess with us, not now and not ever. Our long arm will reach you anywhere, anytime."

articles.title: What the Iran war has done to the world’s energy supply, in charts
articles.body:
What the Iran war has done to the world’s energy supply, in charts
Fossil fuels produce 81 percent of global energy. We look at the Middle East’s role and what happens when supplies are cut.
A major energy conference is going ahead in Riyadh from Sunday despite a Houthi attack on the city’s King Khalid International Airport that killed 12 people and injured 309, according to Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation.
Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Energy said on Sunday that the 25th World Petroleum Council Energy Congress has begun in Riyadh. The 17th International Energy Forum (IEF) Ministerial will be held on the sidelines of the conference, called Riyadh Energy Week, which is to run until Thursday.
But Italy, the cohost of the IEF, will join the meeting via videolink. Nigeria, the other cohost, is sending a representative to the event.
The IEF brings together 68 countries that account for more than 90 percent of global oil and gas supplies and demand. Its members include Saudi Arabia, the United States and Russia. The meeting comes as the US-Israel war on Iran has disrupted energy flows and pushed governments to reassess their energy security.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera looks at where the world’s energy comes from, how much is produced in the Middle East and which countries have strategic reserves to fall back on.
Where does the world’s energy come from?
Energy heats our homes, fuels our cars, keeps the lights on and runs the factories that make what we buy. It comes from fossil fuels such as oil, coal and gas as well as nuclear power and renewables.
Despite rapid growth in renewables, fossil fuels still account for nearly 81 percent of global energy consumption. Oil is the largest source at 31.4 percent, followed by coal at 25.9 percent and natural gas at 23.5 percent. Traditional biomass, nuclear power and other sources make up the rest.
Production is concentrated in a handful of regions, so disruptions in any of them ripple through global markets.
The Middle East is the largest oil-producing region, and North America is the largest natural gas producer. Russia and Central Asia are also major producers of both.
How Middle East energy reaches the world
The Middle East’s importance to energy markets is also about geography. Three narrow waterways connect its producers with consumers around the world.
Before the Iran war, about 27 percent of global seaborne oil trade and almost 20 percent of liquefied natural gas trade transited through the Strait of Hormuz on the eastern side of the Arabian Peninsula.
On the peninsula’s western side, the Bab al-Mandeb strait links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, and the Suez Canal connects the Red Sea with the Mediterranean. As the Iran war has spilled over into other areas of the Middle East and Yemen’s civil war has ramped up, traffic has been reduced through both the strait and canal, forcing some energy shipments on longer routes around Africa.
“That’s probably the first time we’ve really seen a major constriction of a chokepoint,” said Richard Matthews, director of consultancy and research at Gibson Shipbrokers, a London-based shipbroking and maritime advisory service.
He told Al Jazeera that what makes the Strait of Hormuz different from other chokepoints is “there is no alternative maritime route. There are some pipelines, but there’s no alternative, which is why it’s been so significant in terms of cargo volume.”
Gulf ports are where much of the region’s energy begins its journey to the rest of the world.
Which countries rely most on Middle East oil?
Further down the supply chain, people and businesses are feeling the disruption through the rising cost of essentials.
Countries that rely on oil, gas and fertiliser from the Gulf face higher prices, longer waits for shipments and the need to find other suppliers. Even where deals have kept goods moving, the extra costs are being passed down the chain.
Eritrea and Madagascar are the most dependent on Middle Eastern oil, each sourcing about 90 percent of their supply from the region. They are followed by Pakistan (78 percent), Japan (77 percent) and Kenya (77 percent).
Which countries rely most on Middle East gas?
Gas has been even harder to replace than oil because most of it travels as liquefied natural gas from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates through the Strait of Hormuz.
Countries that depend on these shipments are paying more for fuel and electricity and competing for a smaller pool of cargoes. Poorer importers with little storage have struggled the most to find alternatives.
The countries that rely most heavily on Middle Eastern gas are mostly in Asia. South Korea sources 31 percent of the gas it uses from the region, followed by India (29 percent), Pakistan (27 percent) and Taiwan (26 percent).
Who has the largest emergency oil reserves?
Countries keep emergency oil stocks for when supplies are cut off or reduced, and these have been the world’s main cushion during the war. That cushion is now wearing thin.
Western countries have little left to release, energy industry leaders warned, and the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve is at its lowest level since 1982.
“Estimates suggest less than 6 billion barrels of commercial inventories remain today with the vast majority not practically available,” Amin Nasser, head of Saudi Aramco, told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London on Monday.
The International Energy Agency, which coordinates emergency stocks for its members, released a record 400 million barrels of oil in March. It is now preparing to release another 100 million barrels of crude and diesel to ease soaring diesel prices although some of this may be oil from the March release that has yet to reach the market.
A storm in the Gulf of Mexico and attacks in Saudi Arabia are now threatening supplies again, keeping oil prices above $100 a barrel.
Before this year’s releases, China held by far the largest reserves, an estimated 1.4 billion barrels, more than the rest of the list combined. The US was second with 413 million barrels, followed by Japan with 263 million.

articles.title: Trump's diesel deal with Putin: How much, how long, and will It cut prices?
articles.body:
Trump's diesel deal with Putin: How much, how long, and will It cut prices?
TEHRAN - On October 9, US President Donald Trump announced an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin for Russia to supply diesel to the US and global markets, paired with a temporary 6-month US sanctions waiver. The move is aimed at easing record-high US diesel prices weeks before the November 3 midterms. Initial volumes are modest relative to consumption, so analysts expect limited and mostly psychological price effects — unless larger follow-on deliveries materialize and Russian refineries recover.
What exactly was agreed?
Trump said the deal was reached in a phone call with Putin and described it as highly successful. In his words, "vast amounts" of fuel would flow, and he publicly thanked Putin.
Putin confirmed Russia's "readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US market and world markets."
Operationally, the agreement has two parts:
Physical volumes in phases, as outlined by Trump:
300,000+ tons immediately — roughly 2.25 million barrels
500,000 tons in November
1 million tons shortly after
3 million tons more "in a short period," conditional on the state of Russian refineries
Total nominal volume: over 4.8 million tons.
A legal window to deliver it. The US Treasury's OFAC issued a temporary general license allowing the sale, delivery, offloading and import of Russian-origin diesel. The authorization runs for about six months, until April 7, 2027, covering cargoes loaded during that window.
This is the largest fuel-related sanctions relaxation since the Ukraine war began in February 2022. Previous licenses in the context of the ongoing US-Iran conflict were typically 30-day extensions.
How big is this in market terms?
Put in context, the first shipments are small:
The US consumes about 3.6 to 3.8 million barrels of diesel per day and exports about 1.5 million barrels per day. The first 2.25-million-barrel tranche equals roughly half a day of US consumption.
Global diesel demand is around 30 million barrels per day. The early Russian volumes equal 72,000 to 124,000 barrels per day — a fraction of one percent.
The 800,000 tons expected by end-November equals about 6 million barrels, or less than two days of US use.
That is why most market analysts describe the deal as a redirection of existing flows rather than major new net supply: if Russian barrels go to the US, current buyers of Russian diesel must source from elsewhere, leaving global balances broadly unchanged.
Looking back: how did we get here?
US sanctions history: Since 2022, the US has banned imports of Russian oil and petroleum products and, together with allies, imposed price caps and shipping restrictions to limit Moscow's energy revenues.
Only three weeks before the diesel announcement, Trump signed a sweeping bipartisan sanctions law targeting Russia's oil and gas income. The new diesel license therefore represents a sharp, if temporary, reversal — a pause, not a repeal.
Russia's export position: Russia imposed its own restrictions on diesel exports in July after Ukrainian drone strikes damaged several refineries. The International Energy Agency has estimated Russian diesel output fell by about 30%.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Moscow would begin lifting those restrictions ahead of schedule starting in October, adding that the domestic market remains "fully supplied." Russian officials have framed the US deal as a normal commercial operation that also helps stabilize world markets.
Why US diesel is at record levels: Two overlapping disruptions explain the price spike:
Refinery losses in Russia from the Ukraine war, reducing global diesel availability.
Disruption around the Strait of Hormuz and Middle East refining amid the eight-month US-Iran conflict, which has raised freight, insurance and replacement costs.
The result: US average diesel hit a record $6.53 per gallon on September 22, easing only slightly to $6.28 by October 9, according to AAA. A year earlier it was about $3.68. Futures prices dipped modestly on the announcement, but pump prices did not move.
Trump had already tried domestic tools — including a proposed ban on diesel exports and authorization for off-road, tax-exempt diesel use — before turning to external supply.
Why now? The political calendar
The timing is inseparable from US domestic politics. The midterm elections are on November 3, with fuel prices and inflation ranking as voters' top economic concerns. Farm states such as Iowa have been hit particularly hard by diesel costs during harvest season.
Trump has stated the goal explicitly: lower costs for "farmers, ranchers and truckers" as his top priority. Supporters present the deal as pragmatic — using every available barrel to protect consumers. Critics in Congress, including Democrats Chuck Schumer, Jeanne Shaheen and Elizabeth Warren, as well as some Republicans such as Michael McCaul, argue it contradicts the intent of the sanctions law passed weeks earlier and provides revenue to Moscow while the Ukraine war continues.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it a "weak decision" and a "gift to Putin."
Energy analysts, regardless of political view, converge on a narrower technical point: volumes are too small to transform prices, though they could shave the peak off futures and provide localized relief on the US East Coast — New York-New Jersey and Philadelphia — where Russian-origin cargoes would most plausibly land.
What happens next? Three scenarios
Base case — partial delivery, limited price impact:
Russia delivers the first 1.8 million tons (300k + 500k + 1m tons) while keeping the conditional 3 million tons under review. Global diesel futures ease modestly, US retail diesel falls by cents, not dollars. This is the consensus among analysts at Eurasia Group, CSIS and Columbia University.
Prerequisite: Russian refineries stabilize and Hormuz-related freight costs do not worsen.
Upside case — full delivery plus refinery recovery:
If all 4.8+ million tons arrive in November-December and Russian refineries return toward normal throughput, combined with a seasonal demand softening, US diesel could retreat more meaningfully from record highs. Even then, analysts note, prices would remain far above 2025 levels because Middle East refining and shipping constraints persist.
Downside case — logistics and politics interrupt flow:
Tanker availability, insurance disputes, port restrictions, Congressional pressure, or a new escalation in either Ukraine or the Gulf could delay or shrink deliveries — particularly the conditional 3 million tons. In that case, the price effect would be almost entirely symbolic, while the political controversy would remain.
The key variable to watch is not announcements but loadings: how many vessels actually load Russian diesel in October-November, where they discharge, and whether OFAC extends or narrows the license after April 2027.
Bottom line
The agreement opens a narrow, time-limited corridor in an otherwise sanctions-constrained relationship. Economically, it is best understood as a short-term buffer — potentially helpful at the margins, but not a structural fix for a diesel market strained by two conflicts at once. Politically, it signals that in an election season, energy prices can temporarily outweigh sanctions logic.
Whether drivers feel it at the pump will depend less on diplomacy and more on refineries, tankers and the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: North Korea fires unidentified projectile into Sea of Japan: Seoul
articles.body:
South Korea has said that North Korea had fired multiple ballistic missiles into the Sea of Japan.
"Our military detected around 09:20 (0020 GMT) several ballistic missiles launched from the Pyongyang area towards the East Sea," the Joint Chiefs of Staff said in a statement, referring to the Sea of Japan.
"Our military has stepped up surveillance and vigilance against possible additional launches," it added.
The launch follows Pyongyang's test-firing of a ballistic missile earlier this month that it said incorporated artificial intelligence technology.
That missile, fired on October 3, "is capable of changing its flight orbit at a low altitude and AI was introduced into it", Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, said at the time.
Seoul days later announced the successful test of its first homegrown hypersonic glide vehicle (HGV), a weapon carried into the upper atmosphere by rocket boosters or ballistic missiles before gliding towards their targets.
South Korea's presidential office said the HGV offered "a new deterrence capability capable of striking key targets within the Korean Peninsula's operational environment".
Tensions between the two Koreas have been heightened since three South Korean soldiers were injured when two landmines detonated in the Seoul-controlled area of the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) that has served as a buffer since the 1953 armistice.
A joint Seoul-UN investigation alleged that North Korea had planted the landmines over a year ago, something Pyongyang has angrily denied.

articles.title: Republican senator says Trump diesel agreement with Russia may be illegal
articles.body:
Republican senator says Trump diesel agreement with Russia may be illegal
