US President Trump’s bid to bring down diesel prices by easing sanctions on Russia has prompted rare Republican criticism.
United States Senator Thom Tillis has questioned the legality of President Donald Trump’s decision to temporarily relax sanctions on Russian diesel, in an effort to bring down record-high fuel prices caused by the US-Israel war against Iran.
During a Sunday interview on the NBC News television show Meet the Press, Tillis argued that the sanctions relief could violate congressional law.
“I do believe there’s a legitimate case for saying the president’s not following the law,” said Tillis.
Trump’s decision has unsettled some Republican lawmakers who continue to support Ukraine in its war with Russia, which began in February 2022, after Moscow launched a full-scale invasion of the eastern European country.
Tillis warned that his vote in support of Trump’s legislative priorities would be contingent on the White House reversing course.
“If the president wants my support, which I believe he should get for funding military operations and year-end funding beyond baseline funding, I think the president needs to understand this is a problem, and I’m not the only Republican concerned with this,” Tillis said.
Tillis has become a critical voice within the Republican Party, denouncing what he sees as overreach from the Trump administration.
But his time as a senator is nearly at a close. In June 2025, Tillis announced he would not be seeking re-election in the November 3 midterm elections, after Trump threatened him with a primary challenge in his home state of North Carolina. His term ends in January.
Separately on Sunday, Tillis joined a bipartisan group of senators in issuing a letter to denounce the sanctions relief for Russia.
The group included Republicans like Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and John Curtis of Utah, as well as Democrats Jeanne Shaheen and Richard Blumenthal.
“The United States should not provide [Russian President Vladimir] Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course,” the senators wrote.
Another retiring Republican lawmaker, Representative Don Bacon, also said on Friday that “propping up Putin’s war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities”.
The pushback points to schisms within the Republican Party over Russia’s invasion.
Figures from the party’s establishment wing have generally pressed for robust support for Kyiv, while other party members have been sceptical of continued US support for Ukraine.
Trump himself has been critical of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, accusing the government in Kyiv of impeding a US-negotiated ceasefire.
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal, because he could have made many deals, and for some reason, he never does,” Trump said on Saturday. “That’s a war that should have never started, and I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
A day earlier, Trump had announced that a call with Putin had concluded with an agreement to provide 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the global marketplace, with a further 500,000 tonnes to be delivered in November.
In an interview with Fox and Friends on Sunday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent argued that the administration’s decision to ease some sanctions on Moscow was necessary to obtain relief from surging diesel prices.
“We’re going to do it with all the legal authorities we have,” Bessent said.
Analysts have said that the decision is unlikely to bring prices down in the long term. Critics like Tillis have also pointed to previous law barring the importation of Russian fuel, including a 2022 executive order.
A law signed last month — named after the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham — also prohibits US investment in the Russian energy sector.
This year’s rise in global fuel prices has largely been attributed to the US-Israel war against Iran, which began in February. As a result of that war, Iran has limited commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for the fuel trade.
Tillis pointed to those circumstances in his remarks to Meet the Press.
“ If President Trump wants to end the strain on energy supplies, number one, get things right in Iran, and number two, recognise that it was Vladimir Putin, not Zelenskyy, that started this war,” Tillis said.
“It’s Vladimir Putin who owns the responsibility for energy prices to the extent that they come from that part of the world.”
Trump’s decision also garnered international criticism, with the office of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney issuing a statement in support of Ukraine.
“This agreement is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada, and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe,” Carney’s office said in a read-out of a call on Sunday with Zelenskyy. “It will provide additional revenue for Russia and help finance its illegal, unjustifiable war against Ukraine.”

articles.title: Netanyahu condemns deadly Saudi airport attack: ‘On behalf of Israelis, I offer condolences’
articles.body:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu issued an unusual public condemnation on Sunday of a deadly missile attack on Saudi Arabia's main international airport, offering condolences on behalf of Israelis after a strike blamed on Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels killed 12 people and wounded 309 in Riyadh.
"I condemn in the strongest possible terms the shocking terrorist attack at Riyadh airport," Netanyahu said in a statement. "On behalf of the citizens of Israel, I extend our deepest condolences to the families of those murdered and wish the injured a full recovery."
"Terrorism targets innocent people and seeks to spread fear and instability. It must be confronted with determination," he continued. "Israel looks forward to a strong Middle East, one that stands united against threats, protects its people and builds a future of security, cooperation and prosperity for all the peoples of the region."
The unusually direct message of solidarity came as the Houthis threatened further attacks across Saudi Arabia and a new projectile struck a passenger terminal at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Sunday afternoon, less than a day after Saturday's deadly attack.
Houthis threaten further strikes as Riyadh airport remains closed
The Saudi-led coalition reported that another projectile struck Terminal 4 on Sunday, triggering a fire. It also reported intercepting a separate cruise missile. Around the same time, reports emerged of an attack on the airport in Sanaa, Yemen's Houthi-controlled capital.
Earlier Sunday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree reaffirmed the group's intention to enforce what it described as an aerial blockade of Saudi Arabia, warning international airlines, airport employees and passengers against using the kingdom's airports and airspace.
The facilities, he warned, had become "theaters of operations for our forces."
Saree said the Houthis remained determined to enforce their declared principle of "airport for airport, blockade for blockade and escalation for escalation" until their objectives were achieved.
He accused Saudi Arabia of bearing responsibility for the consequences of failed attempts to intercept Houthi missiles and urged the public to take the group's warnings seriously.
The spokesman said all areas of Saudi Arabia were potential targets except Mecca and Medina, Islam's two holiest cities. The clarification followed Saudi accusations last month that the Houthis had fired toward Mecca, home to the Kaaba, one of Islam's most sacred sites.
An aviation industry source in Saudi Arabia told AFP on Sunday morning that operations at Riyadh's international airport remained suspended. Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 reported that the shutdown had been extended, with flights not expected to resume before midnight Sunday local time.
Twelve killed, hundreds injured in deadliest Gulf attack since Iran war began
Saturday's missile struck the area housing terminals 3 and 4 of King Khalid International Airport, which serve domestic flights.
Saudi aviation authorities said the dead included four Saudi nationals, two Bangladeshis and one person each from the United States, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Sudan and the Palestinian territories.
Among the 309 wounded, several were reported to be in critical condition, with hospitals across the Saudi capital treating large numbers of casualties.
The strike was the deadliest attack on a Gulf Arab country since the war involving Iran began in February.
Western sources said information gathered after the attack suggested there had been no advance warning and that no warning sirens sounded before the missile struck.
The attack came just two days after another deadly Houthi strike on the same airport killed three Saudi nationals, including a pilot, and damaged at least one passenger aircraft that was empty at the time.
Several other attacks targeted airports in Riyadh and Abha earlier in the week, killing three more people.
The growing focus on Saudi airports marks a significant escalation in the conflict between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, which is supporting Yemen's internationally recognized government with extensive airstrikes against rebel-held territory.
Trump weighs military intervention as international condemnation grows
U.S. President Donald Trump said Saturday that Washington was considering joining Saudi military operations against the Houthis, although he emphasized that no decision had been made.
Trump later described the attack on Riyadh airport as "terrible" and "unacceptable."
The possibility of direct American involvement comes as the conflict in Yemen increasingly intersects with the broader war involving Iran, a longtime backer of the Houthis.
United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres expressed deep shock over the deadly strike, while European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned what she called a dangerous escalation. Germany also joined the international condemnation.
Why the fighting in Yemen is escalating
The renewed confrontation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis began in July, ending roughly four years of relative calm in Yemen's civil war, which erupted in 2014.
The latest escalation followed Houthi attempts to break the Saudi-imposed air blockade on rebel-held territory, coinciding with renewed fighting involving Iran.
Last month, Houthi forces launched a rapid offensive that brought strategic coastal areas of southwestern Yemen under their control, strengthening their position around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The narrow waterway connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and forms part of a vital shipping route between Europe and Asia through the Suez Canal, carrying approximately 12% of global trade.
Although the Houthis already possessed the ability to strike ships in the Red Sea using missiles and drones, their territorial gains gave them greater control over the strategic passage.
Its importance to Saudi Arabia has increased dramatically because of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula, during the war with Iran.
Earlier last week, Yemeni government forces backed by Riyadh launched a major ground offensive aimed at pushing the Houthis out of their newly captured territory and restoring control over Bab el-Mandeb.
Saudi Arabia has provided extensive air support for the operation, carrying out heavy bombardments of Houthi positions.
Reports indicate that pro-Saudi forces have made advances near the strait, although the extent of those gains remains unclear. The Houthis deny claims by Yemen's internationally recognized government that its forces have already regained control of Bab el-Mandeb.
The intensifying conflict has now brought Saudi Arabia's civilian aviation infrastructure directly into the fighting, while Netanyahu's condemnation and Trump's consideration of military intervention underscore the widening regional repercussions.

articles.title: US says fighter jet struck cargo ship trying to break Iran blockade in Gulf of Oman
articles.body:
The U.S. military said overnight Saturday that it had disabled a commercial cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman after its crew ignored warnings and attempted to breach the naval blockade on Iran. 
"A U.S. fighter jet struck the stern of the Panama-flagged Ocean Molica, also known as the Arika Sun, with a precision-guided munition," U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) said. "The strike completely disabled the vessel's propulsion system without injuring any crew members." CENTCOM said the cargo ship had attempted to navigate regional waters after departing an Iranian port.
"US forces resumed the blockade on all vessels entering or leaving Iranian ports on July 14," CENTCOM said. "During three months of strict enforcement, four commercial vessels have been disabled and 135 ships have been forced to change course and turn back. In addition, U.S. forces destroyed 10 tankers linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' multibillion-dollar shadow shipping network during the same period."
CENTCOM urged all mariners to comply with blockade warnings issued by U.S. forces, continue monitoring official Notices to Mariners and contact U.S. naval forces when sailing in the Gulf of Oman and the approaches to the Strait of Hormuz.
Earlier, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency (UKMTO) reported that a tanker had been struck by an unidentified missile in the Strait of Hormuz, sparking a fire on board. No crew members were injured.
The U.S. operation comes amid heightened regional tensions following a ballistic missile attack on the international airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen. At least 12 people were killed, including an American citizen, and more than 300 were injured. Following the attack, President Donald Trump said the United States might join Saudi Arabia in strikes against the Houthis, but emphasized that he had not yet made a decision.
In recent days, Trump has declared that the United States would not attack Iran before the November 3 midterm elections. He also said Washington and Tehran were holding "productive discussions" and claimed that oil was flowing through the Strait of Hormuz at record levels.
In a post on his Truth Social platform overnight Wednesday, Trump wrote: "We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran. I want to make it clear to everyone that while Iran is in very bad shape, both economically and militarily, and while the blockade will remain in full force, with oil flowing at a record number of barrels through the Strait of Hormuz (22 million barrels just last night, with not a single barrel coming from or going to Iran!), we will not attack Iran at any time before the U.S. midterm elections on November 3. Iran will not have a nuclear weapon!"
Trump's remarks about "productive discussions" came just a day after he said he did not really want another agreement with Iran. Speaking at a campaign rally alongside Republican candidates in San Antonio, Texas, he said: "I don't think another deal is really something I want to do." Despite weeks of stalled negotiations, the president claimed that "Iran is ready to offer us anything." He added that his special envoy, Steve Witkoff, was working on an agreement and "doing very well."

articles.title: Trump tells Ukraine to replace Zelenskyy in Russia diesel deal spat
articles.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump on Saturday called for Ukraine to "get a new leader" following Volodymyr Zelenskyy's criticism of Washington’s decision to ease Russian diesel sanctions, as Trump faces surging fuel prices ahead of midterm elections.
Trump, whose Republicans face dim prospects in next month's vote partly because of soaring energy costs, defended a deal allowing more Russian diesel onto global markets after saying Vladimir Putin strongly wanted to reach a settlement in Ukraine.
Trump accused Zelenskyy of blocking a deal with Moscow and ignoring instructions not to strike Russian refineries, while Kyiv and its European allies warned that easing pressure on Moscow would help fund the Kremlin's war.
Meanwhile, the latest Russian attacks across Ukraine killed at least 21 people, including children.
Trump announced Friday that he had spoken to Putin and agreed Russia would release large amounts of diesel into global markets.
Ukraine and its European allies expressed dismay, with Zelenskyy telling reporters Friday it was a "weak decision."
Asked about the criticism, Trump said Zelenskyy had disobeyed his orders not to strike Russian refineries and that the attacks risked worsening fuel shortages linked to the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.
"He better damn well stop," Trump said.
"I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal, because he could have made many deals that, for some reason, he never does," Trump said.
Trump later said Putin was interested in ending the war.
"Russia would like to make a deal ... but for whatever reason, Zelenskyy does not want to make a deal," he told reporters.
"President Putin would like to see a settlement, strongly."
The U.S. president also criticized Zelenskyy for not holding an election since Russia's 2022 invasion.
"I think he should have an election and he could have settled this thing many times," Trump said.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said lifting sanctions on Russian diesel would only help sustain Russia's war effort.
"This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't," she wrote online.
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham reiterated his "complete solidarity" with Zelenskyy in a call.
Downing Street said Burnham also pledged that Britain would "strengthen its sanctions on Russia."
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga also backed his president. "He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide," he said in a post on X.
On Saturday, a Russian glide bomb attack on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia killed 20 people, including three children, according to Ukraine's state rescue service.
"Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia," Zelenskyy said in a post on X.
A Russian drone attack in the central Dnipropetrovsk region killed an 11-year-old boy, regional officials said.
Russian strikes also caused widespread power cuts in Kyiv.
Russia's Defense Ministry said it had hit a "data center" used by Ukraine's military.
The diesel deal was announced as U.S., Ukrainian and European officials met in Miami in a renewed bid to end the conflict.
Ukraine's delegation was headed home on Saturday, an aide to Zelenskyy said.
U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff said on X the talks involved "the E3, the European Commission, Ukraine and NATO."
He described the discussions as "constructive" and focused on ways to "de-escalate and conclude the war with Russia ahead of winter and advance efforts toward a durable and lasting peace."
The Kremlin said Saturday that Trump had conveyed his ideas about how to de-escalate the war to Putin during a phone call Friday.
Putin received the proposals "with understanding," the Kremlin said, without elaborating.
Russia, which launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, now occupies roughly one-fifth of Ukrainian territory.

articles.title: Hormuz attacks intensify as efforts to end war on Iran stall
articles.body:
Hormuz attacks intensify as efforts to end war on Iran stall
IRGC warns against ignoring the ‘security and rules’ of the strategic waterway as US CENTCOM says it disabled vessel trying to run naval blockade.
US bombs cargo vessel in Gulf of Oman 'trying to run Iran blockade'
Tehran, Iran – Strikes around the strategic Strait of Hormuz have picked up again as mediated efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran remain deadlocked.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said on Saturday night that an unnamed crude oil supertanker hit a naval mine and suffered a major fire while using an unauthorised route in the waterway with navigation systems turned off. In a statement, it warned of a similar fate for any oil tanker that “wishes to ignore the security and rules” of the strait, through which one-fifth of the world’s oil and gas passes in peacetime.
On Sunday, a senior Iranian army official told state television that the country’s forces remain prepared for both defensive and offensive operations, more than seven months since the United States and Israel started the war by attacking Iran on February 28.
“We have struck blows against enemy vessels. If anything else happens against Iran, we will strike them again,” said Habibollah Sayyari, chief of staff and joint coordinator of the army.
His comments came after the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported several incidents of military action or warnings against vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman over the past day. It said ship masters in the vicinity of Ras al-Khaimah, in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), had been directed via radio broadcast overnight to move from their anchorages. And on Sunday afternoon, UKMTO reported an unidentified projectile had struck a tanker heading outbound through the Strait of Hormuz.
Separately, the UAE said its coastguard had rescued 22 crew members after a fire broke out at an unnamed tanker close to its shores, although it did not identify the cause of the blaze.
Early on Sunday, the US Central Command (CENTCOM) released footage of a fighter jet bombing the stern of a Panama-flagged cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman and disabling its propulsion to enforce its naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports.
Since the US reimposed the blockade in mid-July, CENTCOM says its forces have disabled four commercial vessels, turned around 135 ships and destroyed 10 tankers linked with Iran. Washington says Tehran has exported no oil through the blockade line.
This comes as at least a dozen ships were attacked over the week ending on October 5, the highest number since the war began. At least one was hit off the north coast of Qatar, signalling that the danger extends beyond the immediate Hormuz passage as Iran and the US vie for control.
The ship attacks appear to have decreased energy flows that had surpassed pre-war levels at the start of the month. Kpler data cited by CNBC on Friday showed that average crude passing through the strait for the week ended October 7 was 8.5 million barrels per day, roughly 40 percent below the normal level.
To reopen the strait and reach a resolution to the war, Iran has demanded a return to a now-collapsed memorandum of understanding that was agreed in June, as well as Washington’s backing of an already finalised Iran-Oman deal that designates temporary coordinated entry and exit routes for vessels transiting the strait.
Messages continue to be exchanged between the two sides through mediators, although no breakthrough is expected in the coming weeks leading to the US midterm vote, set to take place on November 3, and Israel’s election, due on October 27.
US Vice President JD Vance said last week that Iran must make a “meaningful” reduction in its nuclear enrichment capacity to end the war, signalling a potential easing of the oft-repeated US demand that zero enrichment must take place on Iranian soil.
Tehran has said a nuclear agreement potentially involving diluting its high-enriched uranium can be part of the later stages of talks, but has emphasised it will not abandon enrichment altogether.
“The achievements of our indigenous nuclear industry cannot be stopped,” Iran’s nuclear chief Mohammad Eslami said during a speech on Sunday, pointing to electricity generation as a main use case.
He also renewed criticism against the International Atomic Energy Agency for not condemning repeated US threats to again bomb Iran’s nuclear facilities.
Behrouz Kamalvandi, spokesman of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran, told reporters on Sunday that authorities plan on using military and diplomatic avenues to get what they want.
“The Islamic Republic will decisively pursue the country’s interests,” he said. “If those interests can be secured through diplomacy, that is much better, but if not, we will secure them in the field of battle”.

articles.title: Deadly attack on airport in Saudi Arabia's capital kills 12
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Deadly attack on airport in Saudi Arabia's capital kills 12 people and injures over 300
Saudi Arabia on Sunday extended the closure of the country's main international airport, according to an online flight tracker, a day after a missile attack on the facility killed 12 people from several countries and left more than 300 injured in a major escalation of the war between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and the kingdom.
A Saudi-led coalition blamed Saturday afternoon's attack on the Houthis. It was the latest of several in the past week at King Khalid International Airport in the capital, Riyadh, and marked the deadliest attack in any Gulf Arab country since the start of the Iran war.
Saudi Arabia is the world's top oil exporter, and the attacks have sent up oil prices and rattled markets.
Following the attack, US President Donald Trump said Saturday he was weighing whether the United States would join Saudi strikes against the rebels.
Airport operations were suspended Saturday. Authorities later extended the closure until at least 9PM. Sunday, according to Flightradar24.
Also on Sunday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said 91 Yemenis were killed and 168 injured by the Saudi-led coalition in five weeks. It said 60 percent of those killed were women and children.
Mix of nationalities killed at Saudi airport 
The attack struck an airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorised to speak to the media.
The Saudi statement said the dead included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. It said several hospitals were treating the injured.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged in a social media post that an American citizen had been killed in the attack, which he condemned.
The Egyptian man was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, who worked for the Saudi airline Flybas, according to the Egyptian state-run Al-Qahera New television.
Trump said he would consider joining strikes against rebels.
The attack is expected to increase Saudi pressure on allies, including the United States, to provide military support for the kingdom, which has seemingly tried to avoid all-out war with the Houthis.
Shortly after the attack, Trump said he was evaluating whether the US should join Saudi strikes against the rebels. "We may. We're going to look at it," he said. "We just found out about the recent attack. So we'll make a decision. We move very quickly."
Trump said later Saturday that he planned to speak with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Asked if the US might get involved, Trump responded, "We'll find out."
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis blamed them for the attack, calling it a "fully-fledged war crime" and vowing a firm response. The airport has no military facilities.
There was no immediate statement from the rebels, who earlier on Saturday accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa International Airport in the Houthi-held Yemeni capital.
The Houthis claimed attacks earlier in the week on King Khalid International Airport that killed three Saudis, including a pilot.
The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis.
For Iran, the fighting puts pressure on a key US ally
Until recently, the Houthis had been largely on the sidelines of the war on Iran. Now the rebels are a way for Tehran to apply pressure on a key US ally.
The Saudis and the Houthis began fighting in 2015 when the kingdom entered Yemen's civil war on behalf of the internationally recognised government.
Relative calm after a 2022 ceasefire ended in July when the Houthis resumed attacks, saying the Saudis fired on the Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was trying to land. That revived anger over the Saudi-led blockade that has largely isolated Houthi-run areas.
Now fighting has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea.
Those gains gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping on a corridor that is a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.
Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defence support to the region, regional officials told the AP last month, with one noting that the US has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran.
The Houthis this week warned global airlines "for the last time" about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace, which they described as a theatre for their military operations.
Before the latest attack, Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group, and Pakistan International Airlines suspended flights to and from Riyadh and other Saudi airports for varying periods.

articles.title: War and high debt to dominate IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok
articles.body:
War and high debt to dominate IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok
The US-Israel war on Iran and its inflationary impact will dominate the agenda.
Finance officials from around the world will gather in Bangkok this week under the shadow of a widening war in the Middle East, the biggest-ever energy supply shock and rising interest rates that together pose daunting risks to already-sluggish global economic growth.
The US-Israel war on Iran, now in its eighth month, and its inflationary impact are slated to dominate the agenda and sideline conversations during the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank, held outside Washington for the first time in three years.
IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva told Reuters News Agency that 18,000 people were registered to attend the meetings, 4,000 more than the last off-site meetings held in Morocco in October 2023.
Notably absent will be United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who dispatched two senior officials in his stead while he handles some “domestic engagements”, a US official said. Federal Reserve Board Chairman Kevin Warsh will attend and is slated to participate in a public event with Georgieva on October 16.
Several other finance ministers were also staying home due to domestic budget and election duties, but most central bankers would attend, Georgieva said.
Bessent’s decision to skip the high-profile gathering and a meeting of the Group of 20 (G20) major economies, which the US leads this year, may frustrate counterparts amid rising tensions over the Iran war, Ukraine’s battle against Russia’s invasion, and the US move to impose sanctions on the International Criminal Court.
Fossil energy reserve release
The Group of Seven (G7) countries have agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves under pressure from US President Donald Trump, who is keen to see lower petrol prices before November elections that could see his Republican Party lose control of Congress.
Trump on Friday announced a deal with Russia that would provide even more diesel to global markets and a temporary waiver of US sanctions designed to deprive Moscow of revenues for its war on Ukraine. The move drew swift criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
More than one billion barrels of oil have been released, mainly from onshore commercial inventories, since the start of the war on February 28. But industry executives say the amount of oil in storage that is accessible to the global market is running low, making the market more fragile and fuelling pressure on prices.
The IMF has signalled little change in its forecast for three percent global growth in 2026, and may edge its forecast for next year slightly higher. But some countries will see downgrades, including Ukraine, now in its fifth year of war against Russia’s invasion, and Gulf countries hit by Iranian strikes and sharply reduced energy exports.
IMF research released on Tuesday showed that sharp spikes in food and energy prices are an increasingly common source of crises that drive inflation expectations higher for longer, worsen poverty and threaten economic stability.
One headache for policymakers is the growing public debt burden that is sapping growth and adding inflationary pressures. The IMF says public debt is at the highest level since World War II and will exceed 100 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) before 2030.
Advanced economies, led by the US, have the highest debt-to-GDP ratios, but emerging markets and low-income countries are particularly vulnerable, given a perfect storm of challenges: capital outflows in search of higher US rates, weather extremes triggered by the El Nino climate phenomenon, and a lack of investment in artificial intelligence (AI), which has mitigated negative supply shocks in the US and other rich countries.
Developing countries are particularly vulnerable given high public debt levels that will have to be renegotiated at higher interest rates. Together, they face $400bn in debt payments to external creditors in 2026, and interest payments already exceed 10 percent of revenue on average.
Many lower-income countries are worried about new IMF recommendations for loan programmes that call for fewer but deeper reforms as a condition for approving lending, a change that many fear will lead to painful austerity measures.

articles.title: Deadly Houthi strike on Riyadh airport draws int'l condemnation
articles.body:
The international community joined in unison Sunday to condemn the deadly Houthi attack on Saudi capital Riyadh.
U.N. and EU leaders voiced shock at the attack and warned against an escalation in the deadly conflict.
Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was "deeply shocked" by Saturday's attack on Riyadh's airport, which killed 12 people and wounded over 300, according to aviation authorities.
"Attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are a violation of international law. These attacks must cease immediately," Guterres said in a statement.
U.S. President Donald Trump said Saturday that Washington may join Saudi strikes against the Houthis in Yemen following the attack.
Asked by reporters whether he had decided to take part in the strikes, Trump said: "We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack. We will make a decision. We move very quickly."
EU chief Ursula von der Leyen called the attack a "dangerous escalation" and said the Iran-backed group must halt strikes on civilian targets.
"These attacks by Iran's proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence. They are destabilizing crucial global transport and energy nodes with shockwave sent through the world," von der Leyen said.
"These murderous attacks at civilians must stop at once," she said, adding the EU stands in "solidarity with Saudi Arabia."
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said he "firmly condemns" the attack, which he described as "a terrorist act against Saudi Arabia and civil aviation."
"Our thoughts are with the victims and I send my sincere condolences to their loved ones," he wrote on X.
Meanwhile, U.K. Defense Minister Wes Streeting said the attacks were "contemptible" and a "dangerous escalation"
France also condemned the "heinous attack" and stressed "total solidarity" with Saudi Arabia.
France, which is already lending troops and military equipment to Saudi Arabia, "will continue to remain by its side in its defense of its territory and its infrastructure," a Foreign Ministry statement said, calling on the Houthis to cease their attacks.
Meanwhile, Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif strongly condemned the deadly attack on Saudi capital's international airport.
"Attacks targeting civilians and vital infrastructure are utterly unacceptable and pose a serious threat to regional peace and stability," Sharif posted on X, describing the attack as "heinous" and reaffirming Pakistan's "steadfast commitment to Saudi Arabia's sovereignty, territorial integrity."
Pakistan is close ally of Saudi Arabia and are part of the Mecca mutual defense pact alongside Türkiye.
Another Saudi ally, Syria also condemned "in the strongest terms" Saturday's deadly attack on King Khalid International Airport.
It stressed that the security of Saudi Arabia is an "integral part of the security of Syria and the entire region."
In a statement released on X, the Syrian Foreign Ministry described the attack as "a violation of the Kingdom's sovereignty and a direct threat to its security and stability, as well as to the safety of civilians, civilian facilities, and air navigation."
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim "unequivocally denounced" the attack, saying "there can be no justification for attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure."
Anwar said on X that putting innocent lives at risk "can only deepen the suffering already wrought by this conflict and carry it into places that should remain beyond its reach."
He also said Malaysia stands in solidarity with Saudi Arabia and its people "at this perilous hour," and that Kuala Lumpur remains "steadfast in our hope that diplomacy and reason will prevail before the conflict widens still further."
Bangladesh also "strongly and unequivocally" condemned the attack in an official statement. Two Bangladeshi nationals have been killed in the strike.
"Attacks endangering civilian lives and targeting civilian infrastructure are unacceptable and must cease immediately," the Bangladesh Foreign Ministry said.
The Muslim-majority South Asian nation also called for an "immediate cessation of hostilities, the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, and a peaceful resolution of the ongoing crisis through dialogue and diplomacy, in the interest of regional peace, security and stability."
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia on Sunday kept its main international airport closed and moved Riyadh schools online as Yemen's Houthi rebels threatened new airstrikes across the kingdom.
Saturday's strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh marked a major escalation in the war between Yemen's Iran's-backed Houthis and the kingdom and further complicated sputtering efforts to halt the U.S.-Iran war.

articles.title: Trump says Ukraine and Russia agree to ‘energy ceasefire’
articles.body:
Zelenskyy says Russia violated energy truce announced by Trump
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had pushed for a 60-day full ceasefire.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Russia has attacked its energy sites despite a ceasefire deal announced earlier in the day by US President Trump aimed at sparing fuel infrastructure.
The announcement came after Trump said the two countries had agreed to an “energy ceasefire”, after mutual attacks on energy infrastructure piled pressure on global energy prices.
“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed,” Trump wrote on social media. “Do not break it! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP.”
Zelenskyy initially denied any knowledge of the agreement and said it was “news to him,” according to Axios.
“Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian ‘shaheds’ all day today,” he wrote on X, adding that Kyiv would back such a truce but that Moscow must also comply.
“There have been glide bomb strikes and strikes on our energy infrastructure too. A power plant in Kharkiv was attacked this evening,” he added.”
There was no immediate announcement by the Kremlin addressing the claim.
Zelenskyy previously said on Sunday he would organise elections if Russian President Vladimir Putin agrees to a 60-day full ceasefire.
‘Better stop’
On Saturday, Trump slammed the Ukrainian president for attacking Russian oil refineries, the day after the US temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian fuel that were originally imposed to sap Moscow’s war effort in Ukraine.
“He better damn well stop,” Trump told reporters at the White House. “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” he added.
Earlier on Saturday, Zelenskyy said Trump’s announcement of the diesel deal with Putin had emboldened Moscow. Kyiv instead urged Washington to pressure Moscow for serious negotiations to end the four-and-a-half-year war.
“Today, Russia said thank you for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy said.
“Last night provided yet more confirmation that Russia perceives any easing of pressure as a signal that it can supposedly keep fighting, that it can supposedly keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed.”
‘Up to Ukrainians’
The southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia has been a regular target of Russian bombardment, with attacks intensifying in the past few months.
On Saturday, a six-year-old girl was among those killed in Zaporizhzhia when one attack reduced part of an apartment block to rubble. Her grandfather, Anatoliy Chumniy, stood sobbing over her body, laid on the ground in a white bag, after rescuers pulled her from the wreckage.
In response to Trump’s suggestion of a new leader, Zelenskyy said, “it’s up to Ukrainians” to choose their leader and noted that Putin would also like to change who is leading Ukraine.
Earlier on Sunday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine was ready to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries if Moscow ceases its own attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

articles.title: Houthis defiant after deadly Riyadh airport strike: ‘We’ll keep attacking, don’t fly there’
articles.body:
Yemen's Houthi rebels vowed Sunday to continue enforcing their declared air blockade of neighboring Saudi Arabia, hours after a Houthi missile exploded at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, killing 12 people and wounding 309. 
The rebels renewed their warnings to airlines and passengers as the Saudi capital's main airport remained closed following the unprecedented attack. In an official statement Sunday morning, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned airlines, airport employees and passengers against using Saudi airports or airspace, saying they "serve as theaters of operations for our forces."
In his statement, Saree declared that the Houthis remained determined to enforce the rules they had announced: "Airport for airport, blockade for blockade and escalation for escalation, until our objectives are achieved." He also accused Saudi Arabia of bearing responsibility for the consequences of any failed attempts to intercept missiles launched by the Houthis, urging the public to take the group's warnings seriously. Saree said the Houthis regarded all areas of Saudi Arabia as potential theaters of military operations, except Mecca and Medina, Islam's two holiest cities. His comments followed accusations by Riyadh last month that the Houthis had fired a missile toward Mecca, the destination of the annual Muslim pilgrimage and home to the Kaaba, one of Islam's most sacred sites. The accusation portrayed the rebels as threatening Islam's holy places.
Hours after Saturday's missile attack, flight operations at King Khalid International Airport remained suspended. A source in the Saudi aviation industry told AFP on Sunday morning that the airport was still shut. Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 reported on X that the closure had been extended by another 24 hours, until midnight between Sunday and Monday, Israel time.
According to reports from Saudi Arabia, the Houthi missile exploded in the area housing Terminals 3 and 4, which serve domestic flights. The dead reportedly included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, an American, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Sudanese and a Palestinian. Many of the 309 people wounded were reported to be in serious condition. Reports Sunday morning indicated that hospitals in Riyadh remained filled with casualties from the attack. The strike was the deadliest attack on any Gulf Arab country since the war with Iran began in February.
According to Western sources, information collected following the attack indicates that the missile struck without any advance warning and that no sirens sounded before the impact. The deadly attack came just two days after an earlier Houthi strike on the same airport, in which at least one passenger aircraft, empty at the time, was hit. Three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, were killed in that attack. Several additional attacks targeted airports in Riyadh and the southern Saudi city of Abha earlier last week, killing three more people. The series of attacks marks a new peak in the escalating confrontation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, which has intensified in recent weeks alongside renewed fighting inside Yemen between the rebels and forces loyal to the internationally recognized Yemeni government. Saudi Arabia has supported those government forces with extensive airstrikes on Houthi-controlled territory.
On Saturday, President Donald Trump said the United States could join the fighting and assist Saudi Arabia in conducting strikes against the Yemeni rebels, although he emphasized that no decision had yet been made. Trump subsequently described the Houthi attack on Riyadh as "a terrible thing" and "unacceptable." United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres expressed "deep shock" over the airport attack Sunday morning. Germany also condemned the strike, while European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described it as "a dangerous escalation."
The Houthis have intensified their attacks on Saudi cities in recent days, increasingly targeting airports as part of a campaign to disrupt the kingdom's aviation industry and effectively close its skies. The rebels say the campaign is retaliation for Saudi airstrikes against Houthi positions in Yemen. At the beginning of last week, the Houthis warned international airlines not to operate in Saudi airspace, declaring it an operational zone for attacks against the kingdom. They said they would not accept responsibility for the consequences if airlines continued to fly there.
The renewed confrontation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia began in July, ending a four-year lull in Yemen's civil war. That conflict erupted in 2014, with Riyadh subsequently intervening in support of Yemen's internationally recognized government. The latest escalation began after the Houthis attempted to break the air blockade imposed on them by Saudi Arabia, against the backdrop of an intensifying war involving Iran, their regional ally. Last month, the Houthis launched a rapid territorial offensive, capturing strategic coastal areas in southwestern Yemen overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The territorial gains strengthened their position along one of the world's most important maritime shipping routes. The Houthis had already demonstrated their ability to attack shipping in the Red Sea using long-range missiles and drones, but their advances on the coast gave them tighter control over movement through the strategic passage. Bab el-Mandeb links the Red Sea and Suez Canal shipping route between Europe and Asia, carrying approximately 12% of global trade.
Its strategic importance, particularly for Saudi Arabia, has increased dramatically because of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula during the war with Iran. Early last week, Yemeni government forces aligned with Riyadh launched a major ground offensive aimed at driving the Houthis from their newly captured territory and regaining control of Bab el-Mandeb. Saudi Arabia has provided extensive air support for the operation, including heavy bombardment of Houthi-held areas. Reports indicate that pro-Saudi forces have advanced in the area surrounding the strait, although the extent of those gains remains unclear. The Houthis dispute claims by Yemen's internationally recognized government that its forces have already recaptured Bab el-Mandeb, leaving control of the vital waterway contested as the fighting escalates on both sides of the Arabian Peninsula.

articles.title: Two killed near Israeli-occupied zone in south Lebanon
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Two killed near Israeli-occupied zone in south Lebanon
Two men were killed in south Lebanon on Sunday, one by Israeli fire and the other by an explosive remnant of war, as they took part in the annual olive harvest, according to state media and local officials.
South Lebanon has been the scene of two wars since 2023 between Israel and Hezbollah, and Israeli troops still occupy a band of territory 10 kilometres (six miles) wide running along the border.
The official National News Agency (NNA) said one of the men was killed in Yater, in Bint Jbeil district, when Israeli "shelling targeted the outskirts of the town while he was inspecting his land and olive harvest".
The Lebanese army blamed Israeli tank fire and called the ongoing attacks "a flagrant breach of existing agreements".
Afterwards, the Yater municipality urged residents "to avoid the outskirts of the town and refrain from crossing the earthen barrier separating some unsafe neighborhoods" for fear of Israeli attacks.
In the village of Froun, in the same district, the NNA reported that "a foreign object" left over from previous Israeli operations exploded and killed an engineer as he and others tended their trees.
The engineer had come down from Beirut, where he lives, for the harvest, Froun mayor Hassan Bazzi told AFP.
The incident prompted local residents to call off the harvest and wait for "the Lebanese army to complete the decontamination of the village", Bazzi said.
Since a framework agreement between Lebanon and Israel was struck in June, the violence in the south has diminished but not stopped.
Israel continues to carry out sporadic strikes and demolitions in and around the territory it occupies, while Hezbollah refuses to submit to government plans to disarm it.
About eight kilometres (five miles) away, in Jibshit, volunteers from the north came to help locals with the harvest in a show of solidarity.
"From north to south, one people and one land," said organiser Ahmad Chahhal.
As workers swatted at branches to make the olives fall, an AFP photographer saw drones and heard fighter jets overhead, and explosions could be heard in the distance.
Israel has ramped up its bombardment of Lebanon since March, with intense strikes and a ground invasion.
The framework deal between Israel and Lebanon involves Hezbollah's disarmament, a gradual Israeli withdrawal, and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the region.

articles.title: Trump says Russia and Ukraine agree to 'energy ceasefire'
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump says Russia and Ukraine agree to 'energy ceasefire'
US President Donald Trump said in a brief statement Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt strikes on each other's energy infrastructure, prompting surprise from Ukraine's leader, who said the announcement was "news for me".
There was no immediate comment from Russia on Trump's claim.
Russia has launched waves of attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure since invading in February 2022, knocking out power and heating to millions during freezing temperatures, while Ukraine has systematically struck Russian oil refineries that it says fund the war.
Ukraine's largest private energy provider, DTEK, announced fresh power outages in the capital Kyiv on Sunday amid the attacks.
"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Trump wrote on his Truth Social network, without further details.
Earlier Sunday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reiterated that his country would be ready to stop hitting Russian oil refineries if Russia curbed its own attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
Reacting to Trump's ceasefire announcement, Zelensky told the Axios news outlet that it was "news for me".
Prices at US gasoline and diesel pumps have surged since late February, when joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran prompted Tehran to block the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway used for oil exports from the Gulf.
'Up to our people'
Trump's announcement came amid mounting tensions between Trump and Zelensky over an agreement between Russia and the United States on diesel.
Zelensky said the deal was a "weak decision", while several of Ukraine's European allies pledged to increase pressure on Moscow, despite the agreement.
The deal would see Moscow release large amounts of diesel onto the global market in exchange for temporary sanctions relief.
Addressing the criticism on Saturday, Trump claimed Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries were to blame for rising diesel prices, adding that it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president".
Zelensky pushed back on the suggestion in an interview on Sunday.
"First of all, with all respect to President Trump, it's up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader," Zelensky told ABC News.
Germany's foreign minister said Sunday that Berlin continued to "fully support" Zelensky.
"Europe needs stability and that means that we are very clearly continuing to stay by the side of Ukraine and its government," Johann Wadephul said in Berlin.
And in Kyiv, several residents expressed concern about Trump's call for Zelensky to be replaced.
"I believe our president is the best, and Americans should think about their own president," said 40-year-old local Olesia Goncharuk.
"We Ukrainians decide our own fate and our own freedom, and we are free people," she told AFP.
The row between Zelensky and Trump comes weeks before closely-fought US elections dominated by voter frustration over the cost of living.

articles.title: US Lt-Gen Salene critiques Netanyahu, Israeli government for stalling Trump's Gaza plan
articles.body:
US Security Coordinator Lt.-Gen. Sean M. Salene has made a speech in which he, as softly as possible yet firmly, went after the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for stalling aspects of the Trump administration that strengthen the Palestinian Authority in Gaza, especially regarding training a new Palestinian police force.
Speaking recently at the Reichman University Institute for counterterrorism (ICT), Salene did not name Netanyahu, but said that counterterrorism is a much broader campaign than just using military force.
He stated that counterterrorism, in his view, meant that "you cannot address it only through the military lane. Addressing counterterrorism also has to address the ideology, has to address the education, and has to address the societal conditions which support the evolution of a terrorist organization."
"While some of these would be outside the authorities and the arena that I have, I will also share with you that there are very few serving officers in the United States military who focus on the West Bank problem set, 16 to be exact," he continued.
In contrast to Salene's argument, which is definitely supported by many counterterror academics and also some in the Israeli defense establishment, Netanyahu has focused almost entirely on using military force to defeat Hamas.
US officials accuse Netanyahu of delaying postwar Gaza security, governance plans
Netanyahu has publicly opposed making plans for any "Day After" in Gaza for three years. Regarding even the October 2025 Trump ceasefire plan he signed on to, top US officials have accused him of delaying those aspects designed to replace Hamas with new Palestinian political and security mechanisms in Gaza.
Salene also framed Israeli society as having jumped toward a new state of hyper risk-aversion when facing terrorism and other security dilemmas, "Because in your society and where we are right now, with the open fronts and the open question of Iran, I know that the risk tolerance here is very low, perhaps non-existent. The risk tolerance is low and non-existent."
"I would also share with you a reflection: the way that it appears to me that the IDF and other security professionals view threat. Normally, our doctrine tells us we view threat…as capability plus intent. What I have noticed now is that they reflect threat as capability. That many IDF security professionals view capability as equal in a threat, I think they're reflecting some of the policy guidance they receive and some of the societal pressures that they feel. But in this regard, it's helping to understand this environment," he noted.
In other words, Salene, while sympathetic to Israeli trauma after October 7, was telling his Israeli audience that going to the extreme of always focusing on the worst-case scenario of what enemy capabilities are is counterproductive and problematic.
While he wanted to support Israeli military officials in some respects, he challenged them to consider whether politicized policy guidance and social pressures, rather than expert judgment, are shaping their professional assessments.
Salene warns Hamas threat extends far beyond Gaza, West Bank
Next, he warned that the threat of Hamas itself is also much broader than its immediate forces on the ground confronting Israel.
"Hamas is then not confined just to one place. It's not confined to just Gaza. It's not confined to Judea and Samaria. It exists in Jordan and in Syria, and in Lebanon, and we have financiers in Florida, and in Europe. So this understanding is priority number one for counterterrorism: a broader view of Hamas as an ecosystem," stated the US general.
Here, Salene encouraged Israeli political and defense officials to look beyond the obvious physical battle space before them to think of Hamas as a movement, idea, and series of relationships which extend across the globe, and cannot be shut down by more force in Gaza and the West Bank alone.
In addition, Salene specifically complimented IDF Central Commander Maj.-Gen. Avi Bluth, saying, "You have an incredibly principled leader. An incredibly principled leader in IDF Central Command. Very difficult environment inside of your society. I'm speaking as a military officer to see another military officer attempting to enact his policy with the instruments he had, which now touches your political level."
With these remarks, Salene laid bare problems which Bluth and the Shin Bet have highlighted in terms of a lack of support from the political echelon and from the police in cracking down sufficiently against Jewish extremist violence and terror in the West Bank, even as all Israeli forces have worked well together to keep the larger Palestinian terror problem down.
Discussing security coordination with the PA, he said, "Security coordination. What is it then the United States can do to support the security coordination? There are two parts. The first part, respect and understand what exists and not get in the way."
"The second part is when that begins to break down and becomes very difficult. Where is it the United States can step in in order to assist if it gets difficult, there's tragedies this summer you can tell," he added.
Moreover, Salene said, "Tragedy. How is it that it didn't spiral? I will just share with you. There was effective security coordination. There was communication. There was an effort to de-escalate and contain the crisis so it did not spread. Why? If I zoomed out for a moment and said that if the crisis has spread and destabilized, would the destabilization only be confined to Judea and Samaria?"
Continuing, he asserted, "A destabilization is likely to affect the stability of Jordan. As a US Central Command officer, the stability of Jordan matters. It's important to you. It's important to us. It's important to the bigger picture, to the wider strategic question, which remains open."
Salene highlights role of Israeli-Palestinian security coordination in preventing escalation
Here, Salene was arguing that when Israeli and Palestinian security officials work well together, his office can just stay out of the way, but when they are not, he has stepped in at crucial moments to calm tense situations which could have blown up into much larger unnecessary conflicts.
Salene also reminded everyone that a destabilized West Bank can have concrete national security implications with Jordan, which has been an invaluable ally in counterintelligence against Palestinian terror.
Trying to convince some of the skeptical Israelis listening that US and Israeli security coordination with the PA pays off, he said, "21 years ago, we received funding from my government to provide police forces non-lethal training…we're not paying for an army. We don't support an army. We support police forces, and I offered that there were questions about what it is for the IDF and the security services."
He said that his office helps "enable the training, in accordance with international standards, human rights, and the rule of law, of a security partner to counter Hamas and terrorist threats. This is a particularly difficult conversation today. It's a particularly difficult conversation to have in this environment, but it is a necessary one."
He then asked rhetorically: "Because what is the alternative? What is the alternative? Is the alternative that the security forces in Judea and Samaria are not on the field? Would the gap remain open, or would it be filled? And if it be filled by a terrorist organization, or it be another command upon the IDF."
Realizing how hard it might be to convince some Israelis of the necessity of a US coordinator is necessary to help train PA forces, he volunteered that skeptics exist in the US as well, noting, "There are folks in my own government who say, 'Why should we spend another dollar? Over here in the Palestinian Authority, that's a corrupt institution. Yes, there is corruption. This is the instrument that we have. I am not a politician.
This is a political discussion, and it will quickly get to the political. I will speak to the practical and the technical."
Continuing, he stated, "In a practical and technical institutional capability in accounting, I will share with you that there are people on the other side who work on de-radicalization, who push on education, who know that their structure is wrong."
These comments hit Netanyahu at his most sensitive point. Of all of the aspects of the October 2025 ceasefire which Netanyahu did not like, but signed on to get the Israeli hostages back, allowing PA police into Gaza, trained by the US, Egypt, and Jordan, was the provision he opposed most vehemently.
Yet, where Netanyahu viewed creating a new Gaza police force associated with Fatah as strengthening PA military power which could confront Israel in the Strip, Salene said that any other alternative will lead to Hamas or Palestinian power brokers who disregard human rights and any vision of a stable future for Gazans.
Next, he revealed strengths and weaknesses of the process of the US and other countries coordinating with the PA.
He said that these allies are "a coalition of nations who also support the security of Israel, even when the political place gets very difficult at the technical place, at the military place to maintain this military architecture together for the day when the political winds have shifted, but the architecture remains for the support for defense of Israel."
"Now, the coalition that we lead has nine other nations inside this coalition. The United States coordinates inside this coalition to ensure it is not too far left, not too far right, down the middle to align these efforts. Other actors are on the stage who are not in our coalition. I want to argue there are other actors that have a relationship with the Palestinian authorities that's not in our interest. Russia and China would come to mind," he cautioned.
Salene urges negotiations, de-escalation to counter Hamas recruitment
Waxing philosophical, Salene then asked some additional rhetorical questions about some of the x-factors which go to the heart of the counterterrorism mission, "Back to the fundamental question: Which way is the terrorist ideology the people who are being marketed to being recruited, which way are they going to go? I would argue it is in our interest for those people to stay with the negotiation track, de-escalation, coordination to support a future negotiation, not to succumb to Hamas and the call to jihad."
Next, he stated, "So in this case, the provision of basic social services…undermines the Hamas' argument, which then helps us in the wider picture in a struggle with the movement, which extends far beyond this country."
"These are the ways that we do at the security system to disrupt, coordinate capability, legitimacy, and order, to get to a more durable stability, to one day open the stage for a larger conversation," he added.
Here, Salene tried to convince Israelis that providing a better life to Gazans is in Israel's interest since more stability will bring less conflict.
While a hard sell to Israelis after October 7, Salene argued there is still no real alternative.
CENTCOM and Lt.-Gen. Salene's office declined to comment regarding the article.

articles.title: Trump announces Russia-Ukraine energy truce, but Zelenskyy says it is 'news to him'

US President Donald Trump has announced that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an immediate halt to attacks on each other’s energy infrastructure, but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the announcement was news to him.

Trump-Zelenskyy spat
Earlier Sunday, Zelenskyy said Kiev was prepared to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries if Moscow stopped attacking Ukraine's energy infrastructure, stressing that any de-escalation must be reciprocal and backed by guarantees.
Trump has attributed rising fuel prices to the Russia-Ukraine war rather than the ongoing conflict involving Iran.
The announcement followed a diesel supply agreement Trump unveiled on Friday with Russian President Vladimir Putin, under which Moscow agreed to provide fuel to the US and global markets.
Zelenskyy described the deal as a "weak decision", but Trump said Saturday that Ukraine's strikes were to blame for rising fuel prices.
Ukrainian president criticised the deal as a "gift" to Putin, warning that the easing of restrictions on Russian diesel exports could help finance Moscow's war effort.
