articles.title: Israeli army 'warning against attacking Iran' before election
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israeli army 'warning against attacking Iran' before election
Israeli army officials are warning that any attack on Iran should come after Israel's election on 27 October, over fears that it could delay the vote and erode trust in the military.
Military officials have said that, though intelligence indicates Iran is beefing up its ballistic missile stockpile and production capacity, any attack would have a knock-on effect on public trust and could be viewed as politically motivated, according to Haaretz.
Public trust in Israel's military and security apparatus fell following Hamas's 7 October 2023 attack on Israel, with the military being caught in a political blame game as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu attempts to deflect responsibility.
The warnings against renewed military action against Iran come after reports that Eyal Zamir, Israel's military chief, has told his counterparts that the US is preparing to return to war with Iran within the next three weeks, according to Israel's Channel 12. 
Zamir said that such an attack would lead to the postponement of the election, with Iran expected to attack Israel in response to any US escalation.
Concerns that Netanyahu may delay the upcoming Israeli elections, where polling shows neither he nor the anti-Netanyahu opposition bloc can win enough seats to form a majority, have been voiced by Israel's opposition.
On Wednesday, Netanyahu claimed that Hamas would attack Israel ahead of the elections and had warned the week before that the country's enemies could attack it.
Israeli opposition politician Yair Lapid denounced Netanyahu after being briefed on the intelligence on Hamas, according to the Times of Israel.
Former Prime Minister Ehud Barak told Israel's Channel 12: "Netanyahu is preparing the infrastructure to go to war in a way that would postpone elections," he said, adding that "we must do everything to remove him from power on Oct 27, once and for all."
The army's concern that a return to war could postpone the election comes as US President Donald Trump mulls an attack on Iran, with reports that new plans are being drawn for a short but intense campaign.
Trump, whose Republican Party is also campaigning ahead of midterm elections in November, has publicly ruled out renewed strikes before the vote, despite reports on preparations underway.

articles.title: Saudi coalition fumes after Houthi strike kills 12 at Riyadh airport
articles.body:
The Saudi-led coalition vowed a decisive response Sunday after a strike at Riyadh's international airport killed 12 people, wounded hundreds, marking the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in over a decade.
The coalition blamed the Iran-backed group for the strike on King Khalid International Airport, describing it as a "full-fledged war crime" that a diplomatic source attributed to a missile.
The attack came during an unprecedented wave of Houthi strikes on the kingdom since a truce in the group's long-running war with Yemen's Riyadh-backed government unraveled in July.
The spiraling violence has raised the possibility of a wider escalation, with U.S. President Donald Trump signalling Washington could join military action against the fighters.
One passenger said they witnessed a strike in the airport's domestic terminal.
"I was on gate 403," the witness said. "I saw 401 hit, I saw injured in front of my eyes. Everyone was running."
Four Saudi citizens were among those killed in the attack, as well as two Bangladeshis, one U.S. citizen, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese, the kingdom's civil aviation authority said in a statement.
It said some of the 309 wounded were in serious condition.
Operations at the airport were suspended following the attack and authorities said damage assessments were ongoing.
The attack prompted health officials to activate a rare mass call-up of doctors to deal with the "serious emergency situation," a medical source said.
Two doctors told Agence France-Presse (AFP) that several pilgrims headed to Mecca were among the wounded.
Schools in Riyadh switched to remote learning for the second time in a month.
Parents in the capital received emails Sunday, citing an order from the education ministry, saying "all schools in Riyadh will switch to distance learning for the entire week".
"The cowardly terrorist attack by the Terrorist Houthi Militia ... which resulted in deaths and injuries among civilian passengers and airport staff, constitutes a full-fledged war crime," coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki said in a statement on X.
Earlier, the coalition said it had intercepted missiles targeting Saudi Arabia and destroyed launch platforms.
The Houthis claimed a series of attacks targeting the airport Thursday that killed three people and damaged a plane, though they did not immediately take responsibility for any new strikes Saturday.
Saturday's attack was the deadliest in the kingdom since May 2015, when a suicide bombing by the Daesh terrorist group killed 21 worshippers in a Shiite mosque in the eastern Qatif governorate.
The civil war in Yemen flared back to life in July after a four-year, U.N.-brokered truce collapsed, months into a wider Middle East war that has rocked the region and roiled energy supplies and markets.
Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has supported Yemen's government militarily since 2015 and is now being drawn deeper into its impoverished neighbor's conflict.
Asked Saturday whether he had changed his mind about joining Saudi strikes on the group, Trump said: "We may."
He said he would be speaking with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, calling what happened in the kingdom "not acceptable."
U.S. media outlets have reported that previous Saudi requests for U.S. military assistance in dealing with the Houthis have been rebuffed.
The U.S., Canadian, German and Spanish embassies in Saudi Arabia warned their citizens to avoid the airport.
A senior Western diplomat told AFP that several embassies were banning their staff from using the airport "over the next week."
Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the "heinous attack" and reaffirmed Islamabad's commitment to Saudi Arabia's security under their defense pact.
The latest attack came on the eve of Saudi Arabia's high-profile convention and entertainment season, which begins this month.
Riyadh usually hosts a packed calendar of events, including its flagship investment conference drawing foreign leaders and business titans.
In Yemen, Saudi-supported government forces were advancing against the Houthis in areas the group captured last month around the Bab el-Mandeb strait, military sources told AFP.
The Yemeni government last week announced a counteroffensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis.
The Houthis confirmed that government forces had attacked in the Bab el-Mandeb area – a key choke point for Red Sea oil and cargo shipping – but claimed to have repelled them.
Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia extends Riyadh airport closure after deadly strike
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Saudi Arabia extends Riyadh airport closure after strike kills 12
Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid International Airport will remain closed until at least midnight local time on Sunday following a strike that killed 12 people and injured 309 others, the latest in a series of deadly attacks on the Riyadh transport hub.
The closure was extended until midnight local time on Sunday, according to a notice to air missions, or NOTAM, issued by Saudi aviation authorities. Flights have been cancelled or diverted while officials assess damage to the airport.
The Saudi-led coalition blamed Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis for Saturday’s attack. The dead included four Saudis, two Bangladeshis and one person each from the United States, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt. Some of the injured remain in critical condition, according to the General Authority of Civil Aviation.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree renewed the group’s warning on Sunday against using Saudi airports. His statement, which exempted Mecca and Medina, described other airports as "potential targets and sites for operations by our forces" and urged airlines, airport workers and travellers to take the warning seriously.
The statement also said Saudi Arabia "bears responsibility for any failed interceptions".
Earlier attacks on the airport this week killed four people and damaged a Saudia aircraft on the ground, according to Saudi authorities. The repeated strikes have made the protection of passengers and airport staff an immediate concern alongside the disruption to flights.
Questions remain over whether those inside the airport received an actionable public warning before Saturday’s strike, and what procedures were in place after the earlier attacks.
Saudi Arabia already operates a National Early Warning Platform. The Saudi Civil Defence says it uses cell-broadcast technology to send emergency messages, accompanied by a distinctive tone, to phones connected to mobile networks in the affected area. Its purpose is to warn the public and explain what action people should take to protect themselves.
That public-alert function is distinct from intercepting an incoming missile -- the questions concern both whether a threat was detected and whether information reached people in time to act.
During Iranian attacks in March, at the onset of the war launched by the US and Israel, residents of Riyadh received Arabic- and English-language messages warning of a "hostile aerial threat" and instructing them to remain indoors or in a safe place away from windows and doors. Reporting on a 18 March incident, however, placed the alerts shortly after explosions were heard.
The Civil Defence also issued mobile warnings for Riyadh and nearby Al-Kharj on 19 September amid escalating Houthi attacks, followed by all-clear messages – showing how the platform has been used during the current escalation.
The attacks come as Riyadh hosts major international energy meetings. The WPC Energy Congress, running from Sunday to Thursday, is proceeding as scheduled, while organisers previously said the Future Investment Initiative would go ahead from October 26 to 29. The latter announcement preceded the latest deadly strike.
The US embassy has meanwhile urged American citizens to avoid King Khalid International Airport and its surrounding areas, and to exercise extreme caution when using other major Saudi airports.

articles.title: Ukraine proposed mutual halt to energy infrastructure attacks, Russia refused, source tells 'Post'
articles.body:
Ukraine has repeatedly offered in recent weeks to halt attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, including oil facilities, on the condition that Moscow stop targeting Ukraine’s electricity infrastructure, a diplomatic source told The Jerusalem Post.
The remark came in response to US President Donald Trump’s claim that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had missed several opportunities to end the war. “Ukrainian attacks are worsening diesel shortages and hurting farmers in the United States,” Trump said.
On Sunday, Trump said that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to what he described as an "energy ceasefire."
According to the source, Kyiv proposed a reciprocal arrangement under which both sides would refrain from attacking energy infrastructure. However, Russian President Vladimir Putin ultimately demanded the lifting of sanctions restricting Russian oil and diesel trade.
On Friday, Trump announced an agreement with Putin to increase Russian diesel supplies to the United States and global markets. Trump argued that the move would help lower fuel prices and portrayed Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries as an obstacle to achieving that goal.
“We told him: Do whatever you want, but don’t hit the refineries,” the president said.
Ukraine and European officials have warned that Russia would receive economic benefits without making any corresponding commitment to reduce its attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure.
The US president’s decision was announced on October 9, coinciding with a meeting in Miami led by US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
The Ukrainian delegation included Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Office of the President of Ukraine; Rustem Umerov, the country’s intelligence chief; and David Arakhamia, a senior negotiator.
Advisors from E3 countries invited
National security advisors from the E3 countries - the United Kingdom, France, and Germany - were also invited to the talks and participated alongside representatives of NATO and the European Union.
During the meeting, Witkoff and Kushner informed the delegations that Trump would ease sanctions on Russian fuel, according to a source familiar with the discussions.
The announcement reportedly caught participants by surprise. “Those present could hardly believe their ears,” the source told the Post.
The source said participants discussed various ways to bring the conflict to an end and worked on draft documents outlining possible proposals. Witkoff and Kushner were expected to discuss the drafts with Russian representatives.

articles.title: Kiev pushes back on Trump’s call for a new leader
articles.body:
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky attends a joint news conference with U.S. President Donald Trump’s Special Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner outside the Mariinskyi Palace following negotiations in Kyiv, Ukraine, on September 6, 2026. (Getty Images)
Only Russia is responsible for the war in Ukraine, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 11 as he vowed to press ahead with strikes on Russian oil refineries, despite criticism from U.S. President Donald Trump, who blamed him for high diesel prices and said he should be replaced.
The exchange came as Kiev pressed its campaign against infrastructure deep inside Russia, with a drone attack on Oct. 11 shutting down a data center run by Russian technology giant Yandex, the third strike on the company’s facilities in four days.
“Ukraine will be ready to stop striking Russian oil refineries if Russia stops striking our energy infrastructure,” Zelensky wrote on X.
“It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but [Russian President Vladimir] Putin does not want to do so,” he said, adding that any de-escalation must be reciprocal and backed by real guarantees.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha pushed back on Trump’s comments, writing on X late on Oct. 10 that Zelensky was leading the country through a war for its independence. “He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide. Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well,” Sybiha wrote.
Trump said on Oct. 10 it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelensky has not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S.
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does,” Trump said.
The U.S. president, who on Oct. 9 struck a deal with Putin to buy diesel from Russia in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, has been urging Zelensky for weeks to stop strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
He has sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has driven up world energy prices. Ukrainian and European officials reacted to the diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia’s war effort.
The Ukrainian drone attack on the Yandex data center in the city of Vladimir, east of Moscow, caused outages across the company’s services, leaving users in dozens of Russian cities and in Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia unable to order taxis or access banking services, according to Russian independent news outlet Astra.
“As a result of the drone attack, the infrastructure of Yandex’s data center in Vladimir was damaged. Operations at the data center have been completely halted,” said the Yandex Cloud Telegram channel.
A Moscow resident, Eduard Malyavko, said the outages had “direct impact” and weren’t just about “convenience.”
“It’s also about work,” he said, adding that they also affected “healthcare and everything else.”
Yandex, often described as Russia’s Google, runs the country’s most popular search engine and a wide range of digital services, and is heavily involved in Russia’s artificial intelligence development.

articles.title: Ethiopia, Eritrea ramp up rhetoric: Are they inching towards war?
articles.body:
Ethiopia, Eritrea ramp up rhetoric: Are they inching towards war?
Allegations of Eritrean troop incursions into Tigray deepen the rift with Ethiopia, as fighting in northern Ethiopia rages on.
Ethiopia and Eritrea have exchanged accusations of aggression at the United Nations, raising fears of a new conflict in the Horn of Africa region as fighting intensifies in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region.
The diplomatic spat comes as Ethiopian troops and allied armed groups advanced across Tigray, where forces from Asmara have allegedly crossed the border to support rebels fighting the government forces.
The two neighbours, which fought a deadly border war between 1998 and 2000, were allies during Ethiopia’s devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war.
However, they have since been at loggerheads over the 2022 peace agreement that ended a two-year civil war between the government in Addis Ababa and Tigray rebels, and over Ethiopia’s demands for access to the Red Sea.
So, what did Eritrea and Ethiopia accuse each other of, and are they inching towards war?
What did Eritrea and Ethiopia say at the UN?
Eritrean troops had advanced as far as 60km (37 miles) into Tigray, Ethiopia told the UN Security Council on Friday, accusing its neighbour of violating its sovereignty.
In a letter, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos described the alleged incursion as “a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia’s inherent right to self-defence”.
He invoked Article 51 of the UN Charter, which recognises a country’s right to self-defence, but did not specify what measures Ethiopia was taking.
Eritrea, which won independence from Ethiopia in 1993, rejected the accusations of incursions into Ethiopia, calling them a pretext for an Addis Ababa offensive.
Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh, in his own letter to the UN Security Council on Saturday, urged the body to condemn Ethiopia’s “deplorable declaration of war” and take “deterrent measures”.
He warned that an Ethiopian offensive would cause “huge devastation to the peoples of both countries and destabilise the whole region”.
The accusations come amid a broader dispute over access to the Red Sea.
Landlocked Ethiopia has repeatedly argued that securing direct sea access is essential, while Eritrea fears Addis Ababa intends to seize its port of Assab.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed reiterated on Monday that Ethiopia must have access to the Red Sea.
Hossamaldeen Ibrahim, an analyst at Bloomsbury Intelligence and Security Institute (BISI), said the narratives of both countries contain “verifiable elements”.
“The danger lies in the fact that each side now treats the other’s narrative as existential,” he told Al Jazeera.
Eritrea and Ethiopia fought a deadly border war from 1998 to 2000. Relations improved after Abiy came to power in 2018, but have soured again in recent years.
Professor Matthias Rompel from the Institute of Sociology at the Justus-Liebig-University Giessen in Germany, said that both sides have legitimate security concerns, but their accusations need to be distinguished from independently verified facts.
“Ethiopia’s allegations of Eritrean military incursions into Tigray… and …the scale of Eritrean involvement, and particularly allegations that Asmara is orchestrating the rebellion against Addis Ababa, remain difficult to substantiate independently,” he told Al Jazeera.
He added that the latest developments suggest that the confrontation is no longer merely about Tigray. “Ethiopia’s quest for Red Sea access, Eritrea’s concerns about sovereignty, and Egypt’s strategic rivalry with Ethiopia over the Nile are interconnected,” he said.
“The conflict, therefore, has the potential to destabilise the wider Horn of Africa, with repercussions for Sudan, Somalia and Red Sea security.”
What is the latest fighting about, and how is Eritrea allegedly involved?
Fighting escalated on September 23 when a rebel alliance, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), launched attacks against Ethiopian government forces across Tigray, Amhara and Afar regions.
The rebels captured Tigray’s capital, Mekelle, and its airport before announcing their withdrawal on October 3. Government-allied forces subsequently entered the city.
In the latest on the battlefront, government and allied forces took Idaga Hamus early Friday and Abiy-Adi, in the Tembien area, on Thursday afternoon, according to Ermiyas Ababu, a commander of the government-allied Tigray Peace Force.
Residents, according to Reuters news agency, also reported the takeover of Idaga Hamus. Gebremedhin Kihishen, a business owner in Tembien, said government-allied forces controlled Abiy-Adi.
It was unclear from those accounts who held the towns immediately before the reported government advance or whether Eritrean troops were involved in the fighting.
Ermiyas previously reported Eritrean personnel entering Adigrat on Tuesday and Idaga Hamus on Wednesday, citing reports from his personnel. Al Jazeera was unable to independently verify the claims.
The Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED), a United States-based conflict monitor, reported that Eritrean troops crossed into Ethiopia near Zalambessa and came under Ethiopian drone attack while advancing towards Idaga Hamus. Eritrea has yet to comment on the development.
Addis Ababa accuses Asmara of financing, arming and directing armed groups, as well as deploying troops inside Tigray. Eritrea denies the allegations, which have not been independently verified.
The renewed fighting threatens to unravel the 2022 peace agreement.
That conflict began in November 2020 after months of tensions between Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and the TPLF, which had dominated Ethiopian politics for nearly three decades before Abiy took office in 2018.
Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF, its longtime adversary. The war killed hundreds of thousands of people and was marked by allegations of massacres, sexual violence and widespread hunger.
The November 2022 Pretoria agreement ended major hostilities, but Eritrea was not a party to the deal. Relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara subsequently deteriorated.
Has Ethiopia sent troops north towards Eritrea?
Multiple media reports say Ethiopian government troops and allied militias entered Adigrat, a strategic city roughly 30km (19 miles) from the Eritrean border, on Saturday.
Three residents confirmed their presence to Reuters, while verified footage showed government-allied militia members walking through the city.
Associated Press news agency footage also showed Ethiopian military vehicles entering Adigrat as some residents welcomed the troops.
Government-allied forces have reported capturing Idaga Hamus and Abiy-Adi, while explosions and alleged drone strikes have been reported near Adigrat.
Are Ethiopia and Eritrea inching towards war?
Analysts warn that Ethiopia and Eritrea may already have moved beyond threats and into a dangerous phase of possible military confrontation.
BISI’s Ibrahim said the two countries have moved beyond “inching” towards war, noting that “The situation has entered a high-risk phase of limited but direct military confrontation with a real possibility of rapid escalation into interstate war.”
He warned that the severing of diplomatic ties removed the “last formal mechanism for crisis management”, while Ethiopian military advances towards the Eritrean border increased the risk of “miscalculation”.
Tom Gardner, a correspondent for The Economist, said the current tensions should be understood in the context of decades of hostility between the neighbours.
Their brief alliance during the 2020-2022 Tigray war was an exception and was driven by a shared hostility towards the TPLF, Gardner told Al Jazeera.
“The Ethiopian government’s strategic goal number one is access to the Red Sea, but also removing Eritrea’s government from the picture,” he noted.
“It’s very much looking like the most dangerous moment for the region since that 1998 to 2000 war.”
Rompel from Justus-Liebig-University Giessen said that the current situation is evolving. “The danger of a wider interstate conflict is real, and the situation has already moved beyond a purely diplomatic confrontation,” he said.
“The central danger is not necessarily that either government has decided to launch a full-scale war, but that military miscalculations, mutual distrust and domestic political pressures could trigger a further escalation neither side can easily control.
“A wider conflict is not inevitable, but the space for diplomatic de-escalation is rapidly narrowing,” he said.

articles.title: An estimated quarter of a million join London march marking three years of Gaza genocide
articles.body:
The Palestinian Forum in Britain (PFB) estimates that more than a quarter of a million people took part in a major demonstration in central London on Saturday 10 October, marking the third anniversary of Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza. Protesters called on Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s Government to impose a complete and immediate arms embargo on Israel.
The demonstration was organised by the Palestine Coalition, comprising the Palestinian Forum in Britain, Palestine Solidarity Campaign (PSC), Muslim Association of Britain (MAB), Stop the War Coalition, Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament (CND) and Friends of Al-Aqsa.
The march set off from Victoria Embankment and passed through central London before concluding with a rally and sit-in on Whitehall, near Downing Street. Participants carried Palestinian flags and placards demanding an end to British arms supplies to Israel and accountability for its crimes.
Chants of “Free Palestine”, “Stop Arming Israel”, “From the river to the sea, Palestine will be free” and “Stop the genocide” rang out along the route. Students, healthcare workers, trade unionists, academics and artists joined the demonstration.
Participants demanded a full ban on exports of weapons and military aircraft components to Israel, arguing that partial restrictions are insufficient while British-made components continue to reach the battlefield. They also called on the Government to recognise formally that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza and to turn expressions of sympathy into practical action.
OPINION: One year after ‘Britain Owes Palestine’, London shifts on the occupation but not on its own history
Speakers included former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn MP, John McDonnell MP and Zarah Sultana MP, alongside actor Khalid Abdalla and Dr Omar Abdel-Mannan, representing Health Workers for Palestine. UNISON general secretary Andrea Egan, PSC’s incoming director Aimee Shalan and Palestinian journalist Hala Hanina also addressed the rally, together with representatives of the organising groups.
PFB Chairman Adnan Hmidan participated in the demonstration and spoke at the protest.
Speakers stressed that the continued mobilisation after three years demonstrated the breadth of solidarity with Palestine and sustained public pressure on the Government to change its policies towards Israel. Participants expressed optimism and determination, viewing the turnout as a clear message that the campaign would continue until its demands were met.
The London demonstration coincided with the Global Alliance for Palestine’s call for an international day of solidarity. Actions were called in hundreds of cities across more than 60 countries, with over 200 organisations participating in the wider mobilisation.
PFB reiterated the coalition’s demands for an end to the arms trade with Israel, the suspension of military and intelligence support that facilitates violations of international law, unrestricted humanitarian access to Gaza, and action to stop British institutions and businesses supporting occupation and settlement activity.
The protest continued the series of national marches organised by the Palestine Coalition since October 2023. PFB thanks everyone who took part and urges supporters to maintain pressure through campaigning and engagement with their elected representatives. The campaign for Palestinian freedom and justice must continue.

articles.title: Powers greater than US tried to conquer Iran but ended up in ‘dustbin of history,’ Rezaei says
articles.body:
Powers greater than US tried to conquer Iran but ended up in ‘dustbin of history,’ Rezaei says
TEHRAN — Iran’s top security official says Tehran will determine the outcome of its confrontation with Washington, rules out a return to previous diplomatic norms and warns of potential retaliation against US assets in the event of renewed aggression.
Major General Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council (SNSC), has warned that the United States will face the same fate as previous powers that attempted to subjugate Iran, saying even stronger empires ultimately disappeared into the “dustbin of history.”
In an exclusive interview with Press TV on Saturday, Rezaei said Washington had suffered repeated defeats in its confrontation with Iran and had increasingly resorted to economic warfare, which he characterized as a response to its failure to achieve its objectives through military pressure.
He stressed that Iran, rather than the United States, would determine when the confrontation ends, adding that Tehran would continue to resist until its demands were met.
Addressing the US military presence in West Asia, Rezaei pointed to the withdrawal of American forces from Iraq as evidence, in his assessment, of Washington’s failure to impose its military agenda on the region. He described the development as vindication of Iran’s longstanding opposition to the deployment of US forces in the region.
Rezaei also said more than 30 million Iranians had registered for the Janfada (Sacrifice for Iran) campaign, which was intended to mobilize volunteers prepared to take up arms in the event of US aggression.
On diplomacy, the SNSC secretary said Iran would not return to its previous diplomatic norms, while emphasizing that Tehran was not abandoning diplomacy altogether.
His remarks signaled that, although diplomatic engagement remained an option, Iran’s approach would be shaped by its assessment of the confrontation with Washington and the need to secure its demands.
Rezaei also warned that renewed US aggression could expose American assets to retaliation, including key data systems and artificial intelligence sensors.
Rezaei invokes ancient Rome to counter ‘civilizational war’ narrative
In a separate part of his remarks, Rezaei invoked the defeat of Roman forces by the Sasanian Empire under King Shapur I to challenge the framing of the confrontation with Iran as a civilizational war by US officials.
The reference draws on a significant episode in Iranian history. In 260 AD, Shapur I defeated the Roman emperor Valerian at the Battle of Edessa and captured him, marking a major setback for Rome in its eastern campaigns.
By invoking that episode, Rezaei placed the current confrontation within a broader historical narrative of Iran’s resistance to foreign powers and attempts at domination.
Hormuz tensions and the dispute with Washington
Rezaei also identified Washington and its regional allies as central to the tensions surrounding the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most strategically important maritime corridors for oil and gas shipments.
Iran’s restrictions on passage through the strait followed the latest round of US-Israeli military aggression. The disruption affected a critical route for international energy trade and contributed to heightened concerns over global oil and energy supplies. The resulting market pressures also prompted the United States and the International Energy Agency (IEA) to draw on strategic reserves on multiple occasions.
Following the signing of an Iran-US memorandum of understanding in Islamabad in June, Tehran reopened the waterway. Iran subsequently said Washington had breached the understanding by imposing a blockade on Iranian ports, prompting the country’s armed forces to close the maritime corridor again.
The dispute over the strait has become a major point of contention between Tehran and Washington, linking military developments and diplomatic commitments to the security of international shipping and global energy markets.
Rezaei’s remarks underscored Tehran’s position that any resolution to the confrontation must take account of Iran’s security demands and its role in the region. His comments also made clear that Iran does not regard a return to the previous diplomatic framework as inevitable, even as it continues to leave the door open to diplomacy.

articles.title: Could Egyptian military deployment in Somalia upset Horn of Africa balance of power? - analysis
articles.body:
Egyptian technical military teams, including advisors, trainers, and officers, are reportedly preparing for the deployment of troops to Somalia, in the first such move since the signing of a joint military cooperation agreement between the two sides in 2024, The New Arab reported on Friday.
This potentially important development comes as Pakistan and Turkey may also be deploying forces to Saudi Arabia to support the Kingdom’s defenses against the Houthis.
The report at The New Arab says the deployment to Somalia could come “in light of bilateral security and military cooperation between the two countries and within the African Union Mission, widely known as AUSSOM.” It also comes as Turkey has forces in Somalia. However, despite the support, this has not stabilized Somalia enough.
The report added that “the Egyptian troops will reportedly be positioned in the Ceelcade region which used to house the Cisiley Airfield on the immediate northern outskirts of Mogadishu, within the Middle Shabelle region - in the low-lying semi-arid coastal hinterland just north of the Banaadir administrative boundary, around 400 kilometers from the nearest point to Ethiopia's shared border with Somalia.”
Any deployment could tip the balance of power in the Horn of Africa. In early October, Egypt reached out to leaders in Eritrea, Sudan, and Somalia. Egypt is concerned about the spiraling military conflicts that are taking place to the south of Egypt. It’s worth understanding this. Egypt’s military met Somali Defense Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi in September.
Houthis advance to Bab el-Mandeb strait, target Saudi airports
This all comes amid many developments. On one side of the Red Sea, the Houthis advanced in September to the Bab el-Mandeb strait. Then Saudi Arabia backed a Yemeni government offensive against the Houthis. Now the Houthis are targeting Saudi airports. Riyadh is a friend of Egypt.
Egypt and Somalia have four other major conflicts. Ethiopia's conflicts involve the federal government in Addis Ababa, led by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, and several regional movements. The most devastating recent conflict was the Tigray war, fought from 2020 to 2022 between federal forces and their allies, including Eritrean troops, and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF). On September 21, seven rebel groups in Ethiopia formed a new alliance. Egypt has opposed the Ethiopian Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam.
In Sudan, Egypt backs the Sudanese army. The army is fighting a civil war. The US has tried to push for a ceasefire and banned Sudan from the UN General Assembly. Sudan's civil war began in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), commanded by General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, commonly known as Hemedti.
The SAF represents Sudan's established military institutions and is associated with the internationally recognized state authorities. The RSF emerged from paramilitary networks linked to the Darfur conflict and has developed its own military, economic, and territorial power. Support for both sides fuels Sudan's conflict. For instance, Sudan’s military accuses the UAE of backing the RSF. This conflict has likely destabilized Ethiopia.
Meanwhile, in Somalia, the government is fighting terrorist groups such as al-Shabaab. Somalia’s government also doesn’t control most of the country. Israel recognized Somaliland in December 2025. Puntland also operates as an autonomous state. Egypt sending forces could change things in Somalia and also potentially affect Ethiopia. It could also change Eritrea’s calculations.
Libya split between Turkey-backed GNU, Egypt-backed Haftar
Libya, a bit farther away in North Africa, borders Egypt and Sudan. As such, it also has a role to play.
In western Libya, the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity (GNU) is one part of the mosaic of the country. In eastern Libya, Field Marshal Khalifa Haftar commands the Libyan National Army (LNA), also known as the Libyan Arab Armed Forces. His coalition controls much of eastern and southern Libya and is aligned with the rival eastern-based political authorities.
In the past, Turkey backed the GNU while Egypt, the UAE and others backed Haftar. In September, The New Arab reported that Saddam Haftar, Khalifa's son, went to the UAE for meetings. Whether true or not, what these reports indicate is intense interest in the Horn of Africa by media in the Gulf.
These four conflicts - Sudan, Somalia, Libya, and Ethiopia - are increasingly interconnected. Ethiopia's renewed fighting and tensions with Eritrea threaten wider instability in the Horn of Africa. Sudan's war involves cross-border armed networks, while Somalia's security depends partly on neighboring countries' military commitments. Libya remains influenced by competing interests from the Mediterranean, the Gulf, and elsewhere. Any change in the balance could reverberate to the Red Sea, the Eastern Mediterranean, and the Indian Ocean.

articles.title: German opposition demands Trump-style diesel deal with Russia
articles.body:
German opposition demands Trump-style diesel deal with Russia
Two German opposition parties have called for restoring economic ties with Russia following US President Donald Trump’s example in striking a diesel deal with Moscow, challenging Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s sanctions policy as soaring fuel prices put further pressure on Europe’s largest economy.
The right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the left-wing Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which together command a majority in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt’s parliament, are preparing a joint resolution demanding an end to anti-Russia sanctions and financial support for Kiev amid growing frustration over Berlin’s foreign policy and its economic consequences.
“Germany also needs a diesel deal with Russia,” Claudia Wittig, deputy leader of the BSW parliamentary group, said, according to German media.
Wittig described fuel prices at German filling stations as “a scandal,” arguing that sanctions against Moscow had “failed across the board” and were primarily hurting Germany itself. She insisted that Berlin should go further than a one-off fuel agreement and resume regular imports of Russian oil and gas to help rescue German industry.
“We need policies that think more about Köthen than Kiev,” Wittig said earlier, referring to a German town in Saxony-Anhalt. “We can no longer afford this war.”
AfD co-leader Alice Weidel also hailed Trump’s deal with Moscow, accusing Merz of undermining Germany’s economy with sanctions and expensive liquefied natural gas imports.
“That’s how it’s done!” she wrote on X on Saturday. “While Merz ruins Germany with sanctions and expensive LNG, Trump practices realpolitik. German interests instead of escalation!”
The initiative comes after Trump reached a surprise agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday to ease a global diesel shortage. Washington subsequently suspended sanctions on Russian diesel exports, allowing Moscow to release hundreds of thousands of tons of fuel onto international markets.
Trump has repeatedly blamed Vladimir Zelensky for exacerbating the global energy crisis by targeting Russian oil refineries despite Washington’s warnings. On Saturday, he suggested that Ukrainians should replace their leader, accusing Zelensky of rejecting numerous opportunities to settle the conflict.
The joint resolution is scheduled for a vote in the Saxony-Anhalt parliament in Magdeburg on October 14. AfD and BSW hold a combined majority following September’s regional elections, although the state legislature has no authority to lift federal or EU sanctions against Russia. The initiative also marks a further breach of Germany’s longstanding political “firewall” against the AfD, which mainstream parties have sought to exclude from power despite its growing electoral support.
Merz’s government flatly rejected any prospects of easing its anti-Russia stance and vowed to pursue even more sanctions against Moscow. Government spokesman Stefan Kornelius insisted on Saturday that Berlin’s support for Kiev remained “unwavering.” Meanwhile, Green Party co-leader Franziska Brantner blasted Trump’s agreement with Putin as the height of “unscrupulousness.”
The chancellor, whose popularity has sunk so low that he faces calls to resign from within his own party, has faced mounting criticism over the impact of his policies on Germany. Wagenknecht previously accused him of turning German citizens into “cash cows for Ukraine.” Moscow has likewise accused Merz of acting more like a “Ukrainian chancellor” than a German leader.

articles.title: Iran to pursue legal case over US strike on Minab school in foreign courts: Gharibabadi
articles.body:
Iran to pursue legal case over US strike on Minab school in foreign courts: Gharibabadi
MINAB – Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister for Legal and International Affairs says Tehran is pursuing legal action over the American strike on the Shajareh Tayyebeh school in Minab, with documentation completed and a special committee formed to file lawsuits in foreign courts.
Kazem Gharibabadi made the remarks on Sunday during a visit to the school site and in meetings with the families of the victims, stressing that legal follow-up is underway at both the domestic and international levels.
"The martyrdom of 168 people — mostly schoolchildren, along with a number of parents and teachers — is a great tragedy for the families, the people of Minab and all of Iran, and we share in the grief and suffering of these families," Gharibabadi said.
He said schools, academic and educational centers and hospitals are protected under international humanitarian law during armed conflicts, adding that attacks on such sites constitute a serious violation of those rules.
Gharibabadi said the documentation of the incident has been collected inside the country and that the judicial case will be heard after completing the necessary procedures. He added that relevant bodies are preparing dossiers for filing claims abroad.
"A special committee with the participation of relevant agencies has been formed in Tehran to follow up on this crime, and the documentation received from the judicial system will form the basis for legal action to file lawsuits in several countries," he said.
He noted that the Foreign Ministry, the Legal Vice Presidency and other responsible bodies are deploying their capacities for the legal, political and diplomatic pursuit of the case, adding that the President has emphasized the need to follow up on the crimes committed.
"The families of the martyrs of the Shajareh Tayyebeh school must witness justice being served," Gharibabadi said. "The follow-up of this case will not be limited to inside the country, and we will use international legal capacities to hold the perpetrators accountable."
Referring to other cases related to attacks carried out during the war, including the strike on the Lamerd stadium, Gharibabadi said their legal pursuit is also on the agenda and efforts are underway to pursue the responsibility of the perpetrators in competent authorities.
He also praised the role of the people of Hormozgan in defending the country and stressed support for the martyrs' families and continued pursuit of their legal demands, saying the Foreign Ministry will use its full capacity to help ensure accountability and justice.
On the Strait of Hormuz, Gharibabadi said the waterway has become a symbol of Iranian identity and that Iran will use its capacities to confront enemies. Stressing that Iran was not the initiator of the war, he said the country is defending itself against aggression, has not started a war in the past two centuries, but has stood against aggressors.
He also warned that Iran's response in what he described as the 40-day war differed from that in the 12-day war, cautioning that in the event of renewed military action by the enemy, the Islamic Republic's reaction will be different from the past, and expressed hope that the other sides will act rationally to avoid a repeat of the confrontation.
In the early hours of Feb. 28, 2026 — the first hours of what Tehran describes as the joint US-Israeli aggression against Iran — the Shajareh Tayyebeh school in Minab was hit three times at intervals by missiles. In the incident, 168 people, including schoolgirls and schoolboys, as well as teachers, school staff and parents, were killed.
In a separate incident, five people, including a child, were killed and 68 others, mostly women and children, were injured in a US airstrike late on Sept. 1, 2026, on a residential house in the port of Kuhestak in Sirik County, where people were attending a wedding ceremony. Kuhestak is located in Sirik County in southeastern Hormozgan Province.
Minab, the second most populous county in Hormozgan Province with a population of over 300,000, is located 90 kilometers east of Bandar Abbas.

articles.title: British Prime Minister Burnham reiterates support for Ukraine in call with Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Esra Tekin
11 October 2026•Update: 11 October 2026
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Saturday reaffirmed London’s support for Ukraine during a call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband also reiterated the UK’s backing for Ukraine in talks with Andrii Sybiha, the nation’s foreign minister.
The Prime Minister’s Office said that in a phone call with Zelenskyy, Burnham voiced solidarity with Ukraine amid the challenges caused by Russia’s most recent attacks. The two leaders also discussed sanctions on Russia.
A statement by 10 Downing Street said the call also addressed the importance of maintaining pressure on Russia.
Voicing determination to continue to strengthen sanctions against Russia, building on the measures targeting Russia announced this week, the statement also expressed the UK's readiness to take additional steps to restrict Russia’s ability to wage war.
It urged Moscow to agree to an energy ceasefire covering attacks on energy facilities.
The statement added that infrastructure in Ukraine and maritime trade in the Black Sea should not be targeted.
An energy ceasefire would also have a positive effect on global markets, it said.
US' new diesel fuel deal with Russia
“The UK stands shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine and will continue to stand with them until they prevail," Miliband wrote on US social media company X following his meeting with Sybiha in northern Ukraine.
The statements came after US President Donald Trump said his Friday call with Russian President Vladimir Putin had been “extremely successful.”
Trump said an agreement had been reached for Russia to immediately supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the US and global markets, followed by millions of tons in the near future, depending on the condition of its diesel refineries.
Zelenskyy criticized the deal, saying that easing sanctions on Russia without a de-escalation agreement would be an "obvious weakness.”

articles.title: Yemen breaking the blockade and beginning a new phase
articles.body:
Yemen breaking the blockade and beginning a new phase
LONDON – How Ansarallah succeeded in breaking the Saudi-imposed air blockade on Yemen is worthy of attention. The process began with an Ansarallah delegation’s trip to Tehran to attend the funeral of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, who was assassinated in a joint U.S.-Israeli air raid on his office on February 28.
The delegation flew from Sanaa International Airport to Tehran but was forced to land at Hodeidah Airport on its return after Saudi jets bombed Sanaa airport.
The delegation’s journey to Tehran and its return marked the beginning of a new phase in line with broader regional developments. The message was clear: the emerging balance of power no longer allowed the Saudi-imposed air blockade on Yemen to continue.
Amid the war between the United States and Iran, the message was that any settlement must be comprehensive and include the entire Axis of Resistance, allowing it to exercise its rights without being denied recognition. The new equation became one in which a blockade would be met with a blockade, and the continuation of the blockade on Yemen would lead to countermeasures affecting the other side.
Developments then progressed to the point where the balance of power on the ground began to shift in favor of Ansarallah, representing the extension of the Axis of Resistance towards control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Ansarallah began advancing and taking control of the western coast of the Red Sea, reaching beyond Mokha. This advance extended to a point in the Bab al-Mandab Strait and the island opposite it.
This development was not coincidental. Rather, it formed part of a broader process aimed at changing the balance of power in the region. Ultimately, the situation developed to the point where the Axis of Resistance came to control the Strait of Hormuz, while the Bab al-Mandab Strait also came under the its control.
The combination of control and influence over the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab means that approximately 40% of global energy supplies have come under the influence of the Axis of Resistance. Having this degree of influence over the world's most important energy corridors makes the bloc a far more influential force globally. This shift in the balance of power is ushering all resistance fronts into a new phase.
We are facing a new situation unlike any previous one in terms of the scale of its influence and its capacity to alter existing equations. No previous situation has reached this level of influence. It could bring the Axis of Resistance to a level of influence equal to, or perhaps greater than, that of the U.S.-Israeli alliance, despite the latter’s military and intelligence superiority.
This American-Israeli superiority, which has severely struck the resistance fronts in Gaza, Lebanon, and the West Bank, has now been met by a corresponding counterweight. Control over the Bab al-Mandab is overturning the balance of power, with consequences for the Israeli occupation entity as a whole. The importance of these developments is that they do not concern military confrontation alone; they also affect strategic and economic interests connected to energy and global trade.
This is occurring alongside a transformation in the image of the Israeli occupation entity in global public opinion, where it has become increasingly rejected in the conscience of the world. One indication is that a British minister has declared that Gaza represents a reproach to the global conscience.
Similarly, the actions of settlers in the West Bank, including acts of destruction and violations, have come under condemnation, to the point that some Western officials have described them as terrorists. These developments are new, and they would not have emerged in the same form were it not for the changes that have taken place in the balance of power and influence in the region.
Control over and the ability to influence global energy supplies do not affect the military dimension alone; it also extends to the global economy. Influence over energy supplies affects energy prices and consequently the prices of consumer goods, including food items and metals. It may also have repercussions for global stock exchanges and financial markets. Therefore, control over the corridors that affect the supply of energy, metals, fertilizers, and food gives the Axis of Resistance greater capacity to influence the global economy and financial markets.
Taken together, these developments could constitute a turning point in the course of the world and in the nature of the balance of power that exists within it. We may be facing the possibility of building a new world in which the balance of power differs from that which prevailed during previous periods. In this new world, the resistance bloc could play an influential role. Accordingly, what began as steps to break the blockade on Yemen could extend beyond the borders of Yemen and the region, becoming part of a broader shift in the global balance of power.
The United States does not want to enter this war because direct American involvement would mean preventing US ships from passing through the Red Sea. Washington also does not want to become involved in two wars simultaneously.
The United States is therefore compelled to pursue a piecemeal settlement, one that does not encompass all fronts, including the Yemeni front. There may be a settlement to the U.S.-Iran conflict, but the Yemeni issue itself must ultimately be resolved through a Saudi-Yemeni dialogue.
However, acknowledging the Yemeni situation and the effective control that Ansarallah exercises over parts of Yemen entail an American recognition of the new reality. It would also form part of a broader recognition of Iran and the larger resistance bloc.
The strikes against Saudi Arabia’s oil and energy infrastructure are part of the Yemeni pressure campaign against the Saudi Kingdom. On the one hand, Saudi Arabia is being placed under pressure from the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. On the other hand, pressure on global energy supplies creates additional pressure on Saudi Arabia to accept the situation in Yemen, including the role of Ansarallah.
Yemen is following a principle of responding to siege with siege. When the Yemeni capital is attacked, Yemen also strikes Riyadh’s energy infrastructure.
The persistence of the Yemeni position, combined with Saudi Arabia’s inability to overcome Yemen and the failure of other parties to enter the fighting alongside the kingdom, will ultimately give the Yemenis the upper hand. This could lead to a settlement that recognizes the existence and role of Ansarallah in Yemen. This, in turn, will serve the broader regional context: a U.S.-Iranian agreement that will acknowledges the new balance of power and recognize the right of the Axis of Resistance to exist and maintain its position in the region.

articles.title: Fresh strike sparks fire at Riyadh airport: Saudi-led coalition
articles.body:
A fire broke out at Terminal 4 of King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh on Sunday after it was struck by an unidentified projectile, the Saudi-led coalition said.
In a statement, the coalition said relevant authorities were responding to the fire, without providing details on the extent of the damage or whether there were casualties.
In a subsequent statement, the coalition announced that air defences had intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile near the airport.
It did not clarify whether the intercepted missile was linked to the projectile that struck the terminal or identify who was responsible for the attack.
The incident came a day after an attack on the same airport killed 12 people and injured 309, according to figures announced by Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation overnight Saturday into Sunday.
The authority announced Saturday that operations at the airport were temporarily suspended pending the completion of damage assessments and safety checks on its facilities, in coordination with relevant authorities.
King Khalid International Airport also came under two Houthi militia attacks Thursday, October 8, one targeting its facilities and the other a Saudi Arabian Airlines aircraft.
The aviation authority said Friday that those attacks killed three Saudi citizens and injured several citizens and residents of different nationalities, while also causing material damage.
Earlier Houthi militia attacks targeted Abha and King Khalid International Airport on October 6 and 7, killing three residents of Moroccan, Algerian and Sudanese nationality and injuring 36 people, according to Saudi authorities.
The latest incident brings the number of attacks on King Khalid International Airport since Tuesday to five within a week, according to an Anadolu tally of official Saudi statements.
Saudi authorities have not identified those responsible for the attacks, although the Houthi militia announced Thursday that it had targeted King Khalid International Airport with a ballistic missile.

articles.title: Paying tolls to Iran
articles.body:
Paying tolls to Iran
In a commentary, Kayhan challenged Trump’s claims about the Strait of Hormuz, arguing that the reality on the ground differs from Washington’s narrative. The newspaper cited reports from Western media suggesting that vessels crossing the strategic waterway continue to pay various fees to Iran in exchange for safe passage.
Referring to data from maritime analytics firm Kpler, some oil exporters in the Persian Gulf may be providing Iran with payments amounting to 10 to 20 percent of the value of their oil shipments to ensure security while traveling through the strait. Iran has strengthened its defensive posture and enforcement capabilities in the region.
 
Chinese vessels have continued to move through the waterway despite sanctions pressure and maintained that Iran has demonstrated an ability to bypass American restrictions and preserve a degree of access to international trade.
Shargh: Iran must avoid its opponents’ traps
Shargh devoted its commentary to the challenges and schemes facing a powerful Iran. International politics is not based on ideal concepts of fairness, and genuine “win-win” outcomes rarely exist. In every negotiation, one party typically gains more than the other, making power and influence the principal factors shaping diplomatic results. Iran’s rivals are attempting to create situations that could draw the country into costly and internationally justifiable conflicts. Such efforts are designed to weaken Iran and provide advantages to its foes. For that reason, Shargh stressed the importance of strategic patience and careful decision-making. Diplomacy without power is ineffective in today’s world, and identified the Iranian people as the country’s most valuable source of strength. It concluded that foreign governments increasingly recognize the significance of public support in Iran and therefore seek opportunities to exploit vulnerabilities or create political and social pressure.
Sobh-e-No: military action not in Trump’s interest
Sobh-e-No examined the reasons why the United States is unlikely to launch a military strike against Iran before the November elections. Iran possesses significant capabilities and cannot be easily pressured into accepting Washington’s demands. Any major strategic error by Trump could generate two separate challenges at once: a security crisis abroad and political repercussions inside the United States. The article also noted that Trump has historically preferred avoiding lengthy military engagements and instead favors using military power as leverage to achieve political objectives. According to the paper, launching an attack before an election would eliminate that leverage while exposing Washington to unnecessary risks. As a result, Trump has chosen to postpone any serious military option until after voters cast their ballots. It further argued that years of maximum economic and military pressure have not compelled Iran to surrender. Instead, tensions in the Persian Gulf have become an increasingly sensitive issue that could create political difficulties for Republican leaders in Washington.
Sazandegi: Strengthening regional influence
Sazandegi argued the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) summit in Turkmenistan provided an important opportunity for Tehran to reinforce its regional influence. President Pezeshkian’s trip served two main objectives: expanding cooperation with neighboring countries and discussing political and environmental issues surrounding the Caspian region. The visit allowed Iran to underline its regional role while participating in consultations on the worsening environmental conditions of the Caspian Sea. The trip was more than a routine diplomatic gathering, presenting an opportunity to combine regional diplomacy with environmental cooperation. However, Sazandegi argued that the ultimate success of such efforts will depend on whether discussions and agreements reached during the summit can be transformed into practical policies. In its view, only concrete measures aimed at reducing tensions and addressing ecological challenges will ensure meaningful results for the region.
Arman-e-Emrooz: Looking beyond the West-East divide
Arman-e-Emrooz focused on the need to redefine Iran’s geopolitical position in a rapidly changing Asia. The newspaper argued that the rise of China, India, Indonesia, and other emerging powers demonstrates that Asia is no longer merely an arena for Western competition. Instead, it has become one of the world’s most significant centers of economic growth, political influence, and strategic power. The article suggested that these changes provide Iran with an opportunity to rethink its place in the international system. It argued that Iranian foreign policy should move beyond the traditional choice between the West and the East. Expanding strategic options, the newspaper said, requires a broader and more flexible approach rather than simply replacing one geopolitical orientation with another. Within this framework, Arman-e-Emrooz highlighted the concept of the “Global South” as a useful basis for foreign policy. It argued that the idea allows Iran to connect issues of national identity, geopolitical interests, and economic priorities. By emphasizing shared experiences of independence and development, benefiting from shifts in global power distribution, and expanding cooperation in trade, investment, energy, technology, transportation, and security, Iran could strengthen both its regional and international position.

Intelligence agencies warn against Russian attempts to assassinate European defense CEOs - report

Western intelligence agencies have warned CEOs and other senior employees at defense companies that they are being targeted by Kremlin operatives. According to officials from five European intelligence agencies who spoke with the Financial Times, Europe's defense company bosses that Russia is stepping up efforts to assassinate them, prompting companies to increase personal security around top executives.
With battlefield progress deadlocked in Ukraine and Russia's economy struggling, the Kremlin has ordered an expansion of sabotage and "hybrid" operations in Europe as it seeks to weaken support for Kyiv. Assassinations against European civilian targets, once considered taboo even by Russia's spy agencies, are becoming a prominent part of those plans, according to the intelligence services.
Executives at smaller companies, especially those making drones or components, are also being targeted. "The threat level has risen in Europe. To property but also to people," one senior European intelligence official said.
Sinan Selen, head of Germany's domestic intelligence service BfV, told German lawmakers on Monday, "Russia is engaged in the deliberate planning of acts of violence against individuals by state or state-controlled actors." Selen also stated, "We are observing a further development of these actions in terms of the targets, the methods and the actors involved, including the use of organised crime structures."
Suggested articles
Several defence executives, speaking anonymously, told the FT they escalated close-protection arrangements in the past six months on the advice of government security services.
"The main goal from the Russian perspective is still psychological," one intelligence official said. "Just by making people feel they might be a target, they are having their effect. They want individuals to think twice before doing business with Ukraine."
One official stressed that many Russian efforts remain amateurish and easily countered. In August, the two holidaymakers arrested in Sweden near the property of Saab CEO Micael Johansson were released shortly afterwards.

articles.title: Year into cease-fire, promised peace never arrived for Gazans
articles.body:
A year after a U.S.-brokered cease-fire took effect in the Gaza Strip, residents still living in displacement camps under near-daily Israeli airstrikes say the truce has not brought the promised peace.
Israel has reduced its attack intensity but continues strikes and now controls over 70% of Gaza. The cease-fire plan's promised reconstruction of the devastated Palestinian territory has not materialized.
"Nothing has changed for the better; everything has got worse, they lie to us, it is all lies," Fatima Awkal, a displaced woman in Gaza City, said.
"Martyrs are still falling, people are still being injured, the shelling continues and we cannot even find a moment's peace from the constant buzzing of the drones overhead."
On the streets of Gaza City, rows of white tents line passageways cleared of rubble from destroyed homes, while in the distance, blown-out windows gape from building facades still standing.
Ahmed Jonaid, another displaced Palestinian in Gaza City, said he had hoped to return home after the cease-fire.
"We thought we would experience some happiness and return to our homes. Instead, we see ourselves suffering in refugee camps, sleeping on makeshift mats," the 51-year-old said as he carried two jerrycans of water back to his tent.
Israel's genocidal war, which broke out after the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas incursion, has displaced almost all of Gaza's more than 2 million residents at least once.
With 82% of all standing structures in Gaza either damaged or destroyed as of mid-2026, according to the U.N., many residents still live in tents or makeshift shelters, where lack of hygiene has led to outbreaks of disease.
Ahmed Shawan, a doctor at a hospital in the southern city of Khan Younis, said he had yet to see the cease-fire take effect.
"It has been a full year since the cease-fire was declared, yet it exists only on paper," he said.
The agreement's second phase called for a political transition away from Hamas rule, with technocrat Ali Shaath appointed head of a new National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG).
Five countries, including Morocco, have agreed to join the International Stabilization Force (ISF) tasked with post-war preparations, but its troops have not yet started operating in Gaza.
Israel controls all entry points into the territory and continues to allow only a limited amount of aid, keeping the price of basic goods too high for ordinary Gazans like Ismail Hamouda.
The 47-year-old father, displaced from Jabalia in the north to Gaza City, listed what residents still lack: potable water, food, financial assistance.
"Here in the displacement camps, we thought that after a year of cease-fire things would improve," he said. "Unfortunately, the situation is worsening gradually. We are still displaced."

articles.title: FAA warns US airlines to exercise caution in Saudi Arabia flights
articles.body:
The Federal Aviation Administration told US airlines on Sunday to exercise caution when flying to or over Saudi Arabia, citing safety threats tied to ongoing military activity and interference with navigation systems.
The FAA Notice to Airmen, which lasts until December 10, follows Saturday and Sunday strikes at Riyadh's international airport by the Houthis. The attack on Saturday killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.
Another attack on Sunday killed one and injured 11 more people.
"Threats could pose a potential risk to aircraft at all altitudes, including overflight, the arrival, and departure phases of flight," the FAA said, warning of the "potentially hazardous situation."
The notice also applies to operators of airplanes that are registered in the US. Riyadh airport remains closed to flights through at least 5 p.m. EDT Monday.
Embassies in Middle East advise against travel to Saudi airports
US carrier Delta Air Lines is set to begin direct flights from Atlanta to Riyadh on October 23.
Delta did not immediately respond to a request for comment Sunday, but CEO Ed Bastian told CNBC last week that "safety is going to make the call" about whether the airline will move forward.
In September 2025, FedEx launched its first dedicated flight into Saudi Arabia. The FedEx Boeing 777 freighter operates six times per week, connecting the Americas and Europe to Riyadh, with connections to Guangzhou and Shanghai.
On Monday, the United Kingdom Embassy in Saudi Arabia also advised "against all but essential travel to the cities of Jeddah and Dammam and to all Saudi airports," according to a statement posted on social media.
The US Embassy in Jordan issued a travel advisory on Friday to Americans in the Middle East in light of current hostilities in the region, specifically pointing to the recent Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia's Riyadh airport.
"Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties," the embassy wrote, adding that "the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly" and that Americans should monitor the situation closely, particularly if they are planning travel to or from the region.
Also on Friday, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency EASA recommended that airlines not operate within additional portions of Saudi airspace after the Houthis attacked Riyadh's airport.

articles.title: A deadly airstrike hits a Sudan-Egypt border gold mine, killing at least 13 miners
