articles.title: Syria between potential intervention in Yemen and domestic crises
articles.body:
Syria between potential intervention in Yemen and domestic crises
TEHRAN – The costs and risks of Syrian intervention in Yemen could begin to mount from the moment a decision is made.
Following Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa’s visit to Riyadh a few days earlier, reports on October 7, citing U.S. officials, said Saudi Arabia and Syria were discussing the possibility of deploying Syrian forces to Yemen to participate in military operations against the Sanaa government.
According to reports, between 10,000 and 20,000 soldiers could be sent, with the 90th and 84th Divisions among the formations under consideration. Al-Sharaa was reportedly seriously weighing the proposal but has not yet made a final decision.
Meanwhile, Ahmad Mowaffaq Zaidan, an adviser to the Syrian presidency, denied that Riyadh had asked Damascus to send troops to Yemen. Syria’s official position has emphasized that rebuilding the country remains the priority and that any military cooperation must proceed through official channels and within existing bilateral frameworks.
The official denial, however, does not negate the existence of multiple reports suggesting that various options are under consideration. Nor do the leaks amount to a finalized agreement. To date, there has been no official announcement of a Syrian decision to intervene, no confirmed Saudi request, and no publicly disclosed agreement on the matter.
The significance of these reports, however, extends beyond the question of whether Syrian forces will ultimately be deployed to Yemen. The very fact that such a possibility is being discussed raises broader questions about the regional role Syria’s new leadership might assume, the limits of its commitments to its allies, and the criteria it will apply when deciding whether to intervene militarily beyond its borders.
Lebanon and Yemen: Why the different calculations?
The debate takes on greater significance when viewed alongside President al-Sharaa’s position on the possibility of intervening in Lebanon against Hezbollah, despite an explicit appeal from U.S. President Donald Trump himself. Al-Sharaa ruled out Syrian military intervention in Lebanon, arguing that such a move would require a request from the Lebanese government and that neither the Syrian army nor the country’s internal situation was ready for such a step.
These considerations are even more consequential in the case of Yemen. Geographically, Yemen is much farther away, and its conflict is exceptionally complex. Military intervention could expose Syria to security and political risks extending well beyond the battlefield.
If the Syrian army’s lack of readiness was sufficient reason to rule out intervention in Lebanon, what has changed to make sending thousands of troops to Yemen a viable option? Have Syria’s military capabilities improved sufficiently within a matter of months to support a large-scale overseas deployment? Or does Damascus’s relationship with Riyadh lead it to assess the risks differently?
What could Damascus gain and lose?
Reports suggesting that Syrian forces could be sent to Yemen are closely linked to the central role Saudi Arabia has played in supporting the new leadership in Damascus.
Riyadh has been one of al-Sharaa’s most prominent political backers and has helped advance Arab and international efforts to restore engagement with Syria. It has also played a role in efforts to lift sanctions and create conditions for the country’s reintegration into the region. For Damascus, relations with Riyadh extend beyond economic interests to encompass the pursuit of political and security support at an exceptionally sensitive stage of the country’s transition.
Damascus may view closer military cooperation with Riyadh as an opportunity to build political trust, secure economic and security assistance, and expand its room for regional maneuver. Through such cooperation, it could also seek to demonstrate that Syria is a capable partner able to contribute to a broader framework of Arab security, rather than simply a country seeking external assistance.
These potential benefits, however, are not enough on their own to justify sending thousands of troops into a foreign conflict. Military intervention abroad inevitably carries serious consequences. In addition to exposing Syrian forces to retaliatory attacks, it could expand the circle of Syria’s enemies and draw the country into a conflict whose outcome and terms of settlement it cannot determine independently.
The risks become even more pronounced if the proposed mission remains poorly defined.
Would Syria’s role be confined to protecting Saudi facilities and strategic sites, with its forces assigned clearly defined defensive responsibilities? Or would Syrian troops participate in offensive operations inside Yemen?
The distinction between these scenarios is fundamental. It would determine the legal, military, and political risks involved, as well as whether the mission would remain limited and time-bound or evolve into a prolonged military entanglement.
Domestic crises cannot be overlooked
These discussions are unfolding as Syria continues to face serious and deeply complex domestic challenges.
The integration of the “Syrian Democratic Forces” into state institutions has yet to produce a final settlement. Arrangements governing control, administration, and security in northeastern Syria remain contested, while ongoing protests and political mobilization in Hasakah Governorate underscore the depth and gravity of the unresolved issue.
The situation is even more precarious in the south, where much of Suwayda Governorate remains outside the Syrian state’s control. The far-reaching demands advanced by the community’s spiritual leader, Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri, reflect the depth of the divisions confronting the government.
At the same time, Israel’s invasions and aggression continue across southern Syria. This is occurring alongside the resumption of excavation and fortification work aimed at completing the occupying regime’s so-called “Sufa 53” line inside Syrian territory, consolidating new realities on the ground at the expense of Syrian sovereignty.
Under these circumstances, the challenge is not simply to restore control over the territory facing aggression but to prevent the fragmentation of central authority in parts of Syria, at a time when the capital itself remains within the reach of the Zionist regime’s military aggression.
How, then, can a state facing a direct threat near its capital and struggling to preserve its territorial integrity in the south seriously consider sending thousands of troops to Yemen, thousands of kilometers away? What strategic imperative could justify diverting troops and resources to a foreign theater while the struggle to consolidate sovereignty within the country’s own borders remains unresolved?
Between a leak and a decision
Potential military involvement could offer Damascus an opportunity to strengthen its relationship with Riyadh and open the door to economic and political benefits. Yet these gains remain speculative unless they translate into tangible results, while the costs and risks of intervention could begin to mount from the moment a decision is made.
A state that has yet to complete the reconstruction of its army, economy, and institutions cannot afford to treat overseas military interventions as bargaining chips in a broader contest for regional influence.

articles.title: Iran’s Medical Council urges global health bodies to act over US sanctions
articles.body:
Iran’s Medical Council urges global health bodies to act over US sanctions
TEHRAN – The Iranian Medical Council has called on the World Health Organization (WHO), the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), and the World Medical Association (WMA) to take immediate action against the use of patients’ lives as a tool of political and military pressure.
In an official letter to the three international organizations, the council said the US government was violating international humanitarian and criminal law through inhumane measures, including economic blockade and pharmaceutical sanctions against Iran, turning patients’ lives into an instrument of political and military coercion.
Mohammad Raiszadeh, head of the Iranian Medical Council, urged the leaders of international health organizations to respond promptly and responsibly to what he described as inhumane acts and the weaponization of medical resources in armed conflicts.
He cited previous reports of direct attacks on healthcare facilities, medical infrastructure, and pharmaceutical facilities, adding that the US attack on the Touska, a vessel carrying medicines and, in particular, vital supplies for dialysis patients, was another clear example of directly endangering patients’ health and lives.
Raiszadeh said Iran’s medical community expected the WHO, WMA, ICRC, and other relevant international bodies to respond appropriately and responsibly to the use of medicines, healthcare facilities, medical shipments, and patients’ lives as instruments of warfare.
He also called for effective measures to ensure safe, rapid, and unhindered routes for the delivery of medicines, medical equipment, and pharmaceutical raw materials.
An effective response from institutions whose very purpose is to protect human health, life, and dignity would represent the fulfillment of their moral and historic responsibilities to humanity, he added.
Raiszadeh stressed that Iran’s medical community and people would not forget these events and would pursue accountability, in accordance with international law, for both those responsible for the actions and institutions that remained silent in the face of them.
As of March 27, data compiled from WHO, the Iranian Red Crescent, and national health agencies reveal a targeted erosion of medical neutrality. A total of 292 medical and relief centres, including hospitals, pharmacies, and primary health clinics, have been damaged or destroyed.
This destruction has forced 13 hospitals completely out of service, while another seven have been fully evacuated under duress because of proximity to danger zones.
The emergency response capacity has been further crippled by the destruction of 48 ambulances and rescue vehicles, as well as an emergency medical helicopter.
The assault on health care is not merely incidental but systemic. Under the Geneva Conventions and the UN Charter, medical personnel and facilities must be protected at all times unless used for military purposes. Yet, verified reports indicate US–Israeli attacks on health facilities and the killing of at least eight health-care workers, doctors, nurses, and emergency first responders in Iran.

articles.title: Mecca defense deal should pass through parliament, Özel says
articles.body:
Yeni Party chairman Özgür Özel (AA Photo)
Opposition leader Özgür Özel urged the government to honor its constitutional duties on foreign troop deployments, demanding that the military pact with Saudi Arabia be submitted to parliament for immediate review.
“Both Article 90 and Article 92 of the Constitution are being undermined. Article 90 of the Constitution tells how an international agreement comes into force,” the New Party leader told daily Cumhuriyet in an interview over the weekend.
Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan announced that they signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement on Aug. 7, paving the way for the foundation of the Mecca Alliance. Since then, the opposition has been urging the government to submit it to parliament.
The text of the agreement has not been made public yet, except for a joint statement that announced the development. Türkiye and Pakistan agreed on Oct. 5 to activate collective deterrence measures under the alliance and to rapidly deploy military forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia following attacks claimed by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis.
Özel stressed that the government must present the agreement for debate and a vote in parliament’s defense and foreign affairs committees before sending it to the General Assembly.
“This is a very serious issue,” Özel said, criticizing the government for discussing deploying troops to Saudi Arabia amid continued escalation with Houthis.
“[The government] is giving promises for deploying troops. Article 92 of the Constitution explicitly requires parliamentary approval to send troops. In other words, even if the agreement is submitted, the approval of parliament is still necessary,” he said.
Özel said they will continue to keep this issue on the agenda to “push President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan to show respect to parliament and the constitution.”

articles.title: Yemeni government approves draft law designating Houthis ‘terrorist organization’
articles.body:
The Yemeni government on Sunday approved a draft law designating the Houthi group a “terrorist organization” and criminalizing its activities and financing, Anadolu reports.
The decision came during a Cabinet meeting in the temporary capital Aden, chaired by Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani, according to a statement from the prime minister’s office.
The Cabinet approved the draft following a presentation by the legal affairs minister and instructed officials to complete the constitutional and legal procedures required for its ratification.
The meeting came a day after a Houthi attack on King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh killed 12 people and injured 309, according to the statement.
READ: EU chief warns of ‘dangerous escalation’ after Houthi attack on Riyadh airport
The attack drew widespread condemnation, while the group threatened to continue targeting Saudi Arabia.
The Cabinet said Yemen was at a “decisive stage” aimed at restoring sovereignty over its entire territory and ending what it described as the Houthi coup “financed and directed by Iran.”
Al-Zindani instructed all executive authorities to move from reacting to events toward proactive action, maximize readiness and meet the needs of the armed forces, military formations, security forces and Popular Resistance.
The Houthis had not commented on the proposed designation as of 1445GMT.
READ: Yemeni government forces say 1,370 Houthis ‘neutralized’ in 1,729 strikes

articles.title: 'Flagrant violation of int'l law': World leaders rally behind Riyadh after Houthi airport strike
articles.body:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Sunday that the Houthi attack on Riyadh's international airport, which left at least 12 people dead and over 300 wounded, was a "horrific terrorist attack."
"On behalf of the people of Israel, I extend our deepest condolences to the families of those murdered and our wishes for a full recovery to the injured," the Prime Minister's Office said in a statement shared on X. "Terrorism targets innocent people and seeks to spread fear and instability. It must be confronted with resolve."
"Israel looks forward to a strong Middle East -- one that stands united against threats, protects its people, and builds a future of security, cooperation, and prosperity for all the peoples of our region," he added.
Members of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement condemned the attack, with Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif calling the Houthis’ actions a “flagrant violation of international law” that must be stopped immediately.
“Attacks targeting civilians and critical infrastructure are completely unacceptable and constitute a serious threat to regional peace and stability,” Sharif stated, extending condolences to those wounded and the bereaved families.
“Pakistan stands in unwavering solidarity with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, its leadership and brotherly people.”
“In accordance with the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement and the enduring bonds of brotherhood between our two countries, we reaffirm our steadfast commitment to Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and security.”
Turkey’s Foreign Ministry released a statement condemning the strikes and wishing a quick recovery to the wounded.
Calling for an immediate end to the strikes, “which target civilians and civilian infrastructure,” Turkey reaffirmed its “full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and reiterated our call for the resolution of ongoing conflicts through dialogue and diplomacy.”
Similarly, the Russian Foreign Ministry said on Sunday that it condemned the attack, Russian news agency Interfax reported.
"The situation in the Middle East can only be resolved through diplomatic means, while taking into account the interests of all countries in the region," the ministry said.
'Attack on Saudi Arabia is an attack on Yemen'
The Saudi-backed head of Yemen's Presidential Council, Rashad al-Alimi, denounced the attack on Riyadh’s airport in his own post, extending his condolences to those wounded and the families of those killed.
“This criminal attack reflects the Houthis’ terrorist nature and their disregard for civilian lives and the interests of the Yemeni people,” wrote Alimi. “This comes as Saudi Arabia continues its fraternal support for Yemen’s economy, public budget, and citizens’ welfare, including recent facilities for Yemeni residents.”
“The security of Saudi Arabia and Yemen, and the interests of their peoples, are intertwined. Any attack on Saudi Arabia is an attack on our security, interests, and the future of our generations.”
“We reaffirm our shared resolve to continue the ‘Dawn of Yemen' Operation to end the terrorist threat and restore state institutions, whatever the sacrifices,” he said.
The Qatari Foreign Ministry condemned the strikes as well, “considering them a grave violation of Saudi Arabia's sovereignty and a direct threat to regional security, the safety of civilians, civilian infrastructure, and air navigation.”
It reiterated Qatar’s solidarity with Saudi Arabia, emphasizing “that the security of Saudi Arabia is an integral part of Qatar's security and the collective security system of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) States.”
Jordan's King Abdullah II ibn Al Hussein, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney also condemned the attack in their own X posts.
Trump weighing joining Saudi retaliation against Houthis
US President Donald Trump, speaking to reporters outside the White House, was asked whether Washington planned to join Saudi strikes on the Houthis.
"We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision. We move very quickly," he said.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the attacks, saying they "demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life."
“I am deeply shocked by & strongly condemn Saturday’s lethal attack by the Houthis on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, which reportedly killed 12 people & injured hundreds of civilians,” stated UN Secretary-General António Guterres in an X post.
“Attacks on civilians & civilian infrastructure are a violation of international law. These attacks must cease immediately.”
Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Lebanon ports join IMEC: Can they compete in regional trade?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Beirut and Tripoli join IMEC Ports Club: Can they compete in regional trade?
The ports of Beirut and Tripoli have joined a network linked to the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC), giving Lebanon a potential foothold in regional trade while raising questions over whether the crisis-hit country has the infrastructure and connectivity to compete with hubs such as Israel’s Haifa port.
The administrations of the Port of Beirut and Port of Tripoli signed a joint declaration in New Delhi on 6 October to join the IMEC Ports Club, launched the same day.
"The participation of Beirut and Tripoli in the IMEC Ports Club places Lebanon inside the conversation, as a new trade architecture linking India, the Middle East and Europe is being shaped," Lebanon’s Public Works and Transport Minister Fayez Rasamny told The New Arab.
He said the aim was to turn the two ports into gateways for transit, logistics and regional trade by connecting them to inland transport networks, border crossings and markets beyond Lebanon.
"That is where the real economic value is created: in cargo movement, storage, logistics services, investment and jobs," Rasamny said, pointing to plans for a logistics corridor linking Beirut with the Bekaa Valley and the Syrian border to the east, as well as a proposed railway connecting Tripoli with Abboudieh in northern Lebanon.
"Geography gives us an advantage; connectivity is what will turn that advantage into economic power."
However, joining the Ports Club does not mean Lebanon has formally become a signatory to the original IMEC framework announced in 2023, nor does it guarantee that the corridor’s main route will pass through the country.
Rasamny said the club nevertheless offered Lebanese ports a platform to build partnerships, improve supply-chain and digital connectivity, and position themselves to attract future trade flows.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun welcomed the inclusion of Beirut and Tripoli, describing it as a major achievement that had not received the media attention it deserved, had even been met with scepticism.
Israel, with which Lebanon has no formal diplomatic relations and remains at war, is part of IMEC’s original framework. Haifa port – its largest – is expected to play a role in the proposed corridor, placing the two Lebanese ports' potential involvement in a wider network that also includes Israel.
'It depends on connectivity'
The prospect of Lebanon playing a role in the network raises questions about whether its ports could compete with Haifa for shipping and logistics business, or instead serve complementary routes and markets.
Recent figures point to significant activity at Lebanon’s ports, although the picture is mixed. Beirut handled around 6.4 million tonnes of freight in 2025, an increase of 18.4 percent on the previous year, while container throughput reached approximately 944,000 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs).
In September 2026, Beirut received three large container ships in a single day, including a 366-metre vessel. Yet total freight volumes fell by 10.1 percent year on year in the first seven months of 2026, even as container throughput continued to rise.
Tripoli has also demonstrated its ability to accommodate larger vessels. In June, it received the CMA CGM Eugénie, a container ship more than 360 metres long with capacity for around 15,000 TEUs, reported to be the largest container ship ever to dock at the port.
But the milestone has not translated into an overall increase in freight activity. Tripoli handled 674,000 tonnes of freight in the first five months of 2026, down 32.1 percent year on year, according to Credit Libanais.
The figures highlight the distinction between being able to accommodate large ships and attracting sustained cargo traffic.
Yeghia Tashjian, regional and international affairs cluster coordinator at the Issam Fares Institute for Public Policy and International Affairs at the American University of Beirut, told The New Arab that Lebanon’s inclusion was meaningful, but "more modest than some headlines suggest."
The Ports Club, he said, is "an open platform for port-to-port dialogue and cooperation" rather than a new institutional structure, making Lebanon’s participation "a foothold rather than state-level membership" of IMEC.
Tashjian said Lebanon could realistically seek to become a "secondary Mediterranean transshipment and logistics node," rather than a central land bridge within the corridor.
Beirut and Tripoli could compete with Haifa for some cargo and logistics activity, but joining the club does not mean they will automatically handle the same routes or markets. Their ability to attract business will depend on whether they can offer shippers commercially viable services and reliable connections to destinations beyond Lebanon.
Tripoli could have a particular role because of its proximity to Syria, Tashjian said. If cross-border routes reopen and Syria becomes stable enough to support trade towards Iraq and the Gulf, the northern port could become a link between maritime shipping and regional markets.
But this would require substantial improvements to Lebanon’s transport infrastructure. Tashjian highlighted the lack of adequate connections between ports and inland markets, including the need for north-south rail links to move goods through Syria and onwards to Iraq, Jordan and beyond.
The proposed Tripoli–Abboudieh railway and Beirut’s planned logistics corridor could help address those gaps, but their potential depends on implementation and the development of reliable cross-border routes.
Geopolitical obstacles
Lebanon also faces broader obstacles to attracting investment and cargo. The Port of Beirut continues to bear the legacy of the devastating 2020 explosion, while the country’s fiscal and institutional difficulties and recurring regional conflict risk making shipping companies and investors cautious.
Security and political developments in Syria will also be critical. Without reliable overland connections to regional markets, Lebanon’s ports may struggle to attract the cargo volumes needed to establish themselves as logistics hubs, regardless of their ability to receive larger vessels.
There are also geopolitical complications. Lebanon’s participation in a network that includes Israel does not itself amount to normalisation or formal cooperation between the two countries. But with Haifa part of IMEC’s original plans, Beirut and Tripoli will need to establish what distinct commercial role they can play within the wider network.
The eastern Mediterranean is already the focus of competing efforts to strengthen trade and transport links, with countries including Cyprus, Greece and Egypt seeking to consolidate their positions. Lebanon’s participation in the Ports Club could also feed into wider domestic debate over its engagement with other infrastructure initiatives, including China’s Belt and Road Initiative, IMEC’s main rival.
Ultimately, joining the IMEC Ports Club gives Beirut and Tripoli a platform to develop partnerships and seek a greater role in regional trade. Whether that translates into new investment, jobs and cargo flows will depend less on the declaration itself than on Lebanon’s ability to deliver infrastructure projects, strengthen cross-border connections and provide the stability and governance needed to attract long-term commercial interest.

articles.title: High-tech companies discuss ways to boost ties at 3rd Russia-Iran ICT Forum
articles.body:
High-tech companies discuss ways to boost ties at 3rd Russia-Iran ICT Forum
TEHRAN – Leading Iranian and Russian companies have explored ways to expand bilateral cooperation in advanced technologies at the third Russia-Iran Information and Communication Technology (ICT) Forum.
The forum brought together officials, diplomats, and public- and private-sector representatives from both countries. The participants met on the sidelines of the second Global Digital Forum, held in Moscow from October 8 to 10, IRNA reported.
During the meeting, Alexander Shoitov, Russia’s deputy minister of digital development, communications and mass media, said the participation of Iranian companies in the Global Digital Forum offered a valuable opportunity to exchange information and establish new partnerships.
He noted that Iran and Russia had significant potential to expand bilateral cooperation, particularly in artificial intelligence and cybersecurity.
Shoitov also reaffirmed Russia’s readiness to deepen bilateral ties and develop joint infrastructure in the ICT sector.
For his part, Iran’s ambassador to Russia, Kazem Jalali, highlighted the importance of fostering strategic cooperation between Iran and Russia in the expansion of digital exchanges within a governmental framework. The enhancement of ties helps strengthen the country’s capacity for participation in regional and global markets.
Highlighting the expertise and knowledge of Iranian technology companies in the localization of IT infrastructure equipment, Russian companies can establish joint ventures with reliable partners in Iran, gaining access to the country’s IT and artificial intelligence services market.
Moreover, Iranian and Russian representatives of high-technology companies showcased their latest cutting-edge accomplishments and presented their comprehensive plans and operational proposals for the promotion of cooperation in advanced technologies.
Exchanging best practices and technological solutions, holding B2B meetings, expanding business networks, and exploring opportunities for joint projects were among other key parts of the Forum. Particular attention was given to practical mechanisms for Russian and Iranian companies to enter new markets and develop cooperation with partners from third countries.
The second Global Digital Forum was held at the Mechta multifunctional complex in Gorky Park. As many as 760 delegates from 120 countries took part, including deputy prime ministers, digital development ministers, senior government officials, diplomats, IT company heads, experts, researchers, and representatives of international organizations from Africa, Asia, the Gulf region, Europe, and Latin America.
Sessions were held on artificial intelligence, digital sovereignty, cybersecurity, digital infrastructure, and global cooperation. Participants reviewed global trends in digital transformation, the integration of modern products into national digital systems, and prospects for cooperation between countries in the technology sector.
MOUs to bolster ICT ties
In December 2025, top tech Iranian and Russian companies signed five memoranda of understanding (MOUs) on artificial intelligence (AI), cybersecurity, smart government, blockchain and fintech, regulators, technology parks, and post services, to promote cooperation in the information and communication technology (ICT) sector.
The MOUs were signed in Russia during the fifth Iran-Russia ICT Forum held from December 6 to 7, IRNA reported.
An Iranian delegation led by the deputy ICT Minister for Technology and Innovation, Meysam Abedi, attended the forum.
Referring to the strategic partnership between Iran and Russia, Jalali said the two countries have a high capacity, and the expansion of collaborations will be beneficial to both sides.
For his part, Shoitov said the memoranda of understanding and the agreements reached today are the result of ongoing efforts over the past few years.
“Today, we are celebrating the results of our hard work over many years with the companies collaborating. We can confidently say, cooperation is definitely going on.
So far, the two countries have signed many memoranda of understanding, but there are still new areas of cooperation opening up in our interactions that benefit the people of the two nations,” Shoitov further noted.
Abedi, for his part, said the reached agreements are the result of three years of continuous cooperation between the ICT ministries of the two countries.
He called on Iranian and Russian companies to seriously follow up on the implementation of the MOUs and agreements, and to remove probable obstacles with the help of the government departments of the two countries.
The official went on to propose locating a third country as the joint market for Iranian-Russian products on the agenda, expressing hope that the two countries would sign MOUs on a joint market by the sixth forum.
In May, Russian Presidential Aide Andrei Fursenko emphasized the significance of promoting partnerships and collaborations with Iran in emerging technologies.
It is a fact that focusing on already established technologies will not be beneficial for the two countries. So, it is essential to put on the agenda the technologies that have not (fully) developed yet, which is a much more difficult task, IRNA quoted Fursenko as saying.
For his part, Safarinia said Iran is committed to promoting international scientific cooperation, highlighting that Russia is among the top countries with which Iran is willing to expand ties.
MT/MG

articles.title: Russia’s Yandex says data centre in Vladimir shut down after drone attack
articles.body:
Russia’s Yandex says data centre in Vladimir shut down after drone attack
Third strike on Yandex facilities in a week comes as Russia and Ukraine escalate attacks on tech infrastructure.
A Russian data centre run by technology and AI company Yandex has been shut down after it was hit in a drone attack.
No injuries were reported in the attack on the facility in the city of Vladimir, east of the capital, Moscow, the company said on Sunday.
Emergency services were at the site and several of Yandex’s services were unavailable to users, the company said, as it evaluated ways to restore its systems.
“Operations at the data centre have been completely suspended,” Yandex said in a service alert on Telegram, advising users to activate disaster-recovery plans as the platform operated in emergency mode.
“The remaining resource configuration is considered unstable,” it added, warning that technical support communications could also be disrupted as teams assessed the damage.
It is the third attack on the company’s data centres in the last week, as Russia and Ukraine continue to escalate attacks on each other’s technology infrastructure.
On Friday, Yandex, which is heavily involved in Russia’s AI development and is sometimes referred to as “Russia’s Google”, said its data centre in the Kaluga region southwest of Moscow was struck by Ukrainian drones and partly put out of action.
A day earlier, a Ukrainian attack shut down Yandex’s data hub in Sasovo, southeast of Moscow, where two of the three supercomputers used to develop the company’s AI model are housed.
“We always respond in mirror-like fashion,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday, following the Sasovo strike. “You all know, they have been hitting and continue to hit our data centres. We are responding. I can’t share all the details.”
Russia has struck several Ukrainian data centres and telecommunications infrastructure facilities over the past month, including targets in central Kyiv, in an apparent effort to disrupt the country’s connectivity and digital commerce.

articles.title: Israeli drone strike kills three Palestinians, wounds several in southern Gaza
articles.body:
An Israeli drone strike has killed three Palestinians and wounded several others in southern Gaza after targeting a tent near Nasser Hospital, medical sources confirmed, marking another breach of the fragile ceasefire.
A medical source at Nasser Hospital said the casualties were brought to the facility following the strike in the al-Buraq area of central Khan Younis.
Witnesses told Anadolu Agency that an Israeli drone fired at least one missile directly into the tent, which was being used by displaced civilians as a communal mobile phone charging hub.
Earlier on Sunday, medical officials at al-Shifa Hospital confirmed that six-year-old Jihad Iyad al-Ghandour died of severe wounds sustained on Saturday when Israeli soldiers opened fire inside Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza.
Ground incursions
Separately, Israeli forces expanded territorial control in eastern Gaza City early on Sunday, injuring two Palestinians—including a pregnant woman—and forcing dozens of families to flee.
Local sources reported that Israeli armoured vehicles, accompanied by armed Palestinian militias operating under army support, advanced tens of metres into the Shujaiya neighbourhood under artillery cover and quadcopter fire.
Troops fired heavily across the sector stretching from the eastern vegetable market to the Shujaiya intersection on Salah al-Din Street.
For roughly a week, eastern neighbourhoods including Tuffah and Shujaiya have faced night-time demolitions, artillery bombardment, and armoured patrols along the "yellow line", which demarcates Israeli-held sectors from civilian areas.
According to Gaza's Health Ministry, Israeli violations of the truce agreement enacted on October 10, 2025, have killed 1,488 Palestinians and injured 5,281 as of Sunday.
Since the wider war began in October 2023, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed, over 175,000 wounded, and roughly 90 percent of the enclave's infrastructure destroyed.

articles.title: Two Indian sailors missing after vessel attacked off Oman
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Two Indian sailors missing after vessel attacked off Oman
Two Indian sailors were missing after a commercial vessel was hit by a "drone attack" Sunday off the coast of Oman, New Delhi's shipping minister said.
Shipping minister Sarbananda Sonowal said the tanker MT Petro Dolphin, with 11 Indian seafarers on board, was attacked at the anchorage area for the port of Sohar in northern Oman.
"While nine of our Indian crew members have been successfully rescued and are safe, two Indian nationals currently remain missing," he said on X.
Sonowal said search and rescue operations by local authorities were underway.
"We are continuously coordinating with all relevant authorities to fully support the ongoing rescue efforts and ensure every possible action is taken to safely locate our missing personnel," he said.
Sonowal also said the Marshall Islands-flagged tanker M/T Valthera, carrying 11 Indian crew, was struck Sunday by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz. A fire was sparked, but all Indian crew were reported to be safe.
India is one of the largest contributors of sailors to merchant shipping worldwide, with more than 320,000 active seafarers in 2025, according to the shipping ministry.
Several of its mariners have been killed in attacks in the Strait of Hormuz since the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran on 28 February.
On Tuesday, India's foreign ministry condemned the attack on a Panama-flagged vessel that was struck by a projectile off the coast of Oman while transiting the Strait of Hormuz.
The "continuing incidents of attacks on shipping in the region remain a cause of deep concern," the ministry said.
"We reiterate our call for an immediate cessation of such attacks in the interests of peace and stability in the region."

articles.title: FAA warns US airlines to exercise caution in Saudi Arabia flights due to Houthi airstrikes
articles.body:
The Federal Aviation Administration told U.S. airlines on Sunday to exercise caution when flying to or over Saudi Arabia, citing safety threats tied to ongoing military activities and navigation system interference.
The FAA Notice to Airmen, which lasts until December 10, follows strikes on Saturday and Sunday on Riyadh's international airport. The attack on Saturday killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.
"Threats could pose a potential risk to aircraft at all altitudes, including overflight, the arrival, and departure phases of flight," the FAA said, warning of the "potentially hazardous situation."
The notice also applies to operators of airplanes that are registered in the U.S. Riyadh airport remains closed to flights through at least 5 p.m. EDT Monday.
U.S. carrier Delta Air Lines is set to begin direct flights to Riyadh on October 23 from Atlanta. Delta did not immediately respond to a request for comment Sunday but CEO Ed Bastian told CNBC last week that "safety is going to make the call" about whether the airline will move forward.
Other major US airlines serve Riyadh via codeshare partners.
In September 2025, FedEx launched its first dedicated flight into Saudi Arabia. The FedEx Boeing 777 freighter operates six times per week and connects the Americas and Europe to Riyadh, with connections to Guangzhou and Shanghai.

articles.title: The president who can’t say his name
articles.body:
Three weeks before Michigan decides whether to send the first Muslim senator to Washington, the president still cannot or will not say the man’s name.
“Mike Rogers, the great American Patriot and Republican Candidate for the U.S. Senate from Michigan, completely obliterated Mohammed El-Sayed in the big debate tonight,” Trump wrote on Truth Social after Thursday’s debate.
Rogers had skipped it.
“Mohammed is a Jihadist lunatic who hates our Country, the Black People of Detroit, and wants to see the U.S. fail.”
The candidate’s name is Abdul El-Sayed. Mohamed is his middle name, inherited from his Egyptian immigrant father. He rarely uses it. Yet the president repeats it so relentlessly that it reads less like a mistake than a strategy distilled into a single word.
El-Sayed has stopped pretending to be surprised.
“He knows my name is Abdul,” he said. “He says it every day.”
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called the attacks “bigoted bulls—,” adding that El-Sayed “is on the road to being the next Senator from Michigan no matter how much bigoted bulls— a weak and desperate Donald Trump throws at him.”
Dawud Walid, of the Michigan chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, recognized the tactic for what it was.
“He is intentionally saying his full name, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, to say, ‘Look, this guy is outside what we would consider to be a normative America.’ It’s a political tactic, and we’ve seen it before.
READ: American Senate candidate accuses Netanyahu of pushing US into Iran war
The cruelty is not what is remarkable here. The timing is.
A sitting president does not usually spend the final weeks of a campaign fixated on a single state’s Senate race unless he believes something larger rides on it.
Something does.
Michigan’s open Senate seat, vacated by retiring Democrat Gary Peters, sits inside a chamber Republicans currently control 53 to 47. Democrats need a net gain of four seats on Nov. 3 to take it back, and Michigan would not count among those gains. It is a seat they already hold, and one of the two Democratic-held seats Republicans most want to flip.
A Rogers victory would enlarge the Republican majority and make an already narrow Democratic path elsewhere even tighter. An El-Sayed victory would leave the arithmetic exactly where it stands.
The real stakes, then, are not whether Michigan can flip the Senate in a single stroke. The question is whether Republicans can afford to miss even one opportunity to widen their majority, particularly in a state the president carried twice.
The polling suggests they may not be able to.
El-Sayed led by just over three points in the RealClearPolitics average through Oct. 6, 48.1 to 44.9. Marist put him up seven points in late September. So did Suffolk. Even Fox News, hardly a sympathetic outlet, found him ahead by one point among likely voters in its most recent poll. That marked a reversal from August, when Rogers led by four.
Bettors on Polymarket now give El-Sayed a 69 percent chance of winning.
Money has followed the nerves.
Through Oct. 10, Republican-aligned spending in the race had reached $78 million, compared with $63 million from Democrats. Nearly all of it has been funneled into advertisements branding El-Sayed, a Rhodes Scholar and physician, as “dangerously radical” and “too extreme.”
The ads tie him to Hasan Piker, a streamer who once said America “deserved 9/11,” in the hope that the association will stick where attacks on his policies have not.
Trump himself has yet to set foot in Michigan to campaign for Rogers. El-Sayed has turned the president’s absence into a taunt of his own.
Standing before a crowd in Port Huron this month, dressed in a black V-neck shirt and gripping a handheld microphone, he issued a challenge.
“Donald, if you’re watching, don’t wuss out, man.”
He has called Rogers a coward. He has called the president afraid.
The nerves extend far beyond Michigan.
READ: Former military secretary accuses Netanyahu’s office of falsifying Oct. 7 records
Democrats lead the generic congressional ballot by roughly nine points in Nate Silver’s running average, their widest margin of the cycle. For the first time, they have broken 50 percent support. Trump’s approval rating sits in the high 30s across most tracking polls.
Forecasters now give Democrats an 82 percent chance of retaking the House and better-than-even odds of capturing the Senate.
Should both chambers fall, the final two years of this presidency would unfold before a Congress armed with subpoena power and with nothing left to trade.
That is the arithmetic from which a lame duck is made. It is why one Senate race in one Midwestern state has drawn the kind of presidential attention usually reserved for an election with Trump’s own name on the ballot.
El-Sayed is not without self-inflicted wounds.
Leaked audio captured him declining to take a clear position on the death of Iran’s former supreme leader, out of deference to grieving constituents in Dearborn. The recording gave Republicans an opening they have refused to relinquish.
Some Michigan Democrats, including strategist Adrian Hemond, have worried aloud that El-Sayed’s reluctance to court skeptical factions within his own party could cost Democrats a seat they should hold comfortably.
Sen. Elissa Slotkin, who remained neutral during the primary, has since worked to unify the party behind him. The alternative, she warned, is a senator “beholden to President Trump.”
Even El-Sayed’s allies acknowledge that his candidacy is built on remaking the electorate, not courting its center.
None of this guarantees him a seat in the Senate.
Three weeks is a long time. Leads within a poll’s margin of error can vanish overnight. Michigan Republicans have not won a Senate race since 1994, for reasons that reach far beyond any single candidate.
Rogers knows that history better than most. He lost to Slotkin by less than a point in 2024—close enough to keep him running, but not close enough to make Republicans comfortable about running him again.
Yet a president reduced to repeatedly misnaming his opponent on a platform built for far graver pronouncements is offering an answer of his own.
Strength does not usually sound like that.
Fear sometimes does.

articles.title: Yemen in the Middle East’s energy equation: From natural resources to the right to development
articles.body:
In a mountainous area of Yemen, solar-powered pumps changed how families obtained water. Households that had spent hours collecting it gained access to a system carrying water through tanks at different elevations to their homes. Documented in a World Bank report on electricity access, the experience delivered benefits visible in everyday life: time saved, accessible water and greater opportunities for work and education.
Local electrification projects and the opening of Aden’s solar power plant raise a broader question: how can energy partnerships grow from individual projects into lasting economic capacity?
Yemen’s oil and gas resources, strong solar potential and maritime access provide a basis for economic development. Energy partnerships should connect these assets with domestic production, reliable services and local employment. The terms of investment will determine how much value stays within the country.
Yemen’s share of resource value
Yemen has decades of experience in oil production. The Yemen LNG project’s historical overview records output of approximately 300,000 barrels a day in 2010. This indicates the industry’s past scale; estimating present revenues requires updated production, cost and reservoir data.
Service contracts surrounding extraction determine part of Yemen’s return from oil. Purchasing from domestic suppliers, training technicians and commissioning Yemeni firms to undertake maintenance circulate revenues locally and build skills that can outlast a project. Local content commitments covering these activities can retain more value within Yemen, provided they have measurable targets and effective oversight. A general promise of “technology transfer” offers little basis for assessing delivery.
Refining decisions should begin with markets, feedstock and operating costs. Capital-intensive facilities without dependable sales and maintenance capacity can tie up scarce development funds for years. Assessments should also examine contributions to fuel availability, lower supply costs and domestic services.
Balhaf’s two liquefaction trains have a combined design capacity of 6.7 million tonnes a year, but assessing their economic contribution requires an appraisal of equipment condition, feedstock availability and operating arrangements. Design capacity cannot be treated as current output.
Future decisions should weigh gas export revenues alongside the value of supplying electricity and industry. Reliable power supports workshops and cold storage and enables new investment, while exports generate foreign currency. Infrastructure costs and returns from each use should guide allocation. Agreements with foreign partners need clear information and commitments to support that assessment.
READ: Yemen humanitarian crisis ‘sharply worsens’ as fighting displaces over 200,000: UN
Electricity for services and production
A small system powering lights, a fan and a phone charger may count towards electricity-access statistics, as the World Bank notes in Yemen’s case. It may nevertheless fall short of the power and operating hours required by a health centre or production facility.
Investment planning should begin with the consumer: which equipment must operate, for how many hours and at what affordable cost? The answers determine generation, storage and network requirements. Buying capacity without these connections increases the risk of poor returns.
International cooperation should cover the working life of a project. Equipment suppliers need to provide training and spare-parts access; investors and electricity buyers need clear arrangements for payments, repairs and currency risk. Power purchase agreements (PPAs) must reconcile the project’s revenue requirements with the buyer’s ability to pay. Without maintenance funding, the value of the original investment can deteriorate within a few years.
Solar power: From natural potential to local markets
According to Yemen’s profile published by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), approximately 51 per cent of the country’s land falls within a potential annual solar-output range of 1,900–2,000 kilowatt-hours per kilowatt of installed photovoltaic capacity. These estimates help identify promising areas, with site conditions, dust and maintenance requirements shaping project-level performance.
Small solar systems can expand markets for installers, repair technicians and equipment suppliers. Purchase financing and after-sales services matter: abundant sunlight alone cannot help a household unable to afford the upfront cost. Mini-grids can provide shared generation and storage for groups of consumers, particularly where extending the main grid is expensive.
At a larger scale, the UAE-funded Aden Solar Power Plant began operating in July 2024. Its performance can inform subsequent partnerships. Delivered electricity costs, service quality and local maintenance capacity offer useful measures of success.
Diversifying this mix requires attention to the maturity of each option. IRENA’s data show geographical variations in wind resources, making local measurements essential, while geothermal potential identified in Yemen’s Technology Needs Assessment requires further study. Yemen has no nuclear electricity generation; any long-term consideration would require economic, grid and institutional assessments consistent with the International Atomic Energy Agency’s infrastructure framework.
The right to development as a measurable commitment
The UN Declaration on the Right to Development emphasises people’s participation in development and the fair distribution of its benefits. For energy projects, this has contractual implications: service provision, employment and domestic procurement commitments should be specified, with performance information available for assessment.
Yemen’s ports can facilitate equipment imports, energy trade and industrial services. Investment in skills and domestic firms would increase the value of that maritime position. Negotiations with international partners should incorporate these connections from the outset.
Greater exports, accompanied by reliable electricity and productive opportunities, can help reduce poverty and strengthen economic capacity. The credibility of energy diplomacy will ultimately be measured by people’s share of the value generated from their resources—a share visible in incomes, skills and the quality of services.

articles.title: Iran offers mediation in Saudi-Yemen conflict after Houthi airport strike leaves 13 dead
articles.body:
Iran Offers Mediation in Saudi-Yemen Conflict After Houthi Airport Strike Leaves 13 Dead
Iran's foreign minister says the region's crises have no military solution, telling his Saudi counterpart that diplomacy is the only way forward as tensions escalate following a series of Houthi attacks on Saudi targets
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that Tehran was willing to mediate Saudi-Yemeni talks, after the Iran-aligned Houthis claimed responsibility for a strike on Riyadh's international airport that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300 others.
